0.title: Remember and Obey: The Book of Deuteronomy
0.overview:
On the plains of Moab, within sight of the Promised Land he would never enter, Moses preaches the greatest sermon of his life. Deuteronomy — from the Greek for “second law” — is not a new law but the law repeated, renewed, and pressed home upon the heart of a new generation. The wilderness wanderers are dead; their children stand at the edge of Canaan. Before they cross the Jordan, the aged prophet gathers them and, with the urgency of a dying father, calls them to remember the God who redeemed them and to obey him with all their heart.

The book is structured like an ancient covenant treaty: a historical prologue rehearsing God’s gracious acts (chs. 1–4), the great covenant stipulations (chs. 5–26), the blessings and curses that seal the covenant (chs. 27–28), and the witnesses, succession, and ratification (chs. 29–34). Yet Deuteronomy is no dry legal document. It pulses with love. “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one. You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart” (6:4–5) is its beating heart — the verse Jesus called the greatest commandment of all.

Deuteronomy is the most quoted book in the New Testament after Psalms and Isaiah. Jesus answered every wilderness temptation with words from this book (Matt 4). He named its central command the sum of the Law. Paul drew from it to declare that “the word is near you” (Rom 10), and that Christ became a curse for us to redeem us from the curse of its law (Gal 3:13). To read Deuteronomy is to walk in the footsteps of our Lord and to hear the gospel foreshadowed in shadow and promise.

Above all, Deuteronomy ends with a grave and glorious truth: Moses dies. The mediator of the old covenant, the greatest prophet Israel had known, cannot bring the people into the inheritance. He can only point. It falls to Joshua — Yeshua, the Hebrew name behind Jesus — to lead them in. The law cannot save; it can only show us our need. Christ alone brings us home. Remember, then, and obey — not to earn the land, but because grace has already given it. This is a book to stir the heart to worship.

1.title: Looking Back: The God Who Was Faithful Though We Failed
1.text: <sup>1</sup>These are the words that Moses spoke to all Israel beyond the Jordan in the wilderness, in the Arabah opposite Suph, between Paran and Tophel, Laban, Hazeroth, and Dizahab.<sup>2</sup>It is eleven days' journey from Horeb by the way of Mount Seir to Kadesh-barnea.<sup>3</sup>In the fortieth year, on the first day of the eleventh month, Moses spoke to the people of Israel according to all that the LORD had given him in commandment to them,<sup>4</sup>after he had defeated Sihon the king of the Amorites, who lived in Heshbon, and Og the king of Bashan, who lived in Ashtaroth and in Edrei.<sup>5</sup>Beyond the Jordan, in the land of Moab, Moses undertook to explain this law, saying,<sup>6</sup>"The LORD our God said to us in Horeb, 'You have stayed long enough at this mountain.<sup>7</sup>Turn and take your journey, and go to the hill country of the Amorites and to all their neighbors in the Arabah, in the hill country and in the lowland and in the Negeb and by the seacoast, the land of the Canaanites, and Lebanon, as far as the great river, the river Euphrates.<sup>8</sup>See, I have set the land before you. Go in and take possession of the land that the LORD swore to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, to give to them and to their offspring after them.'<sup>9</sup>"At that time I said to you, 'I am not able to bear you by myself.<sup>10</sup>The LORD your God has multiplied you, and behold, you are today as numerous as the stars of heaven.<sup>11</sup>May the LORD, the God of your fathers, make you a thousand times as many as you are and bless you, as he has promised you!<sup>12</sup>How can I bear by myself the weight and burden of you and your strife?<sup>13</sup>Choose for your tribes wise, understanding, and experienced men, and I will appoint them as your heads.'<sup>14</sup>And you answered me, 'The thing that you have spoken is good for us to do.'<sup>15</sup>So I took the heads of your tribes, wise and experienced men, and set them as heads over you, commanders of thousands, commanders of hundreds, commanders of fifties, commanders of tens, and officers, throughout your tribes.<sup>16</sup>And I charged your judges at that time, 'Hear the cases between your brothers, and judge righteously between a man and his brother or the alien who is with him.<sup>17</sup>You shall not be partial in judgment. You shall hear the small and the great alike. You shall not be intimidated by anyone, for the judgment is God's. And the case that is too hard for you, you shall bring to me, and I will hear it.'<sup>18</sup>And I commanded you at that time all the things that you should do.<sup>19</sup>"Then we set out from Horeb and went through all that great and terrifying wilderness that you saw, on the way to the hill country of the Amorites, as the LORD our God commanded us. And we came to Kadesh-barnea.<sup>20</sup>And I said to you, 'You have come to the hill country of the Amorites, which the LORD our God is giving us.<sup>21</sup>See, the LORD your God has set the land before you. Go up, take possession, as the LORD, the God of your fathers, has told you. Do not fear or be dismayed.'<sup>22</sup>Then all of you came near me and said, 'Let us send men before us, that they may explore the land for us and bring us word again of the way by which we must go up and the cities into which we shall come.'<sup>23</sup>The thing seemed good to me, and I took twelve men from you, one man from each tribe.<sup>24</sup>And they turned and went up into the hill country, and came to the Valley of Eshcol and spied it out.<sup>25</sup>And they took in their hands some of the fruit of the land and brought it down to us, and brought us word again and said, 'It is a good land that the LORD our God is giving us.'<sup>26</sup>"Yet you would not go up, but rebelled against the command of the LORD your God.<sup>27</sup>And you murmured in your tents and said, 'Because the LORD hated us he has brought us out of the land of Egypt, to give us into the hand of the Amorites, to destroy us.<sup>28</sup>Where are we going up? Our brothers have made our hearts melt, saying, "The people are greater and taller than we. The cities are great and fortified up to heaven. And besides, we have seen the sons of the Anakim there."'<sup>29</sup>Then I said to you, 'Do not be in dread or afraid of them.<sup>30</sup>The LORD your God who goes before you will himself fight for you, just as he did for you in Egypt before your eyes,<sup>31</sup>and in the wilderness, where you have seen how the LORD your God carried you, as a man carries his son, all the way that you went until you came to this place.'<sup>32</sup>Yet in spite of this word you did not believe the LORD your God,<sup>33</sup>who went before you in the way to seek you out a place to pitch your tents, in fire by night and in the cloud by day, to show you by what way you should go.<sup>34</sup>"And the LORD heard your words and was angered, and he swore,<sup>35</sup>'Not one of these men of this evil generation shall see the good land that I swore to give to your fathers,<sup>36</sup>except Caleb the son of Jephunneh. He shall see it, and to him and to his children I will give the land on which he has trodden, because he has wholly followed the LORD!'<sup>37</sup>Even with me the LORD was angry on your account and said, 'You also shall not go in there.<sup>38</sup>Joshua the son of Nun, who stands before you, he shall enter. Encourage him, for he shall cause Israel to inherit it.<sup>39</sup>And as for your little ones, who you said would become a prey, and your children, who today have no knowledge of good or evil, they shall go in there. And to them I will give it, and they shall possess it.<sup>40</sup>But as for you, turn, and journey into the wilderness in the direction of the Red Sea.'<sup>41</sup>"Then you answered me, 'We have sinned against the LORD. We ourselves will go up and fight, just as the LORD our God commanded us.' And every one of you fastened on his weapons of war and thought it easy to go up into the hill country.<sup>42</sup>And the LORD said to me, 'Say to them, Do not go up or fight, for I am not in your midst, lest you be defeated before your enemies.'<sup>43</sup>So I spoke to you, and you would not listen; but you rebelled against the command of the LORD and presumptuously went up into the hill country.<sup>44</sup>Then the Amorites who lived in that hill country came out against you and chased you as bees do and beat you down in Seir as far as Hormah.<sup>45</sup>And you returned and wept before the LORD, but the LORD did not listen to your voice or give ear to you.<sup>46</sup>So you remained at Kadesh many days, the days that you remained there.
1.overview:
Deuteronomy opens not with commands but with memory. Before Moses tells Israel what to do, he tells them what God has done. The whole first address (chs. 1–4) is a sermon of remembrance, and chapter 1 begins at the worst wound in the nation’s past: Kadesh-barnea, the place where a whole generation forfeited the Promised Land through unbelief.

Moses rehearses the journey from Horeb (Sinai) to the borders of Canaan. God had given them everything — his presence, his promise, leaders to share the burden, and the land itself laid open before them. All they had to do was believe and go up. Instead they sent spies, listened to fear, and rebelled. “You did not believe the LORD your God” (1:32) is the verdict that hangs over the chapter like a storm cloud.

Yet even here, grace shines. God’s patience, his provision of leaders, his preservation of the children — the very generation now listening — testify that the LORD did not abandon his people even when they spurned his gift. Moses preaches the past so that this new generation will not repeat it.

For us, chapter 1 is a mirror. The same unbelief that kept Israel out of Canaan still keeps hearts out of rest (Heb 3–4). And the same faithful God who bore with Israel bears with us in Christ, who believed where we did not and entered the rest on our behalf.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Word at Horeb: ‘Go, Take Possession’
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses sets the scene on the plains of Moab and recalls how God, after Sinai, commanded Israel to break camp and take the land he had sworn to the patriarchs.
verseByVerse.theology: God’s promises are grounded in his oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The land is sheer gift, secured by covenant, not earned by merit.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel stood on the threshold of inheritance. Now: every believer stands before promises God has already sworn to give in Christ; the call is to go forward in faith.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the words that Moses spoke to all Israel beyond the Jordan in the wilderness, in the Arabah opposite Suph, between Paran and Tophel, Laban, Hazeroth, and Dizahab.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These are the words that Moses spoke to all Israel beyond the Jordan…

The Hebrew Bible names its books from their opening line, and this one is called Debarim — Words. Our title comes by a longer road: the Greek translators rendered a phrase in 17:18 as deuteronomion, a second law, and the name stuck. It is a little misleading. This is not a second law. It is the first law preached — the same commandments taken up and pressed home to a congregation, which is a different thing from a statute book and is why Deuteronomy reads more like a sermon than anything else in the Pentateuch.

And picture the preacher. Moses is a hundred and twenty years old and has been told he has weeks to live. In front of him stands a nation of whom almost nobody remembers Egypt; the adults he brought out are all in the ground behind him except two. He is speaking to the children of the people he began with, and he will not cross the river with them.

He spends the time he has left explaining God’s word to people who will outlive him. There are other things a man in that position might do — settle scores, secure a legacy, or simply go quiet. Everything from here to the end of the book is one old man trying to get the truth into a generation he will not see again.

Note also who is listening: all Israel. Not the elders, not the Levites, not the men who could read. The whole people, standing in the open, hearing the law of God for themselves. That is a decision about how God deals with people, and it has never been reversed.

verseByVerse.quote: It is eleven days' journey from Horeb by the way of Mount Seir to Kadesh-barnea. In the fortieth year, on the first day of the eleventh month, Moses spoke to the people of Israel according to all that the LORD had given him in commandment to them, after he had defeated Sihon the king of the Amorites, who lived in Heshbon, and Og the king of Bashan, who lived in Ashtaroth and in Edrei. Beyond the Jordan, in the land of Moab, Moses undertook to explain this law, saying,
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is eleven days’ journey from Horeb by the way of Mount Seir to Kadesh-barnea.

That sentence is not Moses speaking. It is the narrator, leaning in before the sermon starts, to tell you what you are about to hear a sermon about. Eleven days. Roughly a hundred and fifty miles of walking — a fortnight’s march for a family with children and animals, from the mountain where God gave the law to the border of the land he had promised.

And then verse 3: In the fortieth year.

Set the two figures side by side and you have the book of Deuteronomy in miniature. Eleven days of road, forty years of walking it. Nothing was wrong with the route, the distance, the provisions or the God who was leading. A journey of a fortnight took four decades, and every one of those years has a grave in it.

Somewhere in most lives there is an eleven-day journey that has been taking years. A conversation that should have happened. A sin that should have been confessed and dealt with once. A step of obedience that was clear and got postponed, and postponed, until postponing became the shape of things. The distance never grows; only the years do. And the honest question this verse puts is not how did Israel manage that, but which eleven-day journey you are currently forty years into.

Verse 5 says what Moses is doing about it: he undertook to explain this law. The Hebrew verb means to make plain, to engrave so that it can be read clearly. He is not delivering new revelation. He is taking what God has already said and cutting it deep enough that a new generation cannot miss it.

verseByVerse.quote: "The LORD our God said to us in Horeb, 'You have stayed long enough at this mountain. Turn and take your journey, and go to the hill country of the Amorites and to all their neighbors in the Arabah, in the hill country and in the lowland and in the Negeb and by the seacoast, the land of the Canaanites, and Lebanon, as far as the great river, the river Euphrates. See, I have set the land before you. Go in and take possession of the land that the LORD swore to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, to give to them and to their offspring after them.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD our God said to us in Horeb, “You have stayed long enough at this mountain.”

They had been at Sinai for about eleven months, and what happened there has no parallel in the history of the world. The mountain burned. God spoke the Ten Commandments in an audible voice to a whole nation. The covenant was cut, the tabernacle was raised, the glory came down and filled it. If any place on earth ever deserved to be settled in permanently, it was that one.

And God says: enough. Break camp.

There is a kind of Christian who wants to live at the site of his best experience of God — the conference, the conversion, the year everything was clear — and who measures every subsequent season against it and finds it thin. Sinai was not thin. Sinai was the greatest religious experience any people has ever had, and God moved them off it within the year, because the mountain was never the destination. It was where they were made ready to go somewhere.

Then the commission, and the grammar of it repays attention: See, I have set the land before you. Go in and take possession. The first verb is finished — I have set. The second is a command — go in and take. The land is already given and it still has to be walked into. Grace does not cancel effort; it is the only thing that makes effort anything other than futile.

And underneath both stands an oath older than anybody present: the land that the LORD swore to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob. Four hundred years before this, God had bound himself to a childless man in a country he no longer lived in. Nothing Israel did at Kadesh, and nothing they had done since, put that oath at risk. It was never resting on them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–18 — Leaders Appointed: Sharing the Burden
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses recalls how, as the people multiplied according to God’s promise, he appointed wise and able men to share the burden of judging, charging them to judge justly and without partiality.
verseByVerse.theology: God multiplies his people and provides shepherds to lead them; justice belongs to God, so judges act in his name and must show no partiality.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel grew too numerous for one man. Now: Christ gives shepherds and elders to his church (Eph 4); leadership is shared stewardship under the Chief Shepherd.

verseByVerse.quote: "At that time I said to you, 'I am not able to bear you by myself. The LORD your God has multiplied you, and behold, you are today as numerous as the stars of heaven. May the LORD, the God of your fathers, make you a thousand times as many as you are and bless you, as he has promised you! How can I bear by myself the weight and burden of you and your strife? Choose for your tribes wise, understanding, and experienced men, and I will appoint them as your heads.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses now recalls the day the work became too big for him, and he is candid about it: I am not able to bear you by myself.

But look at what he says in the same breath, because the two halves belong together. The LORD your God has multiplied you, and behold, you are today as numerous as the stars of heaven. That phrase is not decoration. It is the promise God made to Abraham on a night when he had no children at all — Look toward heaven, and number the stars… So shall your offspring be (Gen. 15:5).

So the thing crushing Moses is the fulfilled promise of God. The weight on his shoulders is answered prayer. Stay with that, because it is a common and confusing experience: the ministry that has grown beyond you, the family that is bigger than your energy, the responsibility that arrived because something went well. Not every burden is a sign that something has gone wrong. Some of them are what blessing feels like from underneath.

And then the sentence that shows what kind of man he was. Verse 11: May the LORD, the God of your fathers, make you a thousand times as many as you are and bless you. He is being flattened by the size of this nation, and he stops to ask God to multiply it by a thousand.

Run that test on whatever is currently too much for you. Could you ask God, honestly, to increase it? Most of us can pray for relief. Praying for more of the very thing that is breaking you is only possible if you believe the thing itself is good and God is the one who gave it — which is exactly what Moses believed, and why God could trust him with it.

His solution is not to work harder but to share the load, and the men chosen are wise, understanding, and experienced. Character and judgment, not force of personality. The apostles reached for the same remedy when the church outgrew them (Acts 6:2–4), and for the same reason.

verseByVerse.quote: And you answered me, 'The thing that you have spoken is good for us to do.' So I took the heads of your tribes, wise and experienced men, and set them as heads over you, commanders of thousands, commanders of hundreds, commanders of fifties, commanders of tens, and officers, throughout your tribes. And I charged your judges at that time, 'Hear the cases between your brothers, and judge righteously between a man and his brother or the alien who is with him. You shall not be partial in judgment. You shall hear the small and the great alike. You shall not be intimidated by anyone, for the judgment is God's. And the case that is too hard for you, you shall bring to me, and I will hear it.' And I commanded you at that time all the things that you should do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The charge Moses gives the judges is short and every clause of it has teeth.

Hear the cases between your brothers, and judge righteously between a man and his brother or the alien who is with him. The foreigner gets the same court. Not a separate process, not a lesser standing — the same hearing as a man with a tribe behind him.

You shall not be partial in judgment. The Hebrew idiom is physical: do not recognise faces. The judge is not to look up and see who it is. In the ancient world law bent toward wealth as a matter of course, the way water runs downhill; this forbids the tilt in either direction, and Leviticus makes the second half explicit — you shall not be partial to the poor or defer to the great (Lev. 19:15). Sympathy can corrupt a verdict as surely as a bribe.

You shall hear the small and the great alike. You shall not be intimidated by anyone. A judge who is afraid of the man in front of him cannot do justice, and the cure for that fear is the clause that follows.

For the judgment is God’s. There is the whole thing. The judge is not offering an opinion; he is administering a verdict that belongs to somebody else, and he will answer for how he handled it. That single sentence is why he need not fear the powerful, and why he dare not favour them.

And one more, easily missed: the case that is too hard for you, you shall bring to me. Even the appointed men are allowed a limit. There is no shame in a man in authority saying this one is beyond me, and considerable danger in a man who never does.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–33 — Kadesh-barnea: The Tragedy of Unbelief
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses recounts the journey to Kadesh, the sending of the spies, and the people’s refusal to go up — their fear and grumbling against the LORD who had carried them all the way.
verseByVerse.theology: Unbelief is the root sin; it calls God a liar and recasts his love as hatred. God carries his people like a father, yet they distrust him.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel saw the giants and forgot the God who split the sea. Now: we magnify our obstacles and shrink our God, refusing to enter the rest he offers (Heb 3:19).

verseByVerse.quote: "Then we set out from Horeb and went through all that great and terrifying wilderness that you saw, on the way to the hill country of the Amorites, as the LORD our God commanded us. And we came to Kadesh-barnea. And I said to you, 'You have come to the hill country of the Amorites, which the LORD our God is giving us. See, the LORD your God has set the land before you. Go up, take possession, as the LORD, the God of your fathers, has told you. Do not fear or be dismayed.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then we set out from Horeb and went through all that great and terrifying wilderness that you saw.

Moses does not tidy the journey up. It was great and it was terrifying, and his hearers had seen it with their own eyes — the Negev in high summer, no water, no shade, no road. He is not building his case by minimising what God asked of them.

He is building it the other way. They went through that, and they came out the other side. The wilderness they survived is the evidence he is about to hold up against their fear.

Then the moment: You have come to the hill country of the Amorites, which the LORD our God is giving us. See, the LORD your God has set the land before you. Go up, take possession… Do not fear or be dismayed.

Notice what is packed into those two verses. A gift already given. A command to act. A promise attached. And an explicit word about their emotions — do not fear or be dismayed — spoken before anybody had said they were afraid. God knew what was coming, and he addressed the fear in advance rather than waiting to rebuke it afterwards.

Everything they needed was in Moses’ mouth on that morning. There is no missing piece in this paragraph. Whatever happens next cannot be blamed on insufficient information.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all of you came near me and said, 'Let us send men before us, that they may explore the land for us and bring us word again of the way by which we must go up and the cities into which we shall come.' The thing seemed good to me, and I took twelve men from you, one man from each tribe. And they turned and went up into the hill country, and came to the Valley of Eshcol and spied it out. And they took in their hands some of the fruit of the land and brought it down to us, and brought us word again and said, 'It is a good land that the LORD our God is giving us.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then all of you came near me and said, “Let us send men before us, that they may explore the land for us.”

Two things about this. First, in Numbers the command to send spies comes from God (Num. 13:1–2); here Moses says the people asked. Both are true, and the combination is the point — the request came from below and God permitted it. Second, Moses does not shelter behind that: The thing seemed good to me. He agreed. Forty years later, preaching to their children, he puts his own judgment on the record rather than quietly leaving it out.

Now read the report he says they brought back. They took in their hands some of the fruit of the land and brought it down to us, and brought us word again and said, “It is a good land that the LORD our God is giving us.”

And that is all he tells us. No giants, no fortified cities, no ten men against two. Moses knows perfectly well what else was said that day — he will quote the fear in verse 28 — but when he sets out what the spies reported, he gives the good land and stops.

He is not misremembering. He is preaching. From where he now stands, the bad report was never the substance of the matter; it was noise, and forty years have made that unmistakable. The land was good, God was giving it, they had the fruit in their hands, and they would not go. Strip out the excuse and the refusal stands there with nothing in front of it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Yet you would not go up, but rebelled against the command of the LORD your God. And you murmured in your tents and said, 'Because the LORD hated us he has brought us out of the land of Egypt, to give us into the hand of the Amorites, to destroy us. Where are we going up? Our brothers have made our hearts melt, saying, "The people are greater and taller than we. The cities are great and fortified up to heaven. And besides, we have seen the sons of the Anakim there."'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet you would not go up, but rebelled against the command of the LORD your God. And you murmured in your tents…

In your tents. Not at the tabernacle, not to Moses’ face, not in open assembly where it could be answered. In the dark, at home, to the family — which is where this kind of thing always incubates, because it needs privacy to grow and dies in daylight.

And here is what came out: Because the LORD hated us he has brought us out of the land of Egypt, to give us into the hand of the Amorites, to destroy us.

Hear it properly. The God who broke Egypt for them, opened a sea, drowned an army, fed them every morning off the ground and stood over their camp in fire every night — that God, they said, had done all of it as an elaborate way of getting them somewhere quiet enough to kill them.

Unbelief cannot leave God’s character alone. It never stops at I am not sure this will work; it goes on to he does not mean me well, because a God who is good and able leaves no room for the refusal. And the lie is old. It is the first thing the serpent ever said — God knows that when you eat of it… you will be like God (Gen. 3:5), which is to say: he is keeping something from you, he is not for you.

If you have ever lain awake after a diagnosis, or a bereavement, or a door that shut, and found the thought forming that God is against you — that thought has a history, and this is where it is recorded. It is also where it is answered, though not until much later and not with an argument. He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things? (Rom. 8:32). You cannot hold that sentence and the whisper in the tent at the same time.

Notice too what fear does to measurement. The cities are fortified up to heaven — which is not a report, it is a feeling with numbers on it. Nobody had measured a wall.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I said to you, 'Do not be in dread or afraid of them. The LORD your God who goes before you will himself fight for you, just as he did for you in Egypt before your eyes, and in the wilderness, where you have seen how the LORD your God carried you, as a man carries his son, all the way that you went until you came to this place.' Yet in spite of this word you did not believe the LORD your God, who went before you in the way to seek you out a place to pitch your tents, in fire by night and in the cloud by day, to show you by what way you should go.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses’ answer to their terror is not encouragement. It is evidence, and he lays it out in three pieces.

First, the present: The LORD your God who goes before you will himself fight for you. Second, the past in Egypt: just as he did for you in Egypt before your eyes. And third — the piece that goes deepest — the past in the desert: and in the wilderness, where you have seen how the LORD your God carried you, as a man carries his son, all the way that you went until you came to this place.

Stay with that image, because it is one of the tenderest in the Old Testament and it is put here on purpose. Picture a father at the end of a long day’s walk with a small child who cannot go another step: the child up on his shoulder, asleep, arms round his neck, contributing nothing whatever to the journey and getting there anyway. That, says Moses, is what the last forty years have actually been. The people who said the LORD hated us had been carried the whole way by the one they were accusing.

And then verse 32 falls like a stone. Yet in spite of this word you did not believe the LORD your God.

That is the verdict of the chapter and the diagnosis of the whole wilderness. Not you were outnumbered. Not the giants were real. They did not believe him. Hebrews takes this exact sentence and hands it to the church as the standing warning: So we see that they were unable to enter because of unbelief (Heb. 3:19).

Verse 33 adds the last piece of evidence, and it is quietly devastating: he went before you in the way to seek you out a place to pitch your tents. While they were deciding he meant to destroy them, he was out ahead of them, in the dark, looking for somewhere they could sleep.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 34–46 — The Sentence and the Stubborn Presumption
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God swears that the unbelieving generation will not see the land, sparing Caleb and Joshua; then, when Israel presumptuously tries to go up after all, they are defeated, for the LORD is not among them.
verseByVerse.theology: God’s discipline is real and his oath is sure; presumption is as deadly as cowardice. True faith obeys God’s timing, not its own remorse.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel wept too late and fought without God. Now: belated, self-willed religion that ignores God’s word ends in defeat; only Spirit-wrought faith prevails.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the LORD heard your words and was angered, and he swore, 'Not one of these men of this evil generation shall see the good land that I swore to give to your fathers, except Caleb the son of Jephunneh. He shall see it, and to him and to his children I will give the land on which he has trodden, because he has wholly followed the LORD!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the LORD heard your words and was angered, and he swore…

He heard them. The murmuring in the tents was private only from Moses. And his response is an oath — the same form of words by which he had bound himself to Abraham. God answers an oath with an oath, and the second one closes what the first had opened, for these men: Not one of these men of this evil generation shall see the good land.

This is a moment to resist the modern instinct to explain God’s anger away. It is not a loss of temper and it is not disproportionate. It is what love looks like when it has been told, by people it carried through a desert, that it is hatred.

And then, in the middle of the sentence, one name: except Caleb the son of Jephunneh. The reason given is a phrase to keep — because he has wholly followed the LORD. The Hebrew is more concrete than that: he filled up after the LORD, went all the way behind him, left no gap. The rest of that generation followed God partially and stopped where it got frightening.

Caleb was one man in six hundred thousand. He had heard the same report, seen the same walls, and stood alone in front of a crowd that wanted to stone him. It made no difference to the outcome for anybody else, and God took his name out of the general sentence and wrote it into the promise instead. Faithfulness in a faithless generation is not wasted, and it is not usually noticed by anyone at the time except God, which turns out to be enough.

verseByVerse.quote: Even with me the LORD was angry on your account and said, 'You also shall not go in there. Joshua the son of Nun, who stands before you, he shall enter. Encourage him, for he shall cause Israel to inherit it. And as for your little ones, who you said would become a prey, and your children, who today have no knowledge of good or evil, they shall go in there. And to them I will give it, and they shall possess it. But as for you, turn, and journey into the wilderness in the direction of the Red Sea.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even with me the LORD was angry on your account and said, “You also shall not go in there.”

Moses says this three times in the book, and each time he says on your account (1:37; 3:26; 4:21). It raises a fair question, because Numbers is quite specific that Moses lost the land for his own failure at Meribah, when he struck the rock and spoke to the people in temper (Num. 20:10–12).

Both are true and neither cancels the other. Moses failed, and it was his failure and God named it as such. And he failed at the end of forty years of being ground down by these people, in an argument they started, about water they were blaming him for. The sin was his. The context was theirs. Anyone who has finally snapped after years of provocation knows exactly how both of those can be true at once — and knows that the second does not excuse the first, which is why Moses never once asks to be let off.

Then the succession: Joshua the son of Nun, who stands before you, he shall enter… for he shall cause Israel to inherit it.

The name is Yehoshua, which means the LORD saves, and which comes into Greek as Iesous — Jesus. So the chapter arrives, without comment, at the thing it has been circling. The law-giver dies outside the land. The man called the LORD saves takes the people in. Hebrews makes the point explicitly and then leaves it hanging on purpose: if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken of another day later on (Heb. 4:8). One Joshua brought them into Canaan. That was never going to be the end of it.

And notice the small instruction attached: Encourage him. The man God has chosen, who will do what Moses could not, still needs strengthening from the people he leads. Nobody is so appointed that they can do without that.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then you answered me, 'We have sinned against the LORD. We ourselves will go up and fight, just as the LORD our God commanded us.' And every one of you fastened on his weapons of war and thought it easy to go up into the hill country. And the LORD said to me, 'Say to them, Do not go up or fight, for I am not in your midst, lest you be defeated before your enemies.' So I spoke to you, and you would not listen; but you rebelled against the command of the LORD and presumptuously went up into the hill country. Then the Amorites who lived in that hill country came out against you and chased you as bees do and beat you down in Seir as far as Hormah. And you returned and wept before the LORD, but the LORD did not listen to your voice or give ear to you. So you remained at Kadesh many days, the days that you remained there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends with the strangest turn in it. Told that the door is shut, Israel suddenly wants to go in. We have sinned against the LORD. We ourselves will go up and fight, just as the LORD our God commanded us. They put on their weapons and thought it easy to go up into the hill country.

It sounds like repentance and it is not. Look at what has actually changed. Yesterday God said go and they would not. Today God says do not go up or fight, for I am not in your midst — and they go. The direction has reversed; the disposition has not moved an inch. In both cases what God said was the thing to be got round.

That is the deepest lesson of the chapter and the hardest. There are two ways to refuse God, and the second one looks like zeal. A man can disobey by hanging back and he can disobey by charging ahead, and the second is more dangerous because it feels like courage and can be mistaken for faith by everyone watching, including himself. I am not in your midst is the only difference that matters, and it is invisible until the fighting starts.

Then the humiliation, in a phrase Moses evidently could not forget: the Amorites chased you as bees do. Not a battle — a rout, men running down a hillside from something small and furious and everywhere at once.

And the saddest verse in the chapter: you returned and wept before the LORD, but the LORD did not listen to your voice. They cried, and it was not repentance either; it was grief at the consequences, which is a different thing and God can tell.

What, then, should they have done? Exactly what they were told in verse 40 — turn, and journey into the wilderness. Accept the discipline. Go the long way. Wait for God to open the door again, without knowing whether he would. And the extraordinary thing is that he did: the whole of Deuteronomy is being preached at the foot of that reopened door, to the children of the men who were chased down that hill. If you have missed a window God opened, the answer is not a self-willed charge at it. It is to submit to the wilderness and wait for him to speak again, because he is the God who gave a second generation the land their fathers threw away.

1.theology:
Unbelief as the root sin. Chapter 1 lays bare that Israel’s catastrophe was not military but spiritual: “you did not believe the LORD your God” (1:32). Hebrews 3–4 makes this the great warning for the church. Faith and unbelief are the hinges on which destiny turns, and unbelief always slanders God’s character, recasting his love as hatred (1:27).

The faithfulness of God to his oath. Against the backdrop of Israel’s failure, God’s covenant fidelity blazes. He swore the land to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (1:8), and though a generation perishes, the promise marches on to their children. Grace outlasts and outruns human sin.

The mediator who cannot bring them in. Moses himself is barred from the land (1:37), and Joshua — Yeshua, Jesus — is appointed to lead Israel into the inheritance (1:38). The law shows the land; only the Savior carries us across the Jordan into rest.
1.examples:
Then: Standing at Kadesh-barnea with the fruit of the land in their hands and the promise of God in their ears, Israel looked at the giants instead of God, grumbled in their tents, and forfeited the inheritance — turning an eleven-day journey into forty years of graves.

Now: We do the same whenever we magnify our obstacles and shrink our God, demanding more evidence when he has already spoken, or rushing into self-willed action when he says wait. The cure is the discipline of remembrance — rehearsing how God has carried us “as a man carries his son” (1:31) — and resting in Christ, who believed where we failed, entered the rest on our behalf, and now bids us follow him through the Jordan of death into the everlasting land.

2.title: The Journey Around Edom and Moab: The Sovereign Lord of All Nations
2.text: <sup>1</sup>"Then we turned and journeyed into the wilderness in the direction of the Red Sea, as the LORD told me. And for many days we traveled around Mount Seir.<sup>2</sup>Then the LORD said to me,<sup>3</sup>'You have been traveling around this mountain country long enough. Turn northward<sup>4</sup>and command the people, "You are about to pass through the territory of your brothers, the people of Esau, who live in Seir; and they will be afraid of you. So be very careful.<sup>5</sup>Do not contend with them, for I will not give you any of their land, no, not so much as for the sole of the foot to tread on, because I have given Mount Seir to Esau as a possession.<sup>6</sup>You shall purchase food from them with money, that you may eat, and you shall also buy water from them with money, that you may drink.<sup>7</sup>For the LORD your God has blessed you in all the work of your hands. He knows your going through this great wilderness. These forty years the LORD your God has been with you. You have lacked nothing."'<sup>8</sup>So we went on, away from our brothers, the people of Esau, who live in Seir, away from the Arabah road from Elath and Ezion-geber. "And we turned and went in the direction of the wilderness of Moab.<sup>9</sup>And the LORD said to me, 'Do not harass Moab or contend with them in battle, for I will not give you any of their land for a possession, because I have given Ar to the people of Lot for a possession.'<sup>10</sup>(The Emim formerly lived there, a people great and many, and tall as the Anakim.<sup>11</sup>Like the Anakim they are also counted as Rephaim, but the Moabites call them Emim.<sup>12</sup>The Horites also lived in Seir formerly, but the people of Esau dispossessed them and destroyed them from before them and settled in their place, as Israel did to the land of their possession, which the LORD gave to them.)<sup>13</sup>'Now rise up and go over the brook Zered.' So we went over the brook Zered.<sup>14</sup>And the time from our leaving Kadesh-barnea until we crossed the brook Zered was thirty-eight years, until the entire generation, that is, the men of war, had perished from the camp, as the LORD had sworn to them.<sup>15</sup>For indeed the hand of the LORD was against them, to destroy them from the camp, until they had perished.<sup>16</sup>"So as soon as all the men of war had perished and were dead from among the people,<sup>17</sup>the LORD said to me,<sup>18</sup>'Today you are to cross the border of Moab at Ar.<sup>19</sup>And when you approach the territory of the people of Ammon, do not harass them or contend with them, for I will not give you any of the land of the people of Ammon as a possession, because I have given it to the sons of Lot for a possession.'<sup>20</sup>(It is also counted as a land of Rephaim. Rephaim formerly lived there—but the Ammonites call them Zamzummim—<sup>21</sup>a people great and many, and tall as the Anakim; but the LORD destroyed them before the Ammonites, and they dispossessed them and settled in their place,<sup>22</sup>as he did for the people of Esau, who live in Seir, when he destroyed the Horites before them and they dispossessed them and settled in their place even to this day.<sup>23</sup>As for the Avvim, who lived in villages as far as Gaza, the Caphtorim, who came from Caphtor, destroyed them and settled in their place.)<sup>24</sup>'Rise up, set out on your journey and go over the Valley of the Arnon. Behold, I have given into your hand Sihon the Amorite, king of Heshbon, and his land. Begin to take possession, and contend with him in battle.<sup>25</sup>This day I will begin to put the dread and fear of you on the peoples who are under the whole heaven, who shall hear the report of you and shall tremble and be in anguish because of you.'<sup>26</sup>"So I sent messengers from the wilderness of Kedemoth to Sihon the king of Heshbon, with words of peace, saying,<sup>27</sup>'Let me pass through your land. I will go only by the road; I will turn aside neither to the right nor to the left.<sup>28</sup>You shall sell me food for money, that I may eat, and give me water for money, that I may drink. Only let me pass through on foot,<sup>29</sup>as the sons of Esau who live in Seir and the Moabites who live in Ar did for me, until I go over the Jordan into the land that the LORD our God is giving to us.'<sup>30</sup>But Sihon the king of Heshbon would not let us pass by him, for the LORD your God hardened his spirit and made his heart obstinate, that he might give him into your hand, as he is this day.<sup>31</sup>And the LORD said to me, 'Behold, I have begun to give Sihon and his land over to you. Begin to take possession, that you may occupy his land.'<sup>32</sup>Then Sihon came out against us, he and all his people, to battle at Jahaz.<sup>33</sup>And the LORD our God gave him over to us, and we defeated him and his sons and all his people.<sup>34</sup>And we captured all his cities at that time and devoted to destruction every city, men, women, and children. We left no survivors.<sup>35</sup>Only the livestock we took as spoil for ourselves, with the plunder of the cities that we captured.<sup>36</sup>From Aroer, which is on the edge of the Valley of the Arnon, and from the city that is in the valley, as far as Gilead, there was not a city too high for us. The LORD our God gave all into our hands.<sup>37</sup>Only to the land of the sons of Ammon you did not draw near, that is, to all the banks of the river Jabbok and the cities of the hill country, whatever the LORD our God had forbidden us.
2.overview:
Chapter 2 carries the historical sermon forward from the wasted years to the renewed march. The wilderness generation has died; now the new generation moves north toward the land. And as they go, a striking theme emerges: the LORD is not merely the God of Israel but the sovereign disposer of all nations. He has given Edom to Esau’s descendants, Moab to Lot’s sons, Ammon their land too — and Israel must not touch these inheritances.

This is a stunning expansion of vision. The same God who promises Canaan to Israel has apportioned territories to the surrounding peoples, displacing ancient giants to make room for them. The whole map of the ancient Near East is, in fact, the handiwork of Israel’s covenant LORD. Acts 17:26 echoes this: God “determined allotted periods and the boundaries of their dwelling place.”

The chapter pivots at Sihon king of Heshbon, the first enemy God hands over to Israel in holy war. Here the conquest truly begins, and God declares he will put “dread and fear” of Israel upon the nations. The God who restrained Israel from Edom now unleashes them upon the Amorites — for the timing of judgment is his alone.

For us, chapter 2 enlarges our God. He is no tribal deity but the Lord of history, ruling the rise and fall of every people. And he is the faithful provider who, through forty wilderness years, saw to it that his people “lacked nothing” (2:7).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Passing By Edom: Land You May Not Take
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel skirts the territory of Esau’s descendants, forbidden to provoke them, for the LORD has given Mount Seir to Esau as a possession.
verseByVerse.theology: God’s sovereignty extends to all nations; he grants inheritances even to those outside the covenant line and holds his people accountable to respect them.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel buys food and water rather than seizing Edom’s land. Now: God’s people honor boundaries and deal justly even with those they could overpower.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then we turned and journeyed into the wilderness in the direction of the Red Sea, as the LORD told me. And for many days we traveled around Mount Seir. Then the LORD said to me, 'You have been traveling around this mountain country long enough. Turn northward
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then we turned and journeyed into the wilderness in the direction of the Red Sea… And for many days we traveled around Mount Seir.

That is thirty-eight years in a sentence. Moses gives the whole wandering half a verse and the word around, which is exactly right: they were not going anywhere. They circled a mountain for the best part of four decades while a generation died.

Then: You have been traveling around this mountain country long enough. Turn northward.

Listen to the echo. In 1:6 God had said, You have stayed long enough at this mountain — and that was Sinai, the place of glory. Here the same words are spoken over a wilderness of failure. God ends both seasons with the identical sentence. He will not let his people settle permanently on their highest day, and he will not leave them permanently in their worst one.

The word to hold is long enough. The wandering had a term. From inside it there was no way to know that; every year looked like the year before, and nobody in that camp could have told you how much longer. But it was never open-ended. God knew the date on which he would say turn northward, and he said it.

Anyone in a season that appears to have no edge to it should notice that this verse exists. The circling was not aimless to God, even when it was indistinguishable from aimless to them.

verseByVerse.quote: and command the people, "You are about to pass through the territory of your brothers, the people of Esau, who live in Seir; and they will be afraid of you. So be very careful. Do not contend with them, for I will not give you any of their land, no, not so much as for the sole of the foot to tread on, because I have given Mount Seir to Esau as a possession. You shall purchase food from them with money, that you may eat, and you shall also buy water from them with money, that you may drink. For the LORD your God has blessed you in all the work of your hands. He knows your going through this great wilderness. These forty years the LORD your God has been with you. You have lacked nothing."' So we went on, away from our brothers, the people of Esau, who live in Seir, away from the Arabah road from Elath and Ezion-geber. "And we turned and went in the direction of the wilderness of Moab.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first order given to the newly-turned nation is a restraint, and it is startling. Do not contend with them, for I will not give you any of their land, no, not so much as for the sole of the foot to tread on, because I have given Mount Seir to Esau as a possession.

Not one footprint. Israel is six hundred thousand fighting men, freshly ordered to march, and they may not take a single pace of Edomite ground.

Then the detail that must have stung: You shall purchase food from them with money… and you shall also buy water from them with money. They pay. The nation on its way to conquer Canaan walks past the brother who had once refused them the road (Num. 20:18–21) and buys its dinner from him at the going rate.

Consider whose land this is. Esau despised his birthright and sold it for a bowl of soup; Scripture says so bluntly (Heb. 12:16). And God gave him a country and defends his title to it against the covenant people. The Lord who chooses is not thereby careless of those he did not choose. He made from one man every nation of mankind… having determined allotted periods and the boundaries of their dwelling place (Acts 17:26) — every nation, not merely the one he was writing his covenant through. There is no square mile on earth that is nobody’s business but its inhabitants’.

And in the middle of the restraint sits an extraordinary sentence: These forty years the LORD your God has been with you. You have lacked nothing. Forty years of judgment, and he says they lacked nothing. That is a very hard thing to have said over a generation of funerals, and it is true. The discipline was real; so was the daily bread, all the way through it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–15 — Passing By Moab: The Old Giants Displaced
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel is likewise forbidden to harass Moab, whose land God gave to Lot’s descendants, and Moses notes how God had earlier displaced the giant Emim and other ancient peoples to settle these nations.
verseByVerse.theology: God dispossesses one people to settle another according to his hidden purposes; the death of the wilderness generation fulfills his solemn oath.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: God moved giants like chess pieces to make room for nations. Now: we trust the God who rules history even when the movements of nations bewilder us.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to me, 'Do not harass Moab or contend with them in battle, for I will not give you any of their land for a possession, because I have given Ar to the people of Lot for a possession.' (The Emim formerly lived there, a people great and many, and tall as the Anakim. Like the Anakim they are also counted as Rephaim, but the Moabites call them Emim. The Horites also lived in Seir formerly, but the people of Esau dispossessed them and destroyed them from before them and settled in their place, as Israel did to the land of their possession, which the LORD gave to them.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moab next, and the same order: Do not harass Moab or contend with them in battle… because I have given Ar to the people of Lot for a possession.

The people of Lot. Abraham’s nephew, who chose the well-watered plain and ended up in Sodom, and whose line came out of a cave and a drunken night that Scripture reports without a word of approval (Gen. 19:30–38). That family gets a country too, and God will not have it touched.

Then a historian’s aside that is doing serious work. The Emim formerly lived there, a people great and many, and tall as the Anakim. Like the Anakim they are also counted as Rephaim. Giants — the same stock, the text says explicitly, as the Anakim whose name made the spies at Kadesh go to pieces. And who cleared them out of Moab? God did, so that Lot’s descendants could live there.

Take in what the parenthesis is arguing. While Israel’s fathers were standing at Kadesh saying the giants were too big, God had already been dispossessing giants — routinely, for centuries, on behalf of Edom and Moab, nations with no covenant and no promise. The thing that paralysed the people of God had never once given him any trouble at all, and he had been doing it in that very neighbourhood for people who had never heard of him.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Now rise up and go over the brook Zered.' So we went over the brook Zered. And the time from our leaving Kadesh-barnea until we crossed the brook Zered was thirty-eight years, until the entire generation, that is, the men of war, had perished from the camp, as the LORD had sworn to them. For indeed the hand of the LORD was against them, to destroy them from the camp, until they had perished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now rise up and go over the brook Zered. And then the accounting: the time from our leaving Kadesh-barnea until we crossed the brook Zered was thirty-eight years, until the entire generation, that is, the men of war, had perished from the camp.

A brook. Not a river, not a sea — a seasonal stream in a valley, the sort of thing a man steps over. That is the boundary God set for the end of a generation, and it took thirty-eight years to reach it.

Now read verse 15, and do not soften it: For indeed the hand of the LORD was against them, to destroy them from the camp, until they had perished.

Those years were not simply time passing. Every funeral in that camp was the hand of God, and Moses says so to their children’s faces. It is a sentence modern readers want to reword, and it should be left exactly as it stands, because Scripture never treats God’s judgments as an embarrassment to be managed.

But notice who is being told. The men listening are the boys who dug those graves. They grew up in a camp where somebody was always being buried, and they are now being told what it meant. God buried a generation of redeemed people who would not trust him, and then walked their sons across the stream. Both halves are the same God, and the New Testament puts them in one sentence and asks us to look at both: Note then the kindness and the severity of God (Rom. 11:22).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–25 — The Command to Begin: Ammon Spared, Sihon Devoted
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After sparing Ammon as well, God commands Israel to begin taking possession, starting with Sihon king of Heshbon, and promises to put dread of Israel upon all the peoples.
verseByVerse.theology: God alone sets the time for judgment and conquest; he hardens and he hands over according to his sovereign will, and he goes before his people in holy war.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: God declares ‘this day I will begin’ to give Israel the land. Now: God’s kingdom advances on his timetable, and the dread of the Lord still goes before his cause.

verseByVerse.quote: "So as soon as all the men of war had perished and were dead from among the people, the LORD said to me, 'Today you are to cross the border of Moab at Ar. And when you approach the territory of the people of Ammon, do not harass them or contend with them, for I will not give you any of the land of the people of Ammon as a possession, because I have given it to the sons of Lot for a possession.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
A third nation is placed out of reach — Ammon, also descended from Lot, also holding land God says he gave them.

Three times now: Edom, Moab, Ammon. Not yours. I gave it to somebody else. And the repetition is the point, because Israel is about to be told to take a country by force, and God spends the first half of the chapter establishing that this is not a licence for acquisition. The nation that is about to conquer Canaan walks past three nations it could have crushed, and does not touch them.

Get that distinction clear, because the conquest is often read as a land-grab with religious varnish. A land-grab does not begin by ruling out three softer targets on the way. Israel took the ground God gave her and no other ground, and the boundary was not drawn by what she could reach.

There is a quieter application in it too. Much of a Christian’s life consists of walking past things that are genuinely good and genuinely obtainable, because they were assigned to somebody else. The tenth commandment exists for this. So does contentment, which is not the belief that other people’s portions are worthless but the settled conviction that God has allotted them on purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: (It is also counted as a land of Rephaim. Rephaim formerly lived there—but the Ammonites call them Zamzummim— a people great and many, and tall as the Anakim; but the LORD destroyed them before the Ammonites, and they dispossessed them and settled in their place, as he did for the people of Esau, who live in Seir, when he destroyed the Horites before them and they dispossessed them and settled in their place even to this day. As for the Avvim, who lived in villages as far as Gaza, the Caphtorim, who came from Caphtor, destroyed them and settled in their place.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Another parenthesis, and the same drumbeat. The Rephaim were there before Ammon, and the Ammonites called them Zamzummim — a people great and many, and tall as the Anakim. God destroyed them. The Avvim lived in villages near Gaza; the Caphtorim came out of Crete and destroyed them and settled in their place.

Four peoples in four verses, all gone, all displaced by God, none of them Israel’s doing.

The writer keeps interrupting his own narrative to say this, and the cumulative effect is a particular view of history. Nations rise and are removed. The map of the ancient world, which looked to everyone living on it like the permanent shape of things, was being redrawn constantly by a God most of those nations had never heard of. Empires think they are the subject of the sentence. In Scripture they are the object.

Which is a steadying thing to know in any century. He it is who sits above the circle of the earth, and its inhabitants are like grasshoppers… who brings princes to nothing, and makes the rulers of the earth as emptiness (Isa. 40:22–23). The Zamzummim were the great power of their valley, and we do not even know how to pronounce their name with confidence.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Rise up, set out on your journey and go over the Valley of the Arnon. Behold, I have given into your hand Sihon the Amorite, king of Heshbon, and his land. Begin to take possession, and contend with him in battle. This day I will begin to put the dread and fear of you on the peoples who are under the whole heaven, who shall hear the report of you and shall tremble and be in anguish because of you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And then, after all the restraint, the word changes. Rise up, set out on your journey and go over the Valley of the Arnon. Behold, I have given into your hand Sihon the Amorite, king of Heshbon, and his land. Begin to take possession, and contend with him in battle.

Begin. After forty years of not beginning, the first real order to advance.

Notice the order of the two clauses, because it governs everything that follows. I have given comes before begin to take. The gift is announced as already made, in the past tense, before a sword is drawn. Israel is not fighting in order to obtain something; she is fighting to take up something already handed over. That is the difference between an army hoping and an army collecting.

The same grammar runs through the New Testament and it is the ground of Christian effort. Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you (Phil. 2:12–13). The working out is real and strenuous. It is never the means of getting what God has not already given.

Then the promise widens beyond the battlefield: This day I will begin to put the dread and fear of you on the peoples who are under the whole heaven. God will fight this war in the minds of Canaan long before Israel arrives — and Rahab, forty years later, will describe the effect from the inside: our hearts melted, and there was no spirit left in any man (Josh. 2:11).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–37 — The Defeat of Sihon: The First Victory
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses sends an offer of peace to Sihon, but God hardens his heart so that he comes out to battle, and Israel utterly defeats him, taking his cities and land as the first fruits of the conquest.
verseByVerse.theology: God both offers terms of peace and sovereignly hardens hearts to fulfill his purposes of judgment; the conquest is his gift, devoted wholly to him.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Sihon’s refusal of peace sealed his doom. Now: the gospel goes out with a genuine offer of peace, yet rejection ripens judgment under the sovereign hand of God.

verseByVerse.quote: "So I sent messengers from the wilderness of Kedemoth to Sihon the king of Heshbon, with words of peace, saying, 'Let me pass through your land. I will go only by the road; I will turn aside neither to the right nor to the left. You shall sell me food for money, that I may eat, and give me water for money, that I may drink. Only let me pass through on foot, as the sons of Esau who live in Seir and the Moabites who live in Ar did for me, until I go over the Jordan into the land that the LORD our God is giving to us.' But Sihon the king of Heshbon would not let us pass by him, for the LORD your God hardened his spirit and made his heart obstinate, that he might give him into your hand, as he is this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s first war opens with an offer of peace. Moses sends words of peace to Sihon: let us pass through on the highway, we will turn neither right nor left, we will pay for food and water. It is the same modest request Edom refused, and it is genuine.

Sihon says no. And then the text says something that stops every honest reader: the LORD your God hardened his spirit and made his heart obstinate, that he might give him into your hand.

This is where Deuteronomy first raises the hardest question in the Bible about the will of God and the will of man, so let us take it slowly and not pretend it is simple.

Begin with what Scripture does not say. It never says God put a desire for evil into a good man. Sihon was not a peaceable king whom God corrupted; he was an Amorite warlord who had taken Heshbon by conquest from Moab (Num. 21:26) and who marched out into open desert to attack a nation that had asked to use a road. What God hardened was already there.

Then look at how the Bible handles the parallel case, because it is careful in a way we usually are not. Of Pharaoh, Exodus says three things: God will harden his heart (Exod. 4:21), Pharaoh hardened his own heart (Exod. 8:15), and God hardened Pharaoh’s heart (Exod. 9:12). Both are asserted, repeatedly, without embarrassment and without resolution. Paul quotes the whole business and, far from smoothing it, sharpens it: So then he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills — and then puts our objection into words for us, Why does he still find fault? (Rom. 9:18–19).

What can be said with confidence is this. God never makes a man sin; every man who is hardened is hardened in what he already wanted. And God is not a spectator of human wickedness; he governs it, and it serves his purposes rather than defeating them. Both truths stand, and the line where they meet is not shown to us. Anyone who has tidied this into a system has almost certainly dropped one half of what the text says.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to me, 'Behold, I have begun to give Sihon and his land over to you. Begin to take possession, that you may occupy his land.' Then Sihon came out against us, he and all his people, to battle at Jahaz. And the LORD our God gave him over to us, and we defeated him and his sons and all his people. And we captured all his cities at that time and devoted to destruction every city, men, women, and children. We left no survivors. Only the livestock we took as spoil for ourselves, with the plunder of the cities that we captured. From Aroer, which is on the edge of the Valley of the Arnon, and from the city that is in the valley, as far as Gilead, there was not a city too high for us. The LORD our God gave all into our hands. Only to the land of the sons of Ammon you did not draw near, that is, to all the banks of the river Jabbok and the cities of the hill country, whatever the LORD our God had forbidden us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The battle is over in a verse. The LORD our God gave him over to us, and we defeated him and his sons and all his people. Israel fought — the text says we defeated him — and the credit is placed elsewhere in the same sentence.

Then the hard part: the cities were devoted to destruction, and Moses spells out what that meant. This is the first time the new generation has done it, and Deuteronomy will return to it at length in chapters 7 and 20, where the grounds are set out in full. Two things belong here. The judgment is God’s, executed through Israel at a fixed moment for a stated reason — the Amorites are not being cleared to make room for a favourite but judged for four centuries of accumulated wickedness, at the end of a delay God himself imposed while it ripened (Gen. 15:16). And it is not a pattern for anybody: no nation since has held that commission, and the New Testament removes the possibility outright (2 Cor. 10:3–4).

The chapter ends with a boundary. Israel took Sihon’s land from Aroer… as far as Gilead, and then: Only to the land of the sons of Ammon you did not draw near.

Even in the flush of a first victory, with an army that has just discovered it can win, the restraint holds. They stop at the line God drew. An army that has tasted success and can still be told not that is a rare thing, and it is the whole difference between a nation under orders and a nation on the make.

2.theology:
The sovereignty of God over all nations. Three times God forbids Israel to seize the lands of Edom, Moab, and Ammon, because he himself allotted them (2:5, 9, 19). The God of Israel rules the boundaries of every people (Acts 17:26), raising up and casting down, displacing giants to settle nations according to his hidden counsel.

Divine hardening and human responsibility. Sihon refuses peace of his own pride, yet “the LORD your God hardened his spirit” (2:30). Scripture holds these together without embarrassment: God’s righteous judgment is accomplished even through the free rebellion of the wicked, just as with Pharaoh.

The faithful provision of God. Through forty years in “this great wilderness,” God was with his people and “you have lacked nothing” (2:7). The Lord of history is also the shepherd who counts every need of his children.
2.examples:
Then: Israel marched north restrained by God’s word — buying food from Edom, sparing Moab and Ammon, but devoting Sihon to judgment when the appointed hour came and the Amorite cup of sin was full.

Now: We serve the Lord of all the nations, who still rules the rise and fall of peoples and the shifting of every border. His kingdom advances on his timetable, with a genuine offer of peace in the gospel; those who refuse ripen for judgment, while his people go forward in the certainty that every enemy is already “given over” in Christ, who has disarmed the powers and goes before us to the final victory.

3.title: Victories East of the Jordan: ‘It Is Enough for You’

And Og the king of Bashan came out against us, he and all his people, to battle at Edrei.<sup>2</sup>But the LORD said to me, 'Do not fear him, for I have given him and all his people and his land into your hand. And you shall do to him as you did to Sihon the king of the Amorites, who lived at Heshbon.'<sup>3</sup>So the LORD our God gave into our hand Og also, the king of Bashan, and all his people, and we struck him down until he had no survivor left.<sup>4</sup>And we took all his cities at that time—there was not a city that we did not take from them—sixty cities, the whole region of Argob, the kingdom of Og in Bashan.<sup>5</sup>All these were cities fortified with high walls, gates, and bars, besides very many unwalled villages.<sup>6</sup>And we devoted them to destruction, as we did to Sihon the king of Heshbon, devoting to destruction every city, men, women, and children.<sup>7</sup>But all the livestock and the spoil of the cities we took as our plunder.<sup>8</sup>So we took the land at that time out of the hand of the two kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan, from the Valley of the Arnon to Mount Hermon<sup>9</sup>(the Sidonians call Hermon Sirion, while the Amorites call it Senir),<sup>10</sup>all the cities of the tableland and all Gilead and all Bashan, as far as Salecah and Edrei, cities of the kingdom of Og in Bashan.<sup>11</sup>(For only Og the king of Bashan was left of the remnant of the Rephaim. Behold, his bed was a bed of iron. Is it not in Rabbah of the Ammonites? (All that portion of Bashan is called the land of Rephaim.<sup>14</sup>Jair the Manassite took all the region of Argob, that is, Bashan, as far as the border of the Geshurites and the Maacathites, and called the villages after his own name, Havvoth-jair, as it is to this day.)<sup>15</sup>To Machir I gave Gilead,<sup>16</sup>and to the Reubenites and the Gadites I gave the territory from Gilead as far as the Valley of the Arnon, with the middle of the valley as a border, as far over as the river Jabbok, the border of the Ammonites;<sup>17</sup>the Arabah also, with the Jordan as the border, from Chinnereth as far as the Sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea, under the slopes of Pisgah on the east.<sup>18</sup>"And I commanded you at that time, saying, 'The LORD your God has given you this land to possess. All your men of valor shall cross over armed before your brothers, the people of Israel.<sup>19</sup>Only your wives, your little ones, and your livestock (I know that you have much livestock) shall remain in the cities that I have given you,<sup>20</sup>until the LORD gives rest to your brothers, as to you, and they also occupy the land that the LORD your God gives them beyond the Jordan. Then each of you may return to his possession which I have given you.'<sup>21</sup>And I commanded Joshua at that time, 'Your eyes have seen all that the LORD your God has done to these two kings. So will the LORD do to all the kingdoms into which you are crossing.<sup>22</sup>You shall not fear them, for it is the LORD your God who fights for you.'<sup>23</sup>"And I pleaded with the LORD at that time, saying,<sup>24</sup>'O Lord GOD, you have only begun to show your servant your greatness and your mighty hand. For what god is there in heaven or on earth who can do such works and mighty acts as yours?<sup>25</sup>Please let me go over and see the good land beyond the Jordan, that good hill country and Lebanon.'<sup>26</sup>But the LORD was angry with me because of you and would not listen to me. And the LORD said to me, 'Enough from you; do not speak to me of this matter again.<sup>27</sup>Go up to the top of Pisgah and lift up your eyes westward and northward and southward and eastward, and look at it with your eyes, for you shall not go over this Jordan.<sup>28</sup>But charge Joshua, and encourage and strengthen him, for he shall go over at the head of this people, and he shall put them in possession of the land that you shall see.'<sup>29</sup>So we remained in the valley opposite Beth-peor.
3.overview:
Chapter 3 completes the record of the eastern conquests with the defeat of Og king of Bashan, the last of the giants, and the allotment of the conquered land to the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh. The God who toppled Sihon now topples Og, whose great iron bedstead becomes a museum-piece testifying to the size of the foe — and the greatness of the God who felled him.

The chapter then turns intensely personal. Moses, having tasted these victories, pleads with God to let him cross the Jordan and see the good land. It is one of the most poignant prayers in Scripture. And God’s answer is a firm and final no: “Enough from you; do not speak to me of this matter again.” Yet even in the refusal there is grace — Moses may climb Pisgah and see the land with his eyes, and he must commission and encourage Joshua, who will lead the people in.

Here the great theme of the whole book deepens: the mediator of the law cannot bring the people into the inheritance. Moses, for all his greatness, dies outside. The law shows us the land; only Joshua — Jesus — carries us across the river.

For the believer, chapter 3 holds both the triumph of a God who fights for us against every giant and the tender mystery of unanswered prayer, where God’s “no” is itself wrapped in fatherly love.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Defeat of Og: The Last of the Giants
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel defeats Og king of Bashan, the last of the Rephaim giants, capturing all his fortified cities and devoting them to destruction, just as with Sihon.
verseByVerse.theology: No enemy, however great, can stand before the LORD who fights for his people; the giants of legend fall like grass before him.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Og’s iron bed memorialized a fallen giant. Now: the monuments of our defeated fears testify to the God who conquers what terrifies us.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then we turned and went up the way to Bashan. And Og the king of Bashan came out against us, he and all his people, to battle at Edrei. But the LORD said to me, 'Do not fear him, for I have given him and all his people and his land into your hand. And you shall do to him as you did to Sihon the king of the Amorites, who lived at Heshbon.' So the LORD our God gave into our hand Og also, the king of Bashan, and all his people, and we struck him down until he had no survivor left.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then we turned and went up the way to Bashan. And Og the king of Bashan came out against us, he and all his people, to battle at Edrei.

Of all the enemies Israel could have met first after the wilderness, this is the worst one. Og was the last of the Rephaim — the giant stock the spies had described at Kadesh when they said we seemed to ourselves like grasshoppers (Num. 13:33). The precise terror that destroyed their parents comes down the road at them in person, with an army behind him, in the first campaign of their lives.

And God says: Do not fear him, for I have given him and all his people and his land into your hand. And you shall do to him as you did to Sihon the king of the Amorites.

Notice the argument God actually makes. Not he is smaller than he looks, and not you are stronger than you think. He says: you have seen me do this before, three weeks ago, to Sihon. The cure for fear here is not a reassessment of the enemy but a memory of God.

And it worked. So the LORD our God gave into our hand Og also… and we struck him down until he had no survivor left. The generation that ran from giants they had only heard described raised a son who killed one. Nothing had changed about the giants.

verseByVerse.quote: And we took all his cities at that time—there was not a city that we did not take from them—sixty cities, the whole region of Argob, the kingdom of Og in Bashan. All these were cities fortified with high walls, gates, and bars, besides very many unwalled villages. And we devoted them to destruction, as we did to Sihon the king of Heshbon, devoting to destruction every city, men, women, and children. But all the livestock and the spoil of the cities we took as our plunder.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we took all his cities at that time — there was not a city that we did not take from them — sixty cities… All these were cities fortified with high walls, gates, and bars.

Go back and read 1:28 next to that. The report that broke the nation at Kadesh was: The cities are great and fortified up to heaven. That was the phrase. That was the whole obstacle.

Here are sixty of them, with high walls, gates and bars, and the summary is there was not a city that we did not take. The thing their fathers described as insurmountable is enumerated by their sons like an inventory.

The walls had not got lower. Bashan’s cities were among the most heavily fortified in the region, and the text goes out of its way to say so rather than minimising them. What changed was that this generation went up when God said go.

That is the whole difference, and it needs saying plainly, because most Christians spend a good deal of life in front of some wall or other. The question is almost never whether the obstacle is real. Israel’s fathers were right about the walls and wrong about God, and being right about the walls did not save them.
