(Rom. 8:32). If the cross happened, nothing that remains is a serious question.

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, the LORD your God will send hornets among them, until those who are left and hide themselves from you are destroyed. You shall not be in dread of them, for the LORD your God is in your midst, a great and awesome God. The LORD your God will clear away these nations before you little by little. You may not make an end of them at once, lest the wild beasts grow too numerous for you. But the LORD your God will give them over to you and throw them into great confusion, until they are destroyed. And he will give their kings into your hand, and you shall make their name perish from under heaven. No one shall be able to stand against you until you have destroyed them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God promises to fight — even, oddly, with hornets, an image of panic and rout — and gives the ground: the LORD your God is in your midst, a great and awesome God. Not watching from a distance. In the camp.

And then a verse that surprises everybody: The LORD your God will clear away these nations before you little by little. You may not make an end of them at once, lest the wild beasts grow too numerous for you.

Little by little. God, who could have emptied Canaan in a week, deliberately chooses not to — and the reason he gives is agricultural. A land emptied of people faster than Israel can occupy it goes back to wilderness; the terraces collapse, the vines go wild, and the predators move in. Slow victory is the kindness. Fast victory would have handed them a country they could not hold.

Anyone who has prayed for years about a sin that will not die should hold on to verse 22. God’s usual method with his people is little by little, and it is not because he lacks power or interest. Sudden, total deliverance from everything at once would leave a man with ground he has no character to occupy. Sanctification is slow for the same reason the conquest was slow — the land has to be lived in, not merely cleared.

verseByVerse.quote: The carved images of their gods you shall burn with fire. You shall not covet the silver or the gold that is on them or take it for yourselves, lest you be ensnared by it, for it is an abomination to the LORD your God. And you shall not bring an abominable thing into your house and become devoted to destruction like it. You shall utterly detest and abhor it, for it is devoted to destruction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends with the gold, and it is the sharpest warning in it.

The carved images of their gods you shall burn with fire. You shall not covet the silver or the gold that is on them or take it for yourselves, lest you be ensnared by it.

Here is the temptation, precisely calculated. Nobody in that army is going to be converted to Baal by looking at a statue. But the statues were plated in silver and gold, and Israel was poor. The reasoning writes itself: the idol is destroyed, the god is discredited, the metal is neutral, and we have nothing. Why burn good silver?

God says burn it, and gives the reason in one word: ensnared. A snare is not a wall; it is something that lets you walk in freely and then holds you. The danger was never that Israel would worship the metal. It was that a man who kept one piece of it would find, years later, that he had kept a thread back to the whole thing.

And the language of verse 26 is deliberately extreme: you shall utterly detest and abhor it. Not manage it, not keep it at a safe distance, not admire it as an antique — detest it. Achan would read this command, take a cloak and some silver at Jericho, bury it under his tent, and destroy his family (Josh. 7:21).

Which is exactly how a besetting sin survives in a Christian life. Very few people keep the idol. A great many keep something off it — the friendship that goes with it, the taste for it, the door left unlocked — and reason that the thing itself is gone. If your right hand causes you to sin, cut it off and throw it away (Matt. 5:30) is the same instruction in the same tone, and it was given by the gentlest man who ever lived.

7.theology:
Election grounded in sovereign love. God chose Israel “not because you were more in number… but because the LORD loves you” (7:7–8). Election rests on nothing but God’s free, unmerited love — the love is the cause, not the effect. This is the bedrock of all assurance: if God chose us for no reason in us, nothing in us can unchoose us. Peter applies the same to the church (1 Pet 2:9).

The faithful, covenant-keeping God. The LORD “keeps covenant and steadfast love… to a thousand generations” (7:9). The security of the chosen rests not on our shaky faithfulness but on God’s rock-solid chesed, which finds its yes and amen in Christ (2 Cor 1:20).

Radical separation from idolatry. Israel must make no covenant with the nations and utterly abhor their idols (7:2, 26). Holiness is not polite distance from sin but its renunciation; the believer is called to mortify sin and belong wholly to the God who first loved him.
7.examples:
Then: Israel — the fewest of all peoples — was made God’s treasured possession not by merit but by sheer sovereign love, set apart as a holy nation to make no alliance with Canaanite idolatry and to trust the God who shattered Egypt to clear the land before them little by little.

Now: Every believer is God’s chosen treasure, loved not because we were lovely but because he set his love upon us. We rest our assurance on his covenant faithfulness, conquer fear by remembering the cross and empty tomb, embrace the gradual ‘little by little’ work of sanctification as a mercy, and abhor every idol of the heart, belonging wholly to the Lord who first loved us.

8.title: Remember the LORD Your God: Man Does Not Live by Bread Alone
8.text: <sup>1</sup>"The whole commandment that I command you today you shall be careful to do, that you may live and multiply, and go in and possess the land that the LORD swore to give to your fathers.<sup>2</sup>And you shall remember the whole way that the LORD your God has led you these forty years in the wilderness, that he might humble you, testing you to know what was in your heart, whether you would keep his commandments or not.<sup>3</sup>And he humbled you and let you hunger and fed you with manna, which you did not know, nor did your fathers know, that he might make you know that man does not live by bread alone, but man lives by every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD.<sup>4</sup>Your clothing did not wear out on you and your foot did not swell these forty years.<sup>5</sup>Know then in your heart that, as a man disciplines his son, the LORD your God disciplines you.<sup>6</sup>So you shall keep the commandments of the LORD your God by walking in his ways and by fearing him.<sup>7</sup>For the LORD your God is bringing you into a good land, a land of brooks of water, of fountains and springs, flowing out in the valleys and hills,<sup>8</sup>a land of wheat and barley, of vines and fig trees and pomegranates, a land of olive trees and honey,<sup>9</sup>a land in which you will eat bread without scarcity, in which you will lack nothing, a land whose stones are iron, and out of whose hills you can dig copper.<sup>10</sup>And you shall eat and be full, and you shall bless the LORD your God for the good land he has given you.<sup>11</sup>"Take care lest you forget the LORD your God by not keeping his commandments and his rules and his statutes, which I command you today,<sup>12</sup>lest, when you have eaten and are full and have built good houses and live in them,<sup>13</sup>and when your herds and flocks multiply and your silver and gold is multiplied and all that you have is multiplied,<sup>14</sup>then your heart be lifted up, and you forget the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery,<sup>15</sup>who led you through the great and terrifying wilderness, with its fiery serpents and scorpions and thirsty ground where there was no water, who brought you water out of the flinty rock,<sup>16</sup>who fed you in the wilderness with manna that your fathers did not know, that he might humble you and test you, to do you good in the end.<sup>17</sup>Beware lest you say in your heart, 'My power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth.'<sup>18</sup>You shall remember the LORD your God, for it is he who gives you power to get wealth, that he may confirm his covenant that he swore to your fathers, as it is this day.<sup>19</sup>And if you forget the LORD your God and go after other gods and serve them and worship them, I solemnly warn you today that you shall surely perish.<sup>20</sup>Like the nations that the LORD makes to perish before you, so shall you perish, because you would not obey the voice of the LORD your God.
8.overview:
Chapter 8 is a meditation on memory and danger. The wilderness, Moses explains, was a school — God humbled Israel, let them hunger, and fed them with manna “that he might make you know that man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD” (8:3). This is the very verse Jesus quoted to Satan in the wilderness (Matt 4:4), succeeding where Israel failed. The deepest human need is not physical but spiritual: the Word of God.

The great theme is remembrance and its enemy, forgetfulness. The wilderness taught dependence; the danger is that the abundance of the land will teach self-sufficiency. When Israel is full, settled, and prosperous, the temptation will be to say, “My power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth” (8:17) — to forget the Giver and worship the gift, even to worship the self.

Moses presses the antidote: “You shall remember the LORD your God, for it is he who gives you power to get wealth” (8:18). Every good thing comes from God’s hand, and the heart that remembers this is kept humble and grateful.

The chapter ends with a solemn warning: to forget God is to perish like the nations. For us, chapter 8 is a searching examination of the spiritual perils of comfort and a call to find our true life not in bread but in the Word — supremely in Christ, the Bread of Life and the living Word.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses calls Israel to remember the whole wilderness journey, in which God humbled and tested them and fed them with manna to teach them that life depends on God’s word, disciplining them as a father his son.
verseByVerse.theology: God uses hardship as fatherly discipline to humble, test, and teach dependence; trials are the school of faith, not signs of abandonment.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the wilderness humbled Israel to teach dependence. Now: God uses our hard providences to wean us from self-reliance and teach us to live by his Word.

verseByVerse.quote: "The whole commandment that I command you today you shall be careful to do, that you may live and multiply, and go in and possess the land that the LORD swore to give to your fathers. And you shall remember the whole way that the LORD your God has led you these forty years in the wilderness, that he might humble you, testing you to know what was in your heart, whether you would keep his commandments or not.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And you shall remember the whole way that the LORD your God has led you these forty years in the wilderness, that he might humble you, testing you to know what was in your heart.

Two words in that sentence change how the last forty years are to be read.

The first is led. Not allowed you to wander — led. From inside it, the wilderness looked like the consequence of a disaster at Kadesh, which it was; and Moses now says it was also a route, chosen and walked by God at the head of the column. Both are true. The years were judgment and they were itinerary.

The second is the whole way. Not the highlights. The whole of it — the water from the rock and the graves at Kibroth-hattaavah, the manna and the serpents, the days when God was unmistakable and the far greater number of days when nothing happened at all. Israel is to remember the entire road, because a memory that keeps only the rescues will not be much use when the next stretch is dull.

And then the purpose, in two parts: that he might humble you, testing you to know what was in your heart.

Testing in Scripture is not God gathering information he lacks. The next clause says it plainly enough — the test was to know what was in your heart, and God knew already. The test was so that they would know. Nobody discovers what he actually believes while things are comfortable. Pressure does not create character; it reveals it, and then, in God’s hands, it changes it.

verseByVerse.quote: And he humbled you and let you hunger and fed you with manna, which you did not know, nor did your fathers know, that he might make you know that man does not live by bread alone, but man lives by every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he humbled you and let you hunger and fed you with manna, which you did not know, nor did your fathers know, that he might make you know that man does not live by bread alone, but man lives by every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD.

Read the order of the verbs, because the whole lesson is in the sequence. He humbled. He let you hunger. Then he fed.

God engineered the hunger. That is what the verse says, and it is not softened anywhere in Scripture. He brought two million people into a place with no food, let them get genuinely hungry, and only then sent bread — and he did it deliberately, so that they would learn something they could not have learned in a fertile country.

And what they were to learn is stated: that man does not live by bread alone, but man lives by every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD. The manna itself taught it. Bread that appears on the ground overnight, that cannot be stored, that has to be gathered fresh every morning, and that stops the day you cross into a land with crops — such bread makes the point better than any sermon. Israel was fed for forty years by a word, not by a harvest.

Now, this is not a verse about preferring spiritual things to physical ones. It says man does not live by bread alone, and the manna was real bread that filled real stomachs. The point is about the ultimate source. Bread keeps a man alive because God says so; take away the word and the bread does nothing.

Fifteen centuries later a man stood in a wilderness of his own, forty days without food, and the tempter said: If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become loaves of bread. And he answered with this verse, word for word (Matt. 4:4). Israel was hungry for forty years and grumbled; the true Son was hungry for forty days and quoted the lesson Israel failed. Then he went on and said something no Israelite could have expected: I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger (John 6:35).

verseByVerse.quote: Your clothing did not wear out on you and your foot did not swell these forty years. Know then in your heart that, as a man disciplines his son, the LORD your God disciplines you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two details close the wilderness section, and they are unexpectedly domestic.

Your clothing did not wear out on you and your foot did not swell these forty years.

Nobody would have chosen those as the miracles to record. Not the sea, not the fire, not the water from the rock — clothes and feet. Forty years of walking in a desert, and the cloak lasted and the feet held up. A man who has done any distance on foot knows exactly how much that matters, and how little anybody thanks God for it.

God’s care runs down into things nobody notices, and it is generally the small mercies that go unrecorded. Most Christians could produce a list of the times God answered something dramatic. Very few keep any account of forty years of feet that did not give out.

Then verse 5, which gathers the whole chapter so far into one image: Know then in your heart that, as a man disciplines his son, the LORD your God disciplines you.

The word is yasar — to train, correct, bring up. It is what a father does to a son he intends to make into something, and it includes hardship on purpose. Israel’s forty years were not a father losing his temper; they were a father raising a child, and the hunger in verse 3 was part of the upbringing.

Hebrews takes this exact idea and presses it on Christians who are suffering, and adds the inference that Deuteronomy leaves implicit: It is for discipline that you have to endure. God is treating you as sons… If you are left without discipline, then you are illegitimate children and not sons (Heb. 12:7–8). The hardship is not evidence that God has withdrawn. It is evidence of the relationship.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–10 — The Good Land: Bless the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses describes the rich and good land into which God is bringing Israel — a land of streams, grain, vines, and minerals — where they will eat and be full and bless the LORD.
verseByVerse.theology: God is the generous giver of good gifts; the proper response to abundance is grateful blessing of the Giver.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel was to bless God for the good land. Now: gratitude and thanksgiving are the right response to every good gift from our Father’s hand.

verseByVerse.quote: So you shall keep the commandments of the LORD your God by walking in his ways and by fearing him. For the LORD your God is bringing you into a good land, a land of brooks of water, of fountains and springs, flowing out in the valleys and hills, a land of wheat and barley, of vines and fig trees and pomegranates, a land of olive trees and honey, a land in which you will eat bread without scarcity, in which you will lack nothing, a land whose stones are iron, and out of whose hills you can dig copper. And you shall eat and be full, and you shall bless the LORD your God for the good land he has given you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the land, and Moses lets himself go. A land of brooks of water, of fountains and springs, flowing out in the valleys and hills, a land of wheat and barley, of vines and fig trees and pomegranates, a land of olive trees and honey.

Every item on that list is chosen for people who have spent forty years in a desert eating the same thing every morning. Water that comes up out of the ground by itself. Bread from a field instead of off the sand. Fruit — and not one fruit but four, named, so they can taste them in advance. Then, almost as an afterthought, mineral wealth: a land whose stones are iron, and out of whose hills you can dig copper.

God is not embarrassed to describe the goodness of the material world to his people. He made it, and he is about to give them a great deal of it, and the passage has no trace of the suspicion of physical pleasure that has attached itself to religion in most centuries since.

And then verse 10, which is the hinge of the chapter and the answer to everything that follows: And you shall eat and be full, and you shall bless the LORD your God for the good land he has given you.

Eat, be full, and bless him. That single instruction is the whole defence against the disaster of the next ten verses. Prosperity does not have to ruin a man. It ruins him when it arrives without gratitude, because a full stomach and a short memory are the exact conditions in which people quietly stop needing God. The Jewish practice of saying grace after the meal — when you are full and least inclined to — comes from this verse, and it is wiser than our habit of thanking God while still hungry.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–20 — The Peril of Plenty: Do Not Forget
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses warns that when Israel grows full and prosperous, their heart may be lifted up to forget the LORD and credit their own power for their wealth; they must remember it is God who gives the power to get wealth, lest they perish like the nations.
verseByVerse.theology: Prosperity tempts the heart to pride, self-sufficiency, and forgetfulness of God; remembering that all comes from God keeps the heart humble and grateful.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel was warned not to credit their own strength for the land’s wealth. Now: affluence still tempts us to self-reliance and the forgetting of God.

verseByVerse.quote: "Take care lest you forget the LORD your God by not keeping his commandments and his rules and his statutes, which I command you today, lest, when you have eaten and are full and have built good houses and live in them, and when your herds and flocks multiply and your silver and gold is multiplied and all that you have is multiplied, then your heart be lifted up, and you forget the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery, who led you through the great and terrifying wilderness, with its fiery serpents and scorpions and thirsty ground where there was no water, who brought you water out of the flinty rock, who fed you in the wilderness with manna that your fathers did not know, that he might humble you and test you, to do you good in the end.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take care lest you forget the LORD your God… lest, when you have eaten and are full and have built good houses and live in them, and when your herds and flocks multiply and your silver and gold is multiplied and all that you have is multiplied, then your heart be lifted up, and you forget the LORD your God.

Notice that the catalogue of dangers is a catalogue of blessings. Full stomachs. Good houses. Growing herds. More silver. Everything on the list is something God gives and something any sensible person would pray for, and Moses names them all as the road to ruin.

And the mechanism is precise: then your heart be lifted up, and you forget. First the lifting up — a quiet swelling of self-regard that nobody notices in themselves — and then forgetting, which follows almost automatically. A man who has begun to feel substantial does not usually decide to stop depending on God. He simply finds one day that he has, and cannot say when.

Against that, Moses sets a memory, and the details are chosen with care: the God who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery, who led you through the great and terrifying wilderness, with its fiery serpents and scorpions and thirsty ground where there was no water, who brought you water out of the flinty rock, who fed you in the wilderness with manna.

Serpents. Scorpions. No water. Flint. That is what he wants remembered in the good houses — not a general sense of having been helped but the specific place they were and what it was like there. Prosperity erases detail first, and the detail is the whole point.

Then the purpose, and it is one of the tenderest phrases in Deuteronomy: he humbled and tested them to do you good in the end. Not to break them. Not even, finally, to punish them. The whole hard road had a kindness at the end of it that they could not see from inside it.

verseByVerse.quote: Beware lest you say in your heart, 'My power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth.' You shall remember the LORD your God, for it is he who gives you power to get wealth, that he may confirm his covenant that he swore to your fathers, as it is this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beware lest you say in your heart, “My power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth.”

There is the sentence, and God quotes it back to them before anybody has said it — as he did with their fear in 7:17. He knows what prosperity says in a man’s heart, and he is willing to put it into words so that they will recognise it when they hear themselves think it.

And note that it is said in your heart. Nobody announces this at dinner. It is the private, satisfied assessment a man makes of his own life when he looks at what he has built and draws a straight line back to himself. It is not usually a boast; it is more often just an assumption, and it is all the more dangerous for being unexamined.

The correction is not that Israel did nothing. They did farm the land and build the houses. The correction is one step further back: You shall remember the LORD your God, for it is he who gives you power to get wealth. Even the capacity was a gift. The energy, the health, the intelligence, the opportunity, the decades of peace in which to work — none of it was self-generated, and a man who traces the chain honestly runs out of his own contributions very quickly.

Paul asks the same question of a church that had begun to congratulate itself, and it has never been answered: What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it? (1 Cor. 4:7).

And read twice the reason God gives the power to get wealth: that he may confirm his covenant that he swore to your fathers. The prosperity is not a reward for performance. It is the keeping of an old promise.

verseByVerse.quote: And if you forget the LORD your God and go after other gods and serve them and worship them, I solemnly warn you today that you shall surely perish. Like the nations that the LORD makes to perish before you, so shall you perish, because you would not obey the voice of the LORD your God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends without any softening. And if you forget the LORD your God and go after other gods and serve them and worship them, I solemnly warn you today that you shall surely perish. Like the nations that the LORD makes to perish before you, so shall you perish.

That last comparison is the sharpest thing in the chapter. Israel is at this moment watching God destroy the Canaanites for their idolatry — and Moses says: if you do what they did, you will get what they got. There is no protected status. The covenant is not a charm.

Which is exactly what happened. Seven centuries later the northern kingdom was carried off by Assyria and the southern kingdom by Babylon, for precisely the sin named here, and the prophets told them plainly that they were being treated like Canaanites. Amos put it with brutal compression: You only have I known of all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities (Amos 3:2). Being chosen raised the accountability rather than removing it.

And the reason given for the ruin is not idolatry in the abstract but something more ordinary: because you would not obey the voice of the LORD your God. It goes back to hearing. The book that begins Hear, O Israel ends its warnings with a people who would not listen.

Paul takes the whole chapter and hands it to the church without a word of adjustment: Now these things happened to them as an example, but they were written down for our instruction… Therefore let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall (1 Cor. 10:11–12). The warning was never for Israel only, and the danger it names is not persecution. It is a good house and a full table and a heart that has quietly stopped remembering.

8.theology:
Man does not live by bread alone. God humbled Israel and fed them manna to teach that life is sustained “by every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD” (8:3). Our deepest need is spiritual, not physical. Jesus quoted this verse against Satan (Matt 4:4), succeeding where Israel failed, and is himself the living Word and Bread of Life.

The peril of prosperity. The great danger is plenty, not want: “lest… your heart be lifted up, and you forget the LORD” (8:14). Comfort breeds self-sufficiency, and self-sufficiency breeds forgetfulness. The boast “my power… has gotten me this wealth” (8:17) is the lie at the heart of pride.

Hardship as fatherly discipline. The wilderness was a school: “as a man disciplines his son, the LORD your God disciplines you” (8:5; cf. Heb 12). Trials are not signs of abandonment but the loving training of a Father whose aim is our holiness and our good.
8.examples:
Then: Israel was led through forty years of wilderness to be humbled, tested, and taught dependence on God’s word, and then warned that the abundance of the good land would tempt them to forget the Giver and boast in their own strength.

Now: We are the most prosperous Christians in history, and the same peril stalks us. We must trace every good thing — even our ability to earn — back to God’s hand, receive our hard providences as a Father’s discipline, refuse the lie of self-made success, and feed our souls not on bread alone but on the Word, supremely on Christ the Bread of Life, lest in our plenty we forget the God who is our only true treasure.

9.title: Not Because of Your Righteousness: Grace Alone for a Stubborn People
9.text: <sup>1</sup>"Hear, O Israel: you are to cross over the Jordan today, to go in to dispossess nations greater and mightier than you, cities great and fortified up to heaven,<sup>2</sup>a people great and tall, the sons of the Anakim, whom you know, and of whom you have heard it said, 'Who can stand before the sons of Anak?'<sup>3</sup>Know therefore today that he who goes over before you as a consuming fire is the LORD your God. He will destroy them and subdue them before you. So you shall drive them out and make them perish quickly, as the LORD has promised you.<sup>4</sup>"Do not say in your heart, after the LORD your God has thrust them out before you, 'It is because of my righteousness that the LORD has brought me in to possess this land,' whereas it is because of the wickedness of these nations that the LORD is driving them out before you.<sup>5</sup>Not because of your righteousness or the uprightness of your heart are you going in to possess their land, but because of the wickedness of these nations the LORD your God is driving them out from before you, and that he may confirm the word that the LORD swore to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob.<sup>6</sup>"Know, therefore, that the LORD your God is not giving you this good land to possess because of your righteousness, for you are a stubborn people.<sup>7</sup>Remember and do not forget how you provoked the LORD your God to wrath in the wilderness. From the day you came out of the land of Egypt until you came to this place, you have been rebellious against the LORD.<sup>8</sup>Even at Horeb you provoked the LORD to wrath, and the LORD was so angry with you that he was ready to destroy you.<sup>9</sup>When I went up the mountain to receive the tablets of stone, the tablets of the covenant that the LORD made with you, I remained on the mountain forty days and forty nights. I neither ate bread nor drank water.<sup>10</sup>And the LORD gave me the two tablets of stone written with the finger of God, and on them were all the words that the LORD had spoken with you on the mountain out of the midst of the fire on the day of the assembly.<sup>11</sup>And at the end of forty days and forty nights the LORD gave me the two tablets of stone, the tablets of the covenant.<sup>12</sup>Then the LORD said to me, 'Arise, go down quickly from here, for your people whom you have brought from Egypt have acted corruptly. They have turned aside quickly out of the way that I commanded them; they have made themselves a metal image.'<sup>13</sup>"Furthermore, the LORD said to me, 'I have seen this people, and behold, it is a stubborn people.<sup>14</sup>Let me alone, that I may destroy them and blot out their name from under heaven. And I will make of you a nation mightier and greater than they.'<sup>15</sup>So I turned and came down from the mountain, and the mountain was burning with fire. And the two tablets of the covenant were in my two hands.<sup>16</sup>And I looked, and behold, you had sinned against the LORD your God. You had made yourselves a golden calf. You had turned aside quickly from the way that the LORD had commanded you.<sup>17</sup>So I took hold of the two tablets and threw them out of my two hands and broke them before your eyes.<sup>18</sup>Then I lay prostrate before the LORD as before, forty days and forty nights. I neither ate bread nor drank water, because of all the sin that you had committed, in doing what was evil in the sight of the LORD to provoke him to anger.<sup>19</sup>For I was afraid of the anger and hot displeasure that the LORD bore against you, so that he was ready to destroy you. But the LORD listened to me that time also.<sup>20</sup>And the LORD was so angry with Aaron that he was ready to destroy him. And I prayed for Aaron also at the same time.<sup>21</sup>Then I took the sinful thing, the calf that you had made, and burned it with fire and crushed it, grinding it very small, until it was as fine as dust. And I threw the dust of it into the brook that ran down from the mountain.<sup>22</sup>"At Taberah also, and at Massah and at Kibroth-hattaavah you provoked the LORD to wrath.<sup>23</sup>And when the LORD sent you from Kadesh-barnea, saying, 'Go up and take possession of the land that I have given you,' then you rebelled against the commandment of the LORD your God and did not believe him or obey his voice.<sup>24</sup>You have been rebellious against the LORD from the day that I knew you.<sup>25</sup>"So I lay prostrate before the LORD for these forty days and forty nights, because the LORD had said he would destroy you.<sup>26</sup>And I prayed to the LORD, 'O Lord GOD, do not destroy your people and your heritage, whom you have redeemed through your greatness, whom you have brought out of Egypt with a mighty hand.<sup>27</sup>Remember your servants, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Do not regard the stubbornness of this people, or their wickedness or their sin,<sup>28</sup>lest the land from which you brought us say, "Because the LORD was not able to bring them into the land that he promised them, and because he hated them, he has brought them out to put them to death in the wilderness."<sup>29</sup>For they are your people and your heritage, whom you brought out by your great power and by your outstretched arm.'
9.overview:
Chapter 9 is a sustained assault on self-righteousness. Lest Israel imagine, once they are settled in the land, that their conquest proved their virtue, Moses delivers a relentless reminder: “the LORD your God is not giving you this good land to possess because of your righteousness, for you are a stubborn people” (9:6). Three times he hammers it home (vv. 4, 5, 6). The land is sheer grace — given because of the wickedness of the nations and the promise to the fathers, never because Israel deserved it.

To prove the point, Moses rehearses Israel’s history of rebellion, climaxing in the golden calf at Horeb. While Moses was on the mountain receiving the covenant, the people were below making an idol. They were “rebellious against the LORD from the day that I knew you” (9:24). Far from being righteous, they were stubborn, stiff-necked, provoking God repeatedly.

The chapter’s glory is Moses’ intercession. Forty days and nights he lay prostrate before God, pleading for the people who deserved destruction, appealing not to their merit but to God’s name, his promise, and his great redemption. Moses the mediator stands between the people and the wrath they had earned.

Here the gospel shines: salvation is by grace alone, never by works, for a stubborn people who deserve nothing. And Moses’ intercession foreshadows the greater Mediator who ever lives to intercede for us — Christ, whose plea is grounded not in our righteousness but in his own perfect sacrifice.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Not Because of Your Righteousness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel will cross the Jordan to dispossess nations greater than themselves, but they must not credit their own righteousness; God gives the land because of the wickedness of the nations and his promise to the fathers, for Israel is a stubborn people.
verseByVerse.theology: Salvation and inheritance are by grace alone, never by human merit; God justifies and blesses the undeserving for his own name’s sake.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel’s conquest was grace, not reward. Now: we are saved not by our righteousness but by Christ’s, lest any should boast.

verseByVerse.quote: "Hear, O Israel: you are to cross over the Jordan today, to go in to dispossess nations greater and mightier than you, cities great and fortified up to heaven, a people great and tall, the sons of the Anakim, whom you know, and of whom you have heard it said, 'Who can stand before the sons of Anak?' Know therefore today that he who goes over before you as a consuming fire is the LORD your God. He will destroy them and subdue them before you. So you shall drive them out and make them perish quickly, as the LORD has promised you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear, O Israel: you are to cross over the Jordan today, to go in to dispossess nations greater and mightier than you, cities great and fortified up to heaven, a people great and tall, the sons of the Anakim, whom you know, and of whom you have heard it said, “Who can stand before the sons of Anak?”

Moses is quoting the spies’ report back at them. Fortified up to heaven is the exact phrase from 1:28, and the sons of the Anakim is the terror that broke the last generation. He does not deny a word of it. He repeats it, and adds a proverb the nations evidently used — who can stand before the sons of Anak?

Notice how Scripture handles fear here. Moses’ method is never to shrink the obstacle. He grants the whole report, in the strongest language available, and then says: Know therefore today that he who goes over before you as a consuming fire is the LORD your God.

The comparison decides it. Set the Anakim against Israel and the proverb is right; nobody can stand before them. Set them against a consuming fire and the question does not arise. The last generation did the first sum and got a true answer to the wrong question.

And note the pace of the verse: he will destroy them and subdue them before you, so that you shall drive them out and make them perish quickly. God will do it; Israel will do it. Both, in one sentence, without any sense of contradiction — which is how Scripture always speaks about the work of God and the work of his people.

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not say in your heart, after the LORD your God has thrust them out before you, 'It is because of my righteousness that the LORD has brought me in to possess this land,' whereas it is because of the wickedness of these nations that the LORD is driving them out before you. Not because of your righteousness or the uprightness of your heart are you going in to possess their land, but because of the wickedness of these nations the LORD your God is driving them out from before you, and that he may confirm the word that the LORD swore to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob. "Know, therefore, that the LORD your God is not giving you this good land to possess because of your righteousness, for you are a stubborn people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now the point of the chapter, made three times in three verses because Moses knows exactly what victory does to people.

Do not say in your heart, after the LORD your God has thrust them out before you, “It is because of my righteousness that the LORD has brought me in to possess this land.”

Not because of your righteousness or the uprightness of your heart are you going in to possess their land.

Know, therefore, that the LORD your God is not giving you this good land to possess because of your righteousness, for you are a stubborn people.

Three times, with the ground cut away more sharply each time, and ending in a flat insult. You are a stubborn people — literally, hard of neck, the image of an ox that will not turn under the yoke.

Notice when the temptation comes: after the LORD your God has thrust them out. Not before. It is success that produces this, not failure — the same pattern as chapter 8, where the danger was a full stomach. A man who has just watched God do something remarkable through him is in far more spiritual danger than a man who has just failed.

And Moses gives the two actual reasons, and neither is Israel. First, the wickedness of these nations — this is judgment on Canaan, not reward for Israel. Second, that he may confirm the word that the LORD swore to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob — God is keeping an old promise to men centuries dead.

Which leaves nothing at all on Israel’s side of the ledger. And that is the doctrine of grace, stated in the Pentateuch as plainly as Paul ever states it: not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy (Titus 3:5). Every Christian who has begun to feel that his standing with God has something to do with how the last few months have gone should read these three verses slowly.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–14 — The Golden Calf: Provoking God to Wrath
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses recounts how, even at Horeb while he received the covenant, Israel made the golden calf and provoked God so greatly that he threatened to destroy them and make a nation of Moses instead.
verseByVerse.theology: Sin runs deep even in God’s redeemed people; their history is one of rebellion, proving that grace alone, not merit, secures their standing.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel sinned at the very mountain of covenant. Now: even in our most privileged moments we are prone to wander, exposing our need of grace.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember and do not forget how you provoked the LORD your God to wrath in the wilderness. From the day you came out of the land of Egypt until you came to this place, you have been rebellious against the LORD. Even at Horeb you provoked the LORD to wrath, and the LORD was so angry with you that he was ready to destroy you. When I went up the mountain to receive the tablets of stone, the tablets of the covenant that the LORD made with you, I remained on the mountain forty days and forty nights. I neither ate bread nor drank water. And the LORD gave me the two tablets of stone written with the finger of God, and on them were all the words that the LORD had spoken with you on the mountain out of the midst of the fire on the day of the assembly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remember and do not forget how you provoked the LORD your God to wrath in the wilderness.

In chapter 8 Moses told them to remember what God had done for them. Here he tells them to remember what they had done to God, and the two disciplines belong together. A memory that keeps only the mercies produces sentimentality; a memory that keeps only the failures produces despair. Israel is to hold both.

And then the summary, which is devastating: From the day you came out of the land of Egypt until you came to this place, you have been rebellious against the LORD. The whole period. Not a bad patch — the entire national history to date.

Then the setting, and the timing is what makes the story unbearable. When I went up the mountain to receive the tablets of stone, the tablets of the covenant that the LORD made with you, I remained on the mountain forty days and forty nights. I neither ate bread nor drank water.

Forty days on a mountain without food while God writes the covenant with his own finger. And at the foot of that same mountain, during those same forty days, the nation is casting a calf.

That is the shape of it. The covenant was being broken while it was being written. Not afterwards, when the memory had faded and the generations had turned — while the ink was wet, by people who had heard the voice from the fire six weeks earlier and had said all that the LORD has spoken we will do (Exod. 19:8).

verseByVerse.quote: And at the end of forty days and forty nights the LORD gave me the two tablets of stone, the tablets of the covenant. Then the LORD said to me, 'Arise, go down quickly from here, for your people whom you have brought from Egypt have acted corruptly. They have turned aside quickly out of the way that I commanded them; they have made themselves a metal image.' "Furthermore, the LORD said to me, 'I have seen this people, and behold, it is a stubborn people. Let me alone, that I may destroy them and blot out their name from under heaven. And I will make of you a nation mightier and greater than they.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s words to Moses on the mountain are abrupt and terrible. Arise, go down quickly from here, for your people whom you have brought from Egypt have acted corruptly.

Hear the pronouns. Your people, whom you brought out. God hands them back to Moses. It is the language of a man disowning something — the way a father says your son to his wife when the boy has disgraced himself.

And then: Let me alone, that I may destroy them and blot out their name from under heaven. And I will make of you a nation mightier and greater than they.

Two things in that offer. The first is that it is genuine, and it is everything Moses could have wanted: a fresh start, a nation from his own line, no more of these people. Every leader who has ever been ground down by the people he leads knows what is being dangled here.

The second is the extraordinary phrase let me alone. Why would the Almighty say that to a man on a mountain? He is not being restrained by Moses; nothing restrains God. He says it because it is an invitation dressed as a prohibition. To tell somebody do not hold me back is to inform them that they can — and Moses, who knew God better than anyone alive, heard it exactly that way and immediately began to hold him back.

That is a remarkable window into how God deals with intercessors. He tells a man what he is about to do in terms that all but invite the man to plead against it. Abraham had the same experience over Sodom — Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do? (Gen. 18:17) — and did exactly the same thing with it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–21 — Moses Breaks the Tablets and Destroys the Calf
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses descends, sees the calf, shatters the tablets before their eyes, and grinds the idol to powder; he recalls his fervent intercession even for Aaron.
verseByVerse.theology: The broken tablets dramatize the broken covenant; sin shatters our relationship with God, and the idol is utterly destroyed, for God tolerates no rivals.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Moses ground the calf to dust. Now: the Christian must utterly destroy cherished idols, not merely set them aside.

verseByVerse.quote: So I turned and came down from the mountain, and the mountain was burning with fire. And the two tablets of the covenant were in my two hands. And I looked, and behold, you had sinned against the LORD your God. You had made yourselves a golden calf. You had turned aside quickly from the way that the LORD had commanded you. So I took hold of the two tablets and threw them out of my two hands and broke them before your eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I turned and came down from the mountain, and the mountain was burning with fire. And the two tablets of the covenant were in my two hands.

Picture the descent. A mountain on fire behind him, and in his arms the two stones that God had written on. He is carrying the most valuable objects that have ever existed.

And I looked, and behold, you had sinned against the LORD your God. You had made yourselves a golden calf. You had turned aside quickly from the way that the LORD had commanded you.

Quickly. That is the word that stings. Not after a generation of drift — within weeks, while the man who led them out was still up the hill.

And then: So I took hold of the two tablets and threw them out of my two hands and broke them before your eyes.

This is often read as Moses losing his temper, and there is certainly anger in it. But the detail before your eyes shows what it actually was. He did not drop them on the path where nobody was looking. He smashed them in front of the whole nation, deliberately, as an act of public testimony — because in the ancient world a covenant document was destroyed when the covenant was broken. Moses was not throwing a tantrum. He was showing them what they had already done.

The tablets were the marriage certificate, and he tore it up in front of the bride, on the day, while the other man was still in the house.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I lay prostrate before the LORD as before, forty days and forty nights. I neither ate bread nor drank water, because of all the sin that you had committed, in doing what was evil in the sight of the LORD to provoke him to anger. For I was afraid of the anger and hot displeasure that the LORD bore against you, so that he was ready to destroy you. But the LORD listened to me that time also. And the LORD was so angry with Aaron that he was ready to destroy him. And I prayed for Aaron also at the same time. Then I took the sinful thing, the calf that you had made, and burned it with fire and crushed it, grinding it very small, until it was as fine as dust. And I threw the dust of it into the brook that ran down from the mountain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What Moses does next is the greatest thing about him.

Then I lay prostrate before the LORD as before, forty days and forty nights. I neither ate bread nor drank water, because of all the sin that you had committed.

Forty more days without food. He has just come down from forty days on the mountain, and he goes straight back down onto his face for another forty — not for himself, and not to receive anything, but because of what they had done. Eighty days of fasting inside about three months, on behalf of people who had betrayed him and God while he was away.

And verse 19 lets us see inside him: For I was afraid of the anger and hot displeasure that the LORD bore against you. He was frightened. Not for himself — God had just offered him a dynasty — but for them. Then five words that carry the whole chapter: But the LORD listened to me that time also.

Verse 20 adds a detail easy to skip and impossible to forget once seen: And the LORD was so angry with Aaron that he was ready to destroy him. And I prayed for Aaron also. Aaron — his own brother, the high priest, the man who actually made the calf and then lied about it. That is the man Moses prayed for, and Israel has a priesthood at all because he did.

Then the disposal of the idol, described with a kind of grim thoroughness: I took the sinful thing, the calf that you had made, and burned it with fire and crushed it, grinding it very small, until it was as fine as dust. And I threw the dust of it into the brook. Burned, crushed, ground to powder, and poured into running water so it could not be gathered again. There is a way of dealing with an idol that leaves nothing to come back to, and it is the only way that works.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–29 — Moses’ Great Intercession: For Your Name’s Sake
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses recalls Israel’s repeated rebellions and recounts his prayer that God spare the people not for their sake but for the sake of his name, his promise to the fathers, and his great redemption.
verseByVerse.theology: Effective intercession appeals not to human merit but to God’s name, promise, and redemptive work; Moses foreshadows Christ’s perfect intercession.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Moses pleaded God’s glory and promise. Now: we pray and are heard not on our worthiness but on the merit and intercession of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "At Taberah also, and at Massah and at Kibroth-hattaavah you provoked the LORD to wrath. And when the LORD sent you from Kadesh-barnea, saying, 'Go up and take possession of the land that I have given you,' then you rebelled against the commandment of the LORD your God and did not believe him or obey his voice. You have been rebellious against the LORD from the day that I knew you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses now runs through the list, and it is a geography of failure. At Taberah also, and at Massah and at Kibroth-hattaavah you provoked the LORD to wrath.

Every name is a place where something went wrong. Taberah, burning, where the fire of the LORD fell on the outskirts of the camp. Massah, testing, where they asked whether the LORD was among them or not. Kibroth-hattaavah, the graves of craving, where they demanded meat and were buried in it. Israel’s route across the wilderness is marked by place-names that are all confessions.

And then the worst one, Kadesh-barnea, described in a single sentence that gets to the root: you rebelled against the commandment of the LORD your God and did not believe him or obey his voice. Believe and obey, in that order, with the failure of the first producing the failure of the second.

Then the summary: You have been rebellious against the LORD from the day that I knew you.

From the day that I knew you. Moses has been with these people for forty years, and this is his assessment of the whole span. He is not exaggerating for effect; the previous chapters are the evidence. And it is precisely this honest, unflattering account of God’s own people that makes the next paragraph what it is. Nobody could read Deuteronomy 9 and conclude that Israel deserved to be saved.

verseByVerse.quote: "So I lay prostrate before the LORD for these forty days and forty nights, because the LORD had said he would destroy you. And I prayed to the LORD, 'O Lord GOD, do not destroy your people and your heritage, whom you have redeemed through your greatness, whom you have brought out of Egypt with a mighty hand. Remember your servants, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Do not regard the stubbornness of this people, or their wickedness or their sin, lest the land from which you brought us say, "Because the LORD was not able to bring them into the land that he promised them, and because he hated them, he has brought them out to put them to death in the wilderness." For they are your people and your heritage, whom you brought out by your great power and by your outstretched arm.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And here is the prayer itself, and it is a masterclass in how to intercede.

Look first at what Moses does not say. He does not argue that the people are better than they look; he has just spent eighteen verses proving the opposite. He does not promise they will improve. He does not mention his own record, or the dynasty he has been offered. Every single argument he makes is about God.

First: do not destroy your people and your heritage, whom you have redeemed through your greatness, whom you have brought out of Egypt with a mighty hand. He gives back the pronouns God had taken away. God had said your people, whom you brought out; Moses says your people, whom you redeemed. That is the whole hinge of the prayer, and it is done in one word.

Second: Remember your servants, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. He appeals to a promise made centuries before any of these sinners existed.

Third: Do not regard the stubbornness of this people, or their wickedness or their sin. He does not deny any of the three. He asks God not to look at them — which is precisely what a man asks when he has no case at all.

Fourth, and most boldly: lest the land from which you brought us say, “Because the LORD was not able to bring them into the land that he promised them, and because he hated them, he has brought them out to put them to death in the wilderness.” He puts God’s reputation on the table. Egypt will conclude either that you could not finish what you started, or that you never loved them.

That is how a man prays when there is nothing to plead on his side of the account. He appeals to what God has already done, to what God has already promised, and to who God is — and it works, because those are the only things that ever have. And a greater Intercessor prays on exactly the same ground: not that we deserve to be kept, but that we were bought. Consequently, he is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them (Heb. 7:25).

9.theology:
Salvation by grace alone, not righteousness. Three times Moses insists the land is given “not because of your righteousness, for you are a stubborn people” (9:5–6). God blesses the undeserving for his own name’s sake and his promise to the fathers. This is the Old Testament foundation of justification by grace, fulfilled in the gospel: “not because of works, so that no one may boast” (Eph 2:9).

The depth of human sin. Israel’s whole history was rebellion — “from the day that I knew you” (9:24) — climaxing in the golden calf at the very mountain of covenant. Honest remembrance of our sin guards against pride and magnifies grace; we are more sinful than we dare admit, yet more loved than we dare hope.

The mediator who intercedes. Moses lay prostrate forty days, pleading not Israel’s merit but God’s name, promise, and redemption (9:18, 25–29). He foreshadows the greater Mediator, Christ, who “always lives to make intercession” (Heb 7:25) on the ground of his own perfect sacrifice.
9.examples:
Then: On the brink of conquest, Israel was warned never to credit their own righteousness, for they were a stubborn people whose whole history — climaxing in the golden calf — was rebellion, and who survived only because Moses lay prostrate forty days, interceding on the ground of God’s name and promise.

Now: We are saved not by our righteousness but by Christ’s, lest any should boast. Honest remembrance of our own rebellion keeps us humble and grateful, and we grind our idols to dust rather than negotiate with them. And we pray with confidence — not because we deserve to be heard, but because our great Mediator ever lives to intercede for us on the ground of his own perfect, finished work.

10.title: Circumcise Your Hearts: What Does the LORD Require of You?
10.text: <sup>1</sup>"At that time the LORD said to me, 'Cut for yourself two tablets of stone like the first, and come up to me on the mountain and make an ark of wood.<sup>2</sup>And I will write on the tablets the words that were on the first tablets that you broke, and you shall put them in the ark.'<sup>3</sup>So I made an ark of acacia wood, and cut two tablets of stone like the first, and went up the mountain with the two tablets in my hand.<sup>4</sup>And he wrote on the tablets, in the same writing as before, the Ten Commandments that the LORD had spoken to you on the mountain out of the midst of the fire on the day of the assembly. And the LORD gave them to me.<sup>5</sup>Then I turned and came down from the mountain and put the tablets in the ark that I had made. And there they are, as the LORD commanded me."<sup>6</sup>(The people of Israel journeyed from Beeroth Bene-jaakan to Moserah. There Aaron died, and there he was buried. And his son Eleazar ministered as priest in his place.<sup>7</sup>From there they journeyed to Gudgodah, and from Gudgodah to Jotbathah, a land with brooks of water.<sup>8</sup>At that time the LORD set apart the tribe of Levi to carry the ark of the covenant of the LORD to stand before the LORD to minister to him and to bless in his name, to this day.<sup>9</sup>Therefore Levi has no portion or inheritance with his brothers. The LORD is his inheritance, as the LORD your God said to him.)<sup>10</sup>"I myself stayed on the mountain, as at the first time, forty days and forty nights, and the LORD listened to me that time also. The LORD was unwilling to destroy you.<sup>11</sup>And the LORD said to me, 'Arise, go on your journey at the head of the people, so that they may go in and possess the land, which I swore to their fathers to give them.'<sup>12</sup>"And now, Israel, what does the LORD your God require of you, but to fear the LORD your God, to walk in all his ways, to love him, to serve the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul,<sup>13</sup>and to keep the commandments and statutes of the LORD, which I am commanding you today for your good?<sup>14</sup>Behold, to the LORD your God belong heaven and the heaven of heavens, the earth with all that is in it.<sup>15</sup>Yet the LORD set his heart in love on your fathers and chose their offspring after them, you above all peoples, as you are this day.<sup>16</sup>Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no longer stubborn.<sup>17</sup>For the LORD your God is God of gods and Lord of lords, the great, the mighty, and the awesome God, who is not partial and takes no bribe.<sup>18</sup>He executes justice for the fatherless and the widow, and loves the sojourner, giving him food and clothing.<sup>19</sup>Love the sojourner, therefore, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt.<sup>20</sup>You shall fear the LORD your God. You shall serve him and hold fast to him, and by his name you shall swear.<sup>21</sup>He is your praise. He is your God, who has done for you these great and terrifying things that your eyes have seen.<sup>22</sup>Your fathers went down to Egypt seventy persons, and now the LORD your God has made you as numerous as the stars of heaven.
10.overview:
Chapter 10 moves from the rehearsal of rebellion to the renewal of relationship. God graciously gives new tablets of stone, restoring the covenant Israel had shattered — a vivid picture of grace that rewrites what sin destroyed. The ark is made to house the tablets, and the Levites are set apart for service.

Then the chapter rises to one of the great summary statements of true religion: “And now, Israel, what does the LORD your God require of you, but to fear the LORD your God, to walk in all his ways, to love him, to serve the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul” (10:12). Here is the heart of covenant life distilled — fear, walk, love, serve. Micah 6:8 will echo it; the whole of true religion is summed in reverent, loving, wholehearted devotion.

At the center stands a command that the whole Bible will unfold: “Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart” (10:16). External religion is not enough; the stubborn heart itself must be cut, changed, renewed. This is the great cry that the new covenant will answer (30:6; Jer 31:33; Ezek 36:26).

The chapter also reveals the heart of God himself: the mighty Creator who owns heaven and earth is the One who loves the sojourner, executes justice for the fatherless and the widow, and set his love on Israel’s fathers. The God of glory is the God of compassion, and his people are to love as he loves.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — New Tablets: Grace Rewrites the Covenant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God commands Moses to cut new tablets, rewrites the Ten Commandments upon them, and has them placed in the ark — restoring the covenant Israel had broken.
verseByVerse.theology: God graciously restores the covenant his people shattered; grace rewrites what sin destroyed and preserves his word among his people.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: God renewed the broken covenant on new stone. Now: in Christ, God restores what our sin breaks and writes his law on hearts of flesh.

verseByVerse.quote: "At that time the LORD said to me, 'Cut for yourself two tablets of stone like the first, and come up to me on the mountain and make an ark of wood. And I will write on the tablets the words that were on the first tablets that you broke, and you shall put them in the ark.' So I made an ark of acacia wood, and cut two tablets of stone like the first, and went up the mountain with the two tablets in my hand. And he wrote on the tablets, in the same writing as before, the Ten Commandments that the LORD had spoken to you on the mountain out of the midst of the fire on the day of the assembly. And the LORD gave them to me. Then I turned and came down from the mountain and put the tablets in the ark that I had made. And there they are, as the LORD commanded me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Chapter 9 ended with a smashed covenant and a man on his face for forty days. Chapter 10 opens with God’s answer, and it is the plainest picture of grace in the Pentateuch.

Cut for yourself two tablets of stone like the first, and come up to me on the mountain… And I will write on the tablets the words that were on the first tablets that you broke.

Take the sequence in. Israel broke the covenant while it was being written. Moses broke the tablets in front of them to show what they had done. And God says: cut two more, and bring them up, and I will write the same words again.

Not different words. Not reduced terms, not a lower standard for a people who have proved they cannot keep the higher one. The words that were on the first tablets. God begins again at exactly the point where they failed, with exactly the same demand.

And notice who does what. Moses cuts the stone; God does the writing. Man can prepare the tablets; only God can put anything on them worth having. That distinction will matter enormously six verses from now, when the subject changes from stone to hearts.

Then the ark — a plain wooden box, made to hold the second set of tablets. The most sacred object in Israel’s history existed to house the evidence of a covenant that had been broken before the ink dried, and God chose to sit above it on the mercy seat and speak from there (Num. 7:89). The broken law under the blood-covered lid is the whole gospel in a piece of furniture.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–11 — The Levites Set Apart; Moses Prevails
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A brief travel note records Aaron's death and Eleazar's succession, the setting apart of the Levites to carry the ark and minister, and God's renewed command for Moses to lead the people onward to the land.
verseByVerse.theology: God provides ordered ministry to carry his word and bless his people; the Levites' inheritance is the LORD himself.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the Levites bore the ark and ministered before God. Now: God appoints servants to carry and proclaim his word, whose true inheritance is God himself.

verseByVerse.quote: (The people of Israel journeyed from Beeroth Bene-jaakan to Moserah. There Aaron died, and there he was buried. And his son Eleazar ministered as priest in his place. From there they journeyed to Gudgodah, and from Gudgodah to Jotbathah, a land with brooks of water. At that time the LORD set apart the tribe of Levi to carry the ark of the covenant of the LORD to stand before the LORD to minister to him and to bless in his name, to this day. Therefore Levi has no portion or inheritance with his brothers. The LORD is his inheritance, as the LORD your God said to him.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A short travel note interrupts the sermon — Aaron’s death at Moserah, Eleazar succeeding him — and then, almost in passing, comes one of the great sentences of the Old Testament.

At that time the LORD set apart the tribe of Levi to carry the ark of the covenant of the LORD, to stand before the LORD to minister to him and to bless in his name… Therefore Levi has no portion or inheritance with his brothers. The LORD is his inheritance.

Three duties: carry, stand, bless. Levi carries the ark on the road, stands before God when the camp settles, and pronounces the blessing over the people. And then the consequence, and it is stated as a therefore: because of that, Levi gets no land.

Picture the day the country was divided. Eleven tribes walk away holding a map — this ridge, that valley, the olive terraces, the boundary stone with a grandfather’s name cut into it. Levi is handed nothing. No acres, no deed, no fence, nothing to leave a son.

And instead: The LORD is his inheritance.

Now run the test that verse invites, because it is the sharpest one in Deuteronomy. Suppose you were given everything you have ever wanted — the health returned, the debts cleared, the people you have buried given back — and God himself were not there. Would that be heaven? A man who has to think about it has learned something about where his treasure actually is. Asaph arrived at the same place from the other direction, after nearly losing his faith over the prosperity of the wicked: Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you… God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever (Ps. 73:25–26).

And here is the comfort on the reverse side. Every acre those eleven tribes received could be taken from them, and eventually was — by drought, by debt, by Assyria, by time. A portion that is God cannot be repossessed. Levi held the only inheritance in Israel that no invading army could reach.

verseByVerse.quote: "I myself stayed on the mountain, as at the first time, forty days and forty nights, and the LORD listened to me that time also. The LORD was unwilling to destroy you. And the LORD said to me, 'Arise, go on your journey at the head of the people, so that they may go in and possess the land, which I swore to their fathers to give them.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses returns to the mountain: I myself stayed on the mountain, as at the first time, forty days and forty nights, and the LORD listened to me that time also. The LORD was unwilling to destroy you.

Then the instruction that follows: Arise, go on your journey at the head of the people, that they may go in and possess the land.

Put those two verses side by side and see what has happened. God had said, six weeks earlier, let me alone, that I may destroy them. Now he says: get up and take them into the land I promised. Nothing about the people has changed. The calf is still ground to powder in a stream; the same men are still in the camp. What stands between the two sentences is forty days of a man lying on his face.

And the phrase in the middle is one to keep: the LORD was unwilling to destroy you. Not unable, and not persuaded against his will. Unwilling. When it came to it, he did not want to. The intercession was real and God answered it, and behind the answer was a disposition that had been there all along.

That is the God Moses knew, and it is the reason he dared to pray as he did in chapter 9. A man does not lie on the ground for forty days pleading with somebody he thinks is looking for an excuse to destroy.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–13 — What Does the LORD Require?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses sums up the whole of covenant life in a single sweeping question and answer: to fear, walk in, love, and serve the LORD with all the heart and soul, keeping his commandments for their own good.
verseByVerse.theology: True religion is summed in reverent, loving, wholehearted devotion to God; his commandments are for our good, not our harm.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel's whole duty was distilled into fearing, loving, and serving God. Now: the same fourfold call defines the Christian life, fulfilled in love for God in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, Israel, what does the LORD your God require of you, but to fear the LORD your God, to walk in all his ways, to love him, to serve the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul, and to keep the commandments and statutes of the LORD, which I am commanding you today for your good?
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now, Israel, what does the LORD your God require of you?

After all the history and all the warnings, Moses asks the question directly and then answers it in one sentence. It is one of the great summaries in the Old Testament, and Micah will later write a companion to it (Mic. 6:8).

Five things: to fear the LORD your God, to walk in all his ways, to love him, to serve the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul, and to keep the commandments and statutes of the LORD.

Notice how they run. It begins with the heart’s posture — fear, reverent awe. It ends with actual obedience — keep the commandments. And in the middle, holding the two ends together: love him, and serve him with all your heart and with all your soul. Deuteronomy will not let awe, love, service and obedience be separated. Awe without love is terror; love without obedience is sentiment; obedience without either is drudgery.

And then the phrase that changes the register of the whole list: which I am commanding you today for your good.

That is God’s own account of why he gives commandments. Not to establish his authority, which needs no establishing. Not to make life narrow. For their good. Every command in this book is addressed to their flourishing — which is the precise point the serpent contradicted in Eden and which the human heart has doubted ever since.

The word require can mislead a modern ear, as if this were a fee. Read the whole question again with verse 13 attached and it turns into something else entirely: what does God ask of you, other than the things that are for your good?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–15 — Heaven Belongs to God, Yet He Set His Love on You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Though the highest heavens and the earth belong to God, he set his affection on Israel's fathers and chose their offspring above all peoples.
verseByVerse.theology: The God who owns all things freely chose to love a particular people; election magnifies the condescension of sovereign grace.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the Lord of all set his love on Israel. Now: the God who needs nothing set his love on us in Christ, a wonder of sheer grace.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, to the LORD your God belong heaven and the heaven of heavens, the earth with all that is in it. Yet the LORD set his heart in love on your fathers and chose their offspring after them, you above all peoples, as you are this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now a sentence whose logic takes the breath away.

Behold, to the LORD your God belong heaven and the heaven of heavens, the earth with all that is in it. Yet the LORD set his heart in love on your fathers and chose their offspring after them, you above all peoples.

The first verse establishes the scale. The heaven of heavens is a Hebrew superlative — the highest heaven, everything above and beyond what anybody can see. All of it is his, along with the earth and its entire contents. He lacks nothing and needs nobody.

And then: yet.

The God who owns the heaven of heavens set his heart on a family of nomads and their descendants. Not because he needed them; the previous verse rules that out completely. Not because they were impressive; chapter 9 rules that out. He set his heart in love on them, and the word for set his heart is a word of attachment, of desire, of being drawn.

This is where the doctrine of election stops being an abstraction. The problem people have with it is usually the fear that God chose arbitrarily, like a man picking a number. What Deuteronomy says is that he chose in love — which is not arbitrary at all, but is also not explicable by anything in the chosen. That is exactly what love is like when it is not a response to merit. Nobody asks a man why he loves his own child and expects a list of the child’s qualifications.

And the same astonishment runs through the New Testament in the same shape: See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are (1 John 3:1). The wonder is never that God is loving in general. It is that he settled it on these particular people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–22 — Circumcise Your Hearts; Love as God Loves
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses calls Israel to circumcise their hearts and be no longer stubborn, for their God is the great, impartial, just God who loves the sojourner; they too must love the sojourner and cling to him alone.
verseByVerse.theology: External religion is not enough; the heart itself must be cut and changed. The character of God — just, impartial, compassionate — is the pattern for his people's love.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel was called to inward circumcision. Now: the new covenant gives the circumcised heart, and we love the outsider because God first loved us.

verseByVerse.quote: Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no longer stubborn.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no longer stubborn.

Circumcision was the physical mark of the covenant, cut into the body of every Israelite male on the eighth day. It was the sign that a man belonged to God’s people, and it was visible to nobody. And Moses now takes that sign and turns it inward.

The image is deliberately shocking. There is something in the human heart that is like an uncircumcised foreskin — a covering, a hardness, an insensitivity that has to be cut away before there can be any real belonging. Israel had the outward mark and was, God has just said, stubborn: hard of neck, and now hard of heart. A man may bear every external sign of covenant membership and be untouched underneath it.

Which is the whole burden of the prophets afterwards. Jeremiah says the nations are uncircumcised in flesh and Israel is uncircumcised in heart (Jer. 9:26). Paul says it outright to people trusting their pedigree: no one is a Jew who is merely one outwardly… circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter (Rom. 2:28–29).

But now feel the impossibility of the command. Circumcise your own heart. How? A man can be circumcised in the flesh by somebody else on the eighth day, before he can consent to anything. He cannot reach his own heart. He cannot cut away his own hardness with the very organ that is hard.

And that is exactly the point, and Deuteronomy knows it. Twenty chapters later the same verb appears with a different subject: And the LORD your God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your offspring, so that you will love the LORD your God with all your heart (30:6).

Here it is commanded; there it is promised. The command exposes what we cannot do, and the promise announces that God will do it — which is the shape of the whole Bible, and the reason Ezekiel’s great sentence sounds like the answer to this verse, because it is: I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh (Ezek. 36:26).

verseByVerse.quote: For the LORD your God is God of gods and Lord of lords, the great, the mighty, and the awesome God, who is not partial and takes no bribe. He executes justice for the fatherless and the widow, and loves the sojourner, giving him food and clothing. Love the sojourner, therefore, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the LORD your God is God of gods and Lord of lords, the great, the mighty, and the awesome God, who is not partial and takes no bribe.

Five titles piled up, and then two negatives — and it is the negatives that do the work. The God of gods is not partial; literally, he does not lift up faces. He does not look at who it is. And he takes no bribe, which in the ancient world made him unique among judges, human or divine; the gods of the nations were routinely bought with sacrifices.

And then, having established that he is beyond influence, Moses says what he actually does with his impartiality, and it is not what anyone expects.

He executes justice for the fatherless and the widow, and loves the sojourner, giving him food and clothing.

The God of gods and Lord of lords, who cannot be bribed or impressed, spends his attention on the three groups with nothing to offer him: the orphan, the widow, the foreigner. In that society those three had no legal standing, no advocate and no leverage — which is exactly why the God who is not impressed by leverage takes them up. His impartiality is not a cool neutrality. It is why he ends up on the side of the people nobody else is on the side of.

And note how practical it gets: giving him food and clothing. Not sympathy. Dinner and a coat.

Then the inference for Israel, and it is not therefore admire him: Love the sojourner, therefore, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt. The reason to love the foreigner is that you were one, and somebody came and got you.
