God’s people are to treat the outsider the way God treated them when they were outside — which is the whole logic of Christian mercy in one line, and the reason the parable of the unforgiving servant ends the way it does.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall fear the LORD your God. You shall serve him and hold fast to him, and by his name you shall swear. He is your praise. He is your God, who has done for you these great and terrifying things that your eyes have seen. Your fathers went down to Egypt seventy persons, and now the LORD your God has made you as numerous as the stars of heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends with four commands and two facts, and they are all in one breath.

You shall fear the LORD your God. You shall serve him and hold fast to him, and by his name you shall swear.

Hold fast is dabaq again — cling, stick, be glued to. The same word used of Israel at Peor, where those who clung to God were alive and those who followed Baal were in the ground (4:4). It is not a word about opinions. It is a word about grip.

Then: He is your praise. He is your God, who has done for you these great and terrifying things that your eyes have seen.

He is your praise. Not he deserves your praise — he is it. He is the thing Israel has to boast about, the whole content of anything they could say for themselves. A small nation with no army, no culture and no land had exactly one distinction, and it was not theirs.

And the last verse gives the arithmetic of it: Your fathers went down to Egypt seventy persons, and now the LORD your God has made you as numerous as the stars of heaven.

Seventy. That is a village — one extended family, seventy names listed in Genesis 46, going down into Egypt to escape a famine. Four centuries later, a nation nobody can count, standing on the border of a country God promised to a childless man who once stood outside his tent and was told to try counting the stars.

Seventy people, and a promise. That is all God started with, and he has never needed more than that. Set that beside the way the church began: a hundred and twenty in an upstairs room, and a promise.

10.theology:
Circumcise your heart. “Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart” (10:16). External religion is not enough; the stubborn heart itself must be cut and changed. The command exposes a need it cannot meet — but what is commanded here is promised in 30:6 and fulfilled in the new covenant: God himself circumcises the heart by the Spirit (Jer 31:33; Ezek 36:26; Rom 2:29).

What the LORD requires. The whole of covenant life is distilled into four verbs: to fear, walk, love, and serve God with all the heart (10:12) — and all “for your good” (10:13). Love stands at the center, holding together reverent awe and obedient service; this whole demand is met perfectly in Christ and worked in us by the Spirit.

The God who owns all yet loves the lowly. The Lord of heaven and earth, who needs nothing, set his love on a small and undeserving people (10:14–15), and the awesome God of gods executes justice for the fatherless and loves the sojourner (10:17–19). His character is the pattern of his people's love: we love the outsider because we were once outsiders loved by grace.
10.examples:
Then: God rewrote the covenant Israel had broken on new tablets, set the Levites apart with the LORD himself as their inheritance, and summoned his people to circumcise their hearts and love the sojourner as the God who owns all heaven yet loves the lowly had loved them.

Now: In Christ, God restores what our sin breaks and, by his Spirit, performs the heart-circumcision we could never do for ourselves. We hold fast to him as our portion and our praise, we love the outsider and the vulnerable because we ourselves were strangers brought near by grace, and we render the fourfold devotion — fearing, walking, loving, serving — that finds its perfection in our Lord Jesus and its joy in the God who set his heart in love on us.

11.title: Love and Obey: The Blessing and the Curse Set Before You
11.text: <sup>1</sup>"You shall therefore love the LORD your God and keep his charge, his statutes, his rules, and his commandments always.<sup>2</sup>And consider today (since I am not speaking to your children who have not known or seen it), consider the discipline of the LORD your God, his greatness, his mighty hand and his outstretched arm,<sup>3</sup>his signs and his deeds that he did in Egypt to Pharaoh the king of Egypt and to all his land,<sup>4</sup>and what he did to the army of Egypt, to their horses and to their chariots, how he made the water of the Red Sea flow over them as they pursued after you, and how the LORD has destroyed them to this day,<sup>5</sup>and what he did to you in the wilderness, until you came to this place,<sup>6</sup>and what he did to Dathan and Abiram the sons of Eliab, son of Reuben, how the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them up, with their households, their tents, and every living thing that followed them, in the midst of all Israel.<sup>7</sup>For your eyes have seen all the great work of the LORD that he did.<sup>8</sup>"You shall therefore keep the whole commandment that I command you today, that you may be strong, and go in and take possession of the land that you are going over to possess,<sup>9</sup>and that you may live long in the land that the LORD swore to your fathers to give to them and to their offspring, a land flowing with milk and honey.<sup>10</sup>For the land that you are entering to take possession of it is not like the land of Egypt, from which you have come, where you sowed your seed and irrigated it, like a garden of vegetables.<sup>11</sup>But the land that you are going over to possess is a land of hills and valleys, which drinks water by the rain from heaven,<sup>12</sup>a land that the LORD your God cares for. The eyes of the LORD your God are always upon it, from the beginning of the year to the end of the year.<sup>13</sup>"And if you will indeed obey my commandments that I command you today, to love the LORD your God, and to serve him with all your heart and with all your soul,<sup>14</sup>he will give the rain for your land in its season, the early rain and the later rain, that you may gather in your grain and your wine and your oil.<sup>15</sup>And he will give grass in your fields for your livestock, and you shall eat and be full.<sup>16</sup>Take care lest your heart be deceived, and you turn aside and serve other gods and worship them;<sup>17</sup>then the anger of the LORD will be kindled against you, and he will shut up the heavens, so that there will be no rain, and the land will yield no fruit, and you will perish quickly off the good land that the LORD is giving you.<sup>18</sup>"You shall therefore lay up these words of mine in your heart and in your soul, and you shall bind them as a sign on your hand, and they shall be as frontlets between your eyes.<sup>19</sup>You shall teach them to your children, talking of them when you are sitting in your house, and when you are walking by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise.<sup>20</sup>You shall write them on the doorposts of your house and on your gates,<sup>21</sup>that your days and the days of your children may be multiplied in the land that the LORD swore to your fathers to give them, as long as the heavens are above the earth.<sup>22</sup>For if you will be careful to do all this commandment that I command you to do, loving the LORD your God, walking in all his ways, and holding fast to him,<sup>23</sup>then the LORD will drive out all these nations before you, and you will dispossess nations greater and mightier than you.<sup>24</sup>Every place on which the sole of your foot treads shall be yours. Your territory shall be from the wilderness to the Lebanon, and from the River, the river Euphrates, to the western sea.<sup>25</sup>No one shall be able to stand against you. The LORD your God will lay the fear of you and the dread of you on all the land that you shall tread, as he promised you.<sup>26</sup>"See, I am setting before you today a blessing and a curse:<sup>27</sup>the blessing, if you obey the commandments of the LORD your God, which I command you today,<sup>28</sup>and the curse, if you do not obey the commandments of the LORD your God, but turn aside from the way that I am commanding you today, to go after other gods that you have not known.<sup>29</sup>And when the LORD your God brings you into the land that you are entering to take possession of it, you shall set the blessing on Mount Gerizim and the curse on Mount Ebal.<sup>30</sup>Are they not beyond the Jordan, west of the road, toward the going down of the sun, in the land of the Canaanites who live in the Arabah, opposite Gilgal, beside the oak of Moreh?<sup>31</sup>For you are to cross over the Jordan to go in to take possession of the land that the LORD your God is giving you. And when you possess it and live in it,<sup>32</sup>you shall be careful to do all the statutes and the rules that I am setting before you today.
11.overview:
Chapter 11 closes the second great address (chs. 5–11) and forms a hinge into the detailed laws that follow. It is a stirring call to love and obey, built on the foundation of all that has come before. Moses presses home the lessons of history — what their eyes have seen of God's mighty acts — as motivation for present obedience.

The great theme is the inseparable bond of love and obedience: “You shall therefore love the LORD your God and keep his charge… always” (11:1). To love God is to keep his commandments; obedience is the language of love. And this love, rehearsed daily and taught to children, is the secret of a long and flourishing life in the land.

Moses paints a beautiful picture of the land itself — not like Egypt, watered by human effort, but a land that “drinks water by the rain from heaven, a land that the LORD your God cares for. The eyes of the LORD your God are always upon it” (11:11–12). Israel's life will depend on daily reliance upon God's provision from heaven.

The chapter climaxes in the great choice that runs through the whole book: “See, I am setting before you today a blessing and a curse” (11:26). The blessing and the curse — fulfilled ultimately at Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal (ch. 27) and borne for us by Christ on the tree (Gal 3:13) — confront every generation with the call to choose life by loving and obeying the LORD.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Your Eyes Have Seen: Obey Because You Remember
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses calls Israel to love and obey God, appealing to what their own eyes have seen of his discipline and his mighty acts in Egypt and the wilderness.
verseByVerse.theology: Obedience flows from remembered experience of God's mighty acts; those who have seen God's power have no excuse for unbelief.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel had seen the exodus and the wilderness firsthand. Now: we obey in light of what we have seen of God's grace in Christ and in our own lives.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall therefore love the LORD your God and keep his charge, his statutes, his rules, and his commandments always. And consider today (since I am not speaking to your children who have not known or seen it), consider the discipline of the LORD your God, his greatness, his mighty hand and his outstretched arm, his signs and his deeds that he did in Egypt to Pharaoh the king of Egypt and to all his land, and what he did to the army of Egypt, to their horses and to their chariots, how he made the water of the Red Sea flow over them as they pursued after you, and how the LORD has destroyed them to this day, and what he did to you in the wilderness, until you came to this place, and what he did to Dathan and Abiram the sons of Eliab, son of Reuben, how the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them up, with their households, their tents, and every living thing that followed them, in the midst of all Israel. For your eyes have seen all the great work of the LORD that he did.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You shall therefore love the LORD your God and keep his charge, his statutes, his rules, and his commandments always.

Love and obedience are bound together in a single sentence, and Deuteronomy never separates them. Love that does not obey is sentiment; obedience that does not love is drudgery. The Lord Jesus said the same thing in the same shape: If you love me, you will keep my commandments (John 14:15).

Then Moses makes the appeal, and note who it is addressed to: your eyes have seen all the great work of the LORD that he did. He lists Egypt, the sea closing over Pharaoh’s army, the wilderness, and then the ground opening under Dathan and Abiram.

And in verse 2 he draws a careful line: I am not speaking to your children who have not known or seen it. He is addressing the men old enough to remember, and he is telling them that their memories are an obligation. They saw it; nobody else in the coming generations will. What they do with that is the difference between a nation that knows God and a nation that has heard about him.

Notice too that the list is not all mercies. Pharaoh drowned and Dathan swallowed are acts of judgment, and Moses puts them in the same sentence as the deliverance. Israel is to remember what God did for them and what he did to those who set themselves against him, and both are grounds for love. A God who never acted against evil would not be worth loving.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–17 — The Land God Cares For
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Obedience will bring long life and strength to possess the land — a land unlike Egypt, watered by rain from heaven, on which God's eyes are always set; but turning to idols will shut up the heavens.
verseByVerse.theology: God cares for his people's land and watches over it continually; daily dependence on his provision is the rhythm of covenant life, and idolatry forfeits blessing.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel depended on rain from God's hand. Now: the believer lives in daily dependence on God's provision, looking to heaven for every good gift.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall therefore keep the whole commandment that I command you today, that you may be strong, and go in and take possession of the land that you are going over to possess, and that you may live long in the land that the LORD swore to your fathers to give to them and to their offspring, a land flowing with milk and honey. For the land that you are entering to take possession of it is not like the land of Egypt, from which you have come, where you sowed your seed and irrigated it, like a garden of vegetables. But the land that you are going over to possess is a land of hills and valleys, which drinks water by the rain from heaven, a land that the LORD your God cares for. The eyes of the LORD your God are always upon it, from the beginning of the year to the end of the year.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now one of the loveliest contrasts in the Old Testament, and it turns on how two countries get their water.

For the land that you are entering to take possession of it is not like the land of Egypt, from which you have come, where you sowed your seed and irrigated it, like a garden of vegetables. But the land that you are going over to possess is a land of hills and valleys, which drinks water by the rain from heaven.

Egypt was watered by the Nile. It is one of the most reliable agricultural systems the world has ever known — a river that floods on schedule every year, and a network of channels and foot-pumps to move the water where you want it. An Egyptian farmer did not pray for rain. He dug, and the river came, and the crop grew. Water was a matter of engineering.

Canaan is hills. There is no great river; the water falls out of the sky or it does not, and no amount of digging will produce a drop. A farmer in those hills looked up rather than across, every year, twice a year, and could do nothing whatever about it.

God is deliberately moving his people from a country where they could manage their own supply to one where they could not. That is not a downgrade; it is the whole point. And he says so in the next verse: a land that the LORD your God cares for. The eyes of the LORD your God are always upon it, from the beginning of the year to the end of the year.

Israel is being moved into permanent dependence, and told that this is what being cared for looks like. Anyone whose circumstances have become less controllable than they used to be should hold on to that. The Nile is easier. The hills are where you learn to look up.

verseByVerse.quote: "And if you will indeed obey my commandments that I command you today, to love the LORD your God, and to serve him with all your heart and with all your soul, he will give the rain for your land in its season, the early rain and the later rain, that you may gather in your grain and your wine and your oil. And he will give grass in your fields for your livestock, and you shall eat and be full. Take care lest your heart be deceived, and you turn aside and serve other gods and worship them; then the anger of the LORD will be kindled against you, and he will shut up the heavens, so that there will be no rain, and the land will yield no fruit, and you will perish quickly off the good land that the LORD is giving you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The promise attached to obedience is rain: he will give the rain for your land in its season, the early rain and the later rain — the autumn rain that softened the ground for ploughing and the spring rain that filled the grain. Miss either and the year fails.

And then the warning, and it is precisely calibrated to the geography just described: take care lest your heart be deceived, and you turn aside and serve other gods… then the anger of the LORD will be kindled against you, and he will shut up the heavens, so that there will be no rain.

Consider why that threat bites in Canaan and would have meant nothing in Egypt. The gods of the land Israel was entering were fertility gods; Baal was the storm god, the lord of rain, and every Canaanite farmer knew what you did in a dry spring. So God says: the rain is mine, and if you go to Baal for it I will stop it. He will meet them on the exact ground of the temptation.

Which is what happened. Centuries later Elijah stood in front of Ahab and said there shall be neither dew nor rain these years, except by my word (1 Kgs. 17:1), and three and a half years afterwards four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal spent a whole day on Carmel trying to get their storm god to light a fire. Deuteronomy 11:17 is the text Elijah was standing on.

And note the phrase lest your heart be deceived. Not lest you rebel. Nobody in Israel intended to abandon God for Baal; they meant to keep both, and add a little insurance for the harvest. Idolatry usually arrives as a supplement rather than a replacement.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–25 — Lay Up These Words; Teach Your Children
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses repeats the Shema's instructions to lay up God's words in heart and soul, teach them to children, and write them on doorposts, promising that wholehearted love and obedience will secure the land against all enemies.
verseByVerse.theology: God's word must saturate heart and home across generations; faithful devotion brings God's power against every foe.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel was to weave God's word into daily life and pass it on. Now: Christian discipleship saturates the home and is handed to the next generation.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall therefore lay up these words of mine in your heart and in your soul, and you shall bind them as a sign on your hand, and they shall be as frontlets between your eyes. You shall teach them to your children, talking of them when you are sitting in your house, and when you are walking by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise. You shall write them on the doorposts of your house and on your gates, that your days and the days of your children may be multiplied in the land that the LORD swore to your fathers to give them, as long as the heavens are above the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses now repeats the instructions of the Shema almost word for word — lay up these words in your heart, bind them on your hand, teach them to your children, sitting, walking, lying down, rising, doorposts, gates.

He said all of this five chapters ago. He says it again here, and a preacher who repeats himself at that length is not running out of material. He is doing what he told them to do: teach them diligently, which is the verb for sharpening a blade — the same edge, gone over again.

But there is one addition, and it is at the end: that your days and the days of your children may be multiplied in the land that the LORD swore to your fathers to give them, as long as the heavens are above the earth.

That last clause was not in chapter 6. As long as the heavens are above the earth — the promise is measured against the permanence of the sky. And the mechanism by which it reaches that far is not a monument or an institution. It is parents talking to children in the kitchen and on the road.

Which is a striking thing to put next to a phrase about the heavens. God has tied the long-term future of his people in the land to the most fragile-looking arrangement imaginable — ordinary households keeping up an ordinary conversation. And it is not fragile; it is the only thing that has ever worked. Institutions preserve documents. Families transmit faith.

verseByVerse.quote: For if you will be careful to do all this commandment that I command you to do, loving the LORD your God, walking in all his ways, and holding fast to him, then the LORD will drive out all these nations before you, and you will dispossess nations greater and mightier than you. Every place on which the sole of your foot treads shall be yours. Your territory shall be from the wilderness to the Lebanon, and from the River, the river Euphrates, to the western sea. No one shall be able to stand against you. The LORD your God will lay the fear of you and the dread of you on all the land that you shall tread, as he promised you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if you will be careful to do all this commandment that I command you to do, loving the LORD your God, walking in all his ways, and holding fast to him, then the LORD will drive out all these nations before you.

Three verbs describe the whole life with God, and they recur through this book like a refrain: loving, walking, holding fast. Affection, direction, and grip. Take away the first and you have mere religion; the second, and you have feeling without a life; the third, and you have somebody who lets go the moment it costs.

And the promise attached is extravagant: Every place on which the sole of your foot treads shall be yours… No one shall be able to stand against you. Territory measured by where they actually walk. God gives it, and they still have to put their feet on it.

Then verse 25: The LORD your God will lay the fear of you and the dread of you upon all the land that you shall tread. The war would be won in the minds of Canaan before Israel arrived, and Rahab confirms it from inside: the fear of you has fallen upon us… our hearts melted (Josh. 2:9, 11).

Note carefully that this is a national promise under a specific covenant, and it is not a formula for a Christian’s circumstances. God has not undertaken that every believer who loves and walks and holds fast will find every enemy retreating; the New Testament says something rather different about that, and the men who wrote it were mostly executed. What does carry across is the last clause of the paragraph — that the outcome does not finally depend on the size of what is in front of you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–32 — The Blessing and the Curse Set Before You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses sets before Israel the great choice — a blessing for obedience and a curse for disobedience — to be proclaimed at Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal when they enter the land.
verseByVerse.theology: Every generation faces the decisive choice between blessing and curse, life and death; the curse for disobedience is ultimately borne by Christ (Gal 3:13).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel faced the choice of blessing or curse at Gerizim and Ebal. Now: the gospel sets before us life in Christ, who bore the curse so we might receive the blessing.

verseByVerse.quote: "See, I am setting before you today a blessing and a curse: the blessing, if you obey the commandments of the LORD your God, which I command you today, and the curse, if you do not obey the commandments of the LORD your God, but turn aside from the way that I am commanding you today, to go after other gods that you have not known.
verseByVerse.commentary:
See, I am setting before you today a blessing and a curse.

Here is the spine of the whole book, and it will run all the way to chapter 30, where Moses says it for the last time with everything at stake: I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse. Therefore choose life (30:19).

Two things about the way it is put. First, the word See — literally Behold, look. Moses is not describing an abstraction. He is holding two things up in front of a crowd and telling them to look at what is in his hands.

Second, and more searching: there is no third option. He does not set before them a blessing, a curse, and a comfortable middle where a person might live without deciding. That middle does not exist in Deuteronomy, and it does not exist anywhere else in Scripture either. Whoever is not with me is against me (Matt. 12:30) is the same sentence in a different century.

And notice what the curse is attached to: if you do not obey… but turn aside from the way that I am commanding you today, to go after other gods that you have not known. The alternative to God is never simply nothing. A man who turns aside from the way does not stand still in an empty field; he goes after something, and the text is candid about what it will be — gods that you have not known, which is to say, gods with no track record with him whatever, chosen precisely because they are new.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the LORD your God brings you into the land that you are entering to take possession of it, you shall set the blessing on Mount Gerizim and the curse on Mount Ebal. Are they not beyond the Jordan, west of the road, toward the going down of the sun, in the land of the Canaanites who live in the Arabah, opposite Gilgal, beside the oak of Moreh? For you are to cross over the Jordan to go in to take possession of the land that the LORD your God is giving you. And when you possess it and live in it, you shall be careful to do all the statutes and the rules that I am setting before you today.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter closes with staging instructions for a ceremony that will not happen for years. You shall set the blessing on Mount Gerizim and the curse on Mount Ebal.

The two mountains stand opposite each other with the town of Shechem in the valley between them, and the natural acoustics there are famous: a man can be heard across the whole valley. God chose a place where a nation could stand on two hillsides and hear each other.

The ceremony itself is described in chapter 27 and carried out in Joshua 8:33–35 — half the tribes on one slope for the blessing, half on the other for the curse, the ark and the priests in the valley between, and the words read out to all of them.

Think about what that would have been like. Not a document filed with the elders. A nation divided across two hills, hearing the terms of the covenant shouted between them, with every person present having to stand on one side or the other of a valley while it was read.

God does not deal with his people only in propositions. He builds things they have to stand in, walk through and taste — a Passover meal, a rainbow, water, bread and wine. This is a covenant you had to climb a hill to hear, and Israel would remember where she was standing.

And the last verse gathers it: you shall be careful to do all the statutes and the rules that I am setting before you today. Not admire them, not agree with them. Do them — which is where chapter 12 begins, and where the law proper starts.

11.theology:
Love expressed in obedience. “You shall therefore love the LORD your God and keep his charge… always” (11:1). Love and obedience are inseparable; obedience is love made visible, as Jesus taught (John 14:15). This wholehearted love — loving, walking, holding fast — is the secret of every blessing and victory.

The land God cares for. Unlike self-watered Egypt, Canaan “drinks water by the rain from heaven, a land that the LORD your God cares for. The eyes of the LORD your God are always upon it” (11:11–12). God designed a life of daily, upward dependence, and his unceasing gaze of care never leaves his people (cf. Ps 121).

The blessing and the curse. “See, I am setting before you today a blessing and a curse” (11:26). Every generation faces this decisive choice, with no neutral ground. The curse fell in the exile — yet the gospel's glory is that Christ “became a curse for us” (Gal 3:13), bearing the curse on the tree so that all who trust him receive the blessing.
11.examples:
Then: Having seen God's mighty acts with their own eyes, Israel was called to love and obey him always, to depend daily on the rain of a land on which God's eyes never close, to saturate home and heart with his word across the generations, and to choose between blessing and curse at Gerizim and Ebal.

Now: We obey in the light of all we have seen of God's grace in Christ; we live in daily, upward dependence on the Father who watches over us unsleeping; we weave the gospel into the fabric of our homes and hand it to our children; and we rejoice that the curse we earned by disobedience has been borne by Christ on the tree, so that we stand forever on the mountain of blessing, called to walk gratefully in the ways of the God who first loved us.

12.title: The Central Sanctuary: Worship God His Way, Not Ours
12.text: <sup>1</sup>"These are the statutes and rules that you shall be careful to do in the land that the LORD, the God of your fathers, has given you to possess, all the days that you live on the earth.<sup>2</sup>You shall surely destroy all the places where the nations whom you shall dispossess served their gods, on the high mountains and on the hills and under every green tree.<sup>3</sup>You shall tear down their altars and dash in pieces their pillars and burn their Asherim with fire. You shall chop down the carved images of their gods and destroy their name out of that place.<sup>4</sup>You shall not worship the LORD your God in that way.<sup>5</sup>But you shall seek the place that the LORD your God will choose out of all your tribes to put his name and make his habitation there. There you shall go,<sup>6</sup>and there you shall bring your burnt offerings and your sacrifices, your tithes and the contribution that you present, your vow offerings, your freewill offerings, and the firstborn of your herd and of your flock.<sup>7</sup>And there you shall eat before the LORD your God, and you shall rejoice, you and your households, in all that you undertake, in which the LORD your God has blessed you.<sup>8</sup>"You shall not do according to all that we are doing here today, everyone doing whatever is right in his own eyes,<sup>9</sup>for you have not as yet come to the rest and to the inheritance that the LORD your God is giving you.<sup>10</sup>But when you go over the Jordan and live in the land that the LORD your God is giving you to inherit, and when he gives you rest from all your enemies around, so that you live in safety,<sup>11</sup>then to the place that the LORD your God will choose, to make his name dwell there, there you shall bring all that I command you: your burnt offerings and your sacrifices, your tithes and the contribution that you present, and all your finest vow offerings that you vow to the LORD.<sup>12</sup>And you shall rejoice before the LORD your God, you and your sons and your daughters, your male servants and your female servants, and the Levite that is within your towns, since he has no portion or inheritance with you.<sup>13</sup>Take care that you do not offer your burnt offerings at any place that you see,<sup>14</sup>but at the place that the LORD will choose in one of your tribes, there you shall offer your burnt offerings, and there you shall do all that I am commanding you.<sup>15</sup>"However, you may slaughter and eat meat within any of your towns, as much as you desire, according to the blessing of the LORD your God that he has given you. The unclean and the clean may eat of it, as of the gazelle and as of the deer.<sup>16</sup>Only you shall not eat the blood; you shall pour it out on the earth like water.<sup>17</sup>You may not eat within your towns the tithe of your grain or of your wine or of your oil, or the firstborn of your herd or of your flock, or any of your vow offerings that you vow, or your freewill offerings or the contribution that you present,<sup>18</sup>but you shall eat them before the LORD your God in the place that the LORD your God will choose, you and your son and your daughter, your male servant and your female servant, and the Levite who is within your towns. And you shall rejoice before the LORD your God in all that you undertake.<sup>19</sup>Take care that you do not neglect the Levite as long as you live in your land.<sup>20</sup>"When the LORD your God enlarges your territory, as he has promised you, and you say, 'I will eat meat,' because you crave meat, you may eat meat whenever you desire.<sup>21</sup>If the place that the LORD your God will choose to put his name there is too far from you, then you may kill any of your herd or your flock, which the LORD has given you, as I have commanded you, and you may eat within your towns whenever you desire.<sup>22</sup>Just as the gazelle or the deer is eaten, so you may eat of it. The unclean and the clean alike may eat of it.<sup>23</sup>Only be sure that you do not eat the blood, for the blood is the life, and you shall not eat the life with the flesh.<sup>24</sup>You shall not eat it; you shall pour it out on the earth like water.<sup>25</sup>You shall not eat it, that all may go well with you and with your children after you, when you do what is right in the sight of the LORD.<sup>26</sup>But the holy things that are due from you, and your vow offerings, you shall take, and you shall go to the place that the LORD will choose,<sup>27</sup>and offer your burnt offerings, the flesh and the blood, on the altar of the LORD your God. The blood of your sacrifices shall be poured out on the altar of the LORD your God, but the flesh you may eat.<sup>28</sup>Be careful to obey all these words that I command you, that it may go well with you and with your children after you forever, when you do what is good and right in the sight of the LORD your God.<sup>29</sup>"When the LORD your God cuts off before you the nations whom you go in to dispossess, and you dispossess them and dwell in their land,<sup>30</sup>take care that you be not ensnared to follow them, after they have been destroyed before you, and that you do not inquire about their gods, saying, 'How did these nations serve their gods?—that I also may do the same.'<sup>31</sup>You shall not worship the LORD your God in that way, for every abominable thing that the LORD hates they have done for their gods, for they even burn their sons and their daughters in the fire to their gods.<sup>32</sup>"Everything that I command you, you shall be careful to do. You shall not add to it or take from it.
12.overview:
Chapter 12 opens the detailed covenant code (chs. 12–26), and it begins where all of life begins for the people of God: with worship. The great theme is that God is to be worshiped at the place he chooses, in the way he prescribes — not as the nations worship their gods, and not according to human invention. This is the principle that Reformed theology has called the regulative principle of worship: we worship God only as he has commanded.

Israel is first to destroy utterly the places and paraphernalia of Canaanite worship — the high places, altars, pillars, and Asherim. The land is to be cleansed of idolatry. Then they are to seek “the place that the LORD your God will choose… to put his name” (12:5), the central sanctuary where the nation's worship would be unified and purified.

The chapter repeatedly warns against doing “whatever is right in his own eyes” (12:8) in worship, and against the deadly curiosity that asks how the nations served their gods, intending to copy them (12:30). “You shall not worship the LORD your God in that way” (12:31). God will not be worshiped on our terms.

And the closing command crowns it all: “Everything that I command you, you shall be careful to do. You shall not add to it or take from it” (12:32). True worship is regulated by God's Word — neither diminished nor embellished by human cleverness. To worship God his way is the first duty and the highest joy of the redeemed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Destroy the Places of Idolatry
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel must utterly destroy all the Canaanite places of worship — on the mountains, hills, and under every green tree — and not worship the LORD as the nations worshiped their gods.
verseByVerse.theology: The land must be cleansed of idolatry; God will not be worshiped in the manner of false gods, and every rival shrine must be destroyed.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel tore down the high places. Now: believers root out every idolatrous practice and refuse to worship God by the world's methods.

verseByVerse.quote: "These are the statutes and rules that you shall be careful to do in the land that the LORD, the God of your fathers, has given you to possess, all the days that you live on the earth. You shall surely destroy all the places where the nations whom you shall dispossess served their gods, on the high mountains and on the hills and under every green tree. You shall tear down their altars and dash in pieces their pillars and burn their Asherim with fire. You shall chop down the carved images of their gods and destroy their name out of that place. You shall not worship the LORD your God in that way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law proper begins, and it begins with worship — and worship begins with demolition. You shall surely destroy all the places where the nations whom you shall dispossess served their gods, on the high mountains and on the hills and under every green tree.

Altars torn down, pillars broken, Asherim burnt, carved images cut to pieces, the very names of the places wiped out. Before Israel is told how to worship, she is told what to knock down.

And note where those shrines were: hilltops and shady trees. Canaanite worship was set in beautiful places, and that was part of its power. The high place caught the wind and the view; the great tree gave shade and a sense of age. False religion has almost always understood atmosphere better than true religion does, and Israel is being warned that a site can do a great deal of a god’s work for him.

Then verse 4, which is the hinge: You shall not worship the LORD your God in that way.

Read that carefully, because it is not what the paragraph seemed to be about. The danger being addressed is not that Israel will worship Baal. It is that Israel will worship the LORD in Baal’s manner — right God, borrowed method. That is a much subtler failure than idolatry and a much commoner one, and the rest of the chapter is built on it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–14 — The Place the LORD Will Choose
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel is to seek the one place God chooses to put his name, bringing their offerings and sacrifices there and rejoicing before him, rather than offering wherever they please.
verseByVerse.theology: God determines where and how he is to be worshiped; centralized worship at his chosen place guards purity and unity and points to Christ, the true meeting place with God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel worshiped at the place God chose. Now: we come to God through Christ, the true temple and the only mediator, not by our own devised paths.

verseByVerse.quote: But you shall seek the place that the LORD your God will choose out of all your tribes to put his name and make his habitation there. There you shall go, and there you shall bring your burnt offerings and your sacrifices, your tithes and the contribution that you present, your vow offerings, your freewill offerings, and the firstborn of your herd and of your flock. And there you shall eat before the LORD your God, and you shall rejoice, you and your households, in all that you undertake, in which the LORD your God has blessed you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Over against the shrines on every hill, God appoints one address: the place that the LORD your God will choose out of all your tribes to put his name and make his habitation there.

Notice that it is not named. Not Shechem, not Shiloh, not Jerusalem — Deuteronomy will say the place the LORD will choose more than twenty times and never once say where. Israel is told to go where God decides, and to find out later where that is. The choosing is God’s, and withholding the name keeps it his.

And what he puts there is his name. That is the language of ownership and of presence: to put your name on something is to claim it, and Israel’s worship was to happen at the one spot on earth God had signed.

Then verse 7, which is a surprise in a chapter about demolition and restriction. And there you shall eat before the LORD your God, and you shall rejoice, you and your households, in all that you undertake.

The centre of Israel’s worship is a family meal, eaten in God’s presence, with rejoicing. Not a rite performed at a distance by a specialist while everybody watches — a household sitting down to eat in front of God and being glad. That is what the one place was for.

Whatever else the restriction of this chapter is, it is not miserly. God narrows the location of worship to one place and then fills that place with roast meat, wine, family and joy — which is, in the end, exactly how the story finishes: Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb (Rev. 19:9).

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not do according to all that we are doing here today, everyone doing whatever is right in his own eyes, for you have not as yet come to the rest and to the inheritance that the LORD your God is giving you. But when you go over the Jordan and live in the land that the LORD your God is giving you to inherit, and when he gives you rest from all your enemies around, so that you live in safety, then to the place that the LORD your God will choose, to make his name dwell there, there you shall bring all that I command you: your burnt offerings and your sacrifices, your tithes and the contribution that you present, and all your finest vow offerings that you vow to the LORD. And you shall rejoice before the LORD your God, you and your sons and your daughters, your male servants and your female servants, and the Levite that is within your towns, since he has no portion or inheritance with you. Take care that you do not offer your burnt offerings at any place that you see, but at the place that the LORD will choose in one of your tribes, there you shall offer your burnt offerings, and there you shall do all that I am commanding you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You shall not do according to all that we are doing here today, everyone doing whatever is right in his own eyes.

That last phrase should stop the reader, because it is the sentence the book of Judges uses to explain its own horrors. Twice Judges says there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes (Judg. 17:6; 21:25), and it says it just before the worst chapters in the Old Testament.

Moses is describing the wilderness arrangement as improvised and temporary — in a moving camp you cannot have a fixed sanctuary, and things were done as circumstances allowed. That was tolerable on the march. Settled in the land it would become anarchy, and each family would end up with a hilltop and a preference.

And the point is not that everyone was doing what was wrong in his own eyes. It is that his own eyes had become the standard. Sincerity is not the issue; the reference point is. A man can be perfectly earnest and entirely his own authority, and the result over three generations is what Judges records.

The corrective offered is rest — when he gives you rest from all your enemies… so that you live in safety — and a place God chooses rather than one they like the look of. Which is why the New Testament, for all its freedom about location, is so insistent that worship is not a private construction: God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth (John 4:24). The place has changed. The principle has not moved an inch.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–28 — Eating Meat, Blood, and Bringing Offerings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel may slaughter and eat meat in their towns as a gift of God, but must not eat the blood, which is to be poured out; their holy offerings and tithes must still be brought to the chosen place.
verseByVerse.theology: Life belongs to God, symbolized by the blood that must not be eaten; God's gifts are to be enjoyed with gratitude, and his holy things brought to him.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel poured out the blood in reverence for life. Now: we honor the blood of Christ, by which life is given, and enjoy God's gifts with thanksgiving.

verseByVerse.quote: "However, you may slaughter and eat meat within any of your towns, as much as you desire, according to the blessing of the LORD your God that he has given you. The unclean and the clean may eat of it, as of the gazelle and as of the deer. Only you shall not eat the blood; you shall pour it out on the earth like water. You may not eat within your towns the tithe of your grain or of your wine or of your oil, or the firstborn of your herd or of your flock, or any of your vow offerings that you vow, or your freewill offerings or the contribution that you present, but you shall eat them before the LORD your God in the place that the LORD your God will choose, you and your son and your daughter, your male servant and your female servant, and the Levite who is within your towns. And you shall rejoice before the LORD your God in all that you undertake. Take care that you do not neglect the Levite as long as you live in your land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now a generous concession, and it needs its background. Under the wilderness arrangement, killing an animal for food was a sacrificial act done at the tent. In a settled country spread over a hundred miles, that would be impossible — so God releases it: you may slaughter and eat meat within any of your towns, as much as you desire, according to the blessing of the LORD your God.

As much as you desire. The chapter that restricts where sacrifice may happen simultaneously frees ordinary eating entirely, and does it in warm language. God is not a minimalist about his people’s dinner tables.

But two things are pinned down. The blood must be poured out on the ground, not eaten. And the tithes and offerings must still go to the chosen place — you shall eat them before the LORD your God… you and your son and your daughter, your male servant and your female servant, and the Levite who is within your towns.

Then verse 19, tucked in almost as an aside: Take care that you do not neglect the Levite as long as you live in your land.

That is a small verse with a long reach. The Levite had no field. When Israel prospered, he would prosper only if people remembered him, and there is nothing automatic about being remembered. God does not leave the support of his servants to spontaneous goodwill; he commands it, by name, in the middle of a paragraph about meat — because the people most likely to be forgotten are the ones with no way of pressing their case.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the LORD your God enlarges your territory, as he has promised you, and you say, 'I will eat meat,' because you crave meat, you may eat meat whenever you desire. If the place that the LORD your God will choose to put his name there is too far from you, then you may kill any of your herd or your flock, which the LORD has given you, as I have commanded you, and you may eat within your towns whenever you desire. Just as the gazelle or the deer is eaten, so you may eat of it. The unclean and the clean alike may eat of it. Only be sure that you do not eat the blood, for the blood is the life, and you shall not eat the life with the flesh. You shall not eat it; you shall pour it out on the earth like water. You shall not eat it, that all may go well with you and with your children after you, when you do what is right in the sight of the LORD. But the holy things that are due from you, and your vow offerings, you shall take, and you shall go to the place that the LORD will choose, and offer your burnt offerings, the flesh and the blood, on the altar of the LORD your God. The blood of your sacrifices shall be poured out on the altar of the LORD your God, but the flesh you may eat. Be careful to obey all these words that I command you, that it may go well with you and with your children after you forever, when you do what is good and right in the sight of the LORD your God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The concession about meat is repeated and widened — whenever you desire, twice — and then the one restriction is stated with a reason attached: Only be sure that you do not eat the blood, for the blood is the life, and you shall not eat the life with the flesh.

Blood is treated in Scripture as the carrier of life, and life belongs to God. To pour the blood out on the ground was to hand back to God what was his and to acknowledge that the animal’s death was a real thing, not a triviality. Israel’s cooks were made to think, every time, about the cost of the meal.

That principle is older than Israel — it was given to Noah, for all mankind (Gen. 9:4) — and it runs straight through to the one place where God does the opposite of pouring life out on the ground. Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life (John 6:54) was so shocking to the people who first heard it precisely because of this verse. The life that was never to be consumed is offered to be received.

And the promise attached is quietly domestic: that all may go well with you and with your children after you. Even a rule about draining a carcass is framed as being for the good of a family two generations on.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–32 — Do Not Inquire How the Nations Worship
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel must not be ensnared into copying how the nations served their gods — even their abominable practices like child sacrifice — but must worship only as God commands, adding nothing and taking nothing away.
verseByVerse.theology: Worship is regulated by God's word alone; the curiosity that imitates pagan worship leads to abomination, and nothing may be added to or subtracted from God's commands.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel was forbidden to imitate Canaanite worship. Now: the church worships by God's word, neither borrowing the world's methods nor inventing its own.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the LORD your God cuts off before you the nations whom you go in to dispossess, and you dispossess them and dwell in their land, take care that you be not ensnared to follow them, after they have been destroyed before you, and that you do not inquire about their gods, saying, 'How did these nations serve their gods?—that I also may do the same.' You shall not worship the LORD your God in that way, for every abominable thing that the LORD hates they have done for their gods, for they even burn their sons and their daughters in the fire to their gods. "Everything that I command you, you shall be careful to do. You shall not add to it or take from it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends with a warning about a very particular temptation, and it is not the one you would expect.

Take care that you be not ensnared to follow them, after they have been destroyed before you, and that you do not inquire about their gods, saying, “How did these nations serve their gods?—that I also may do the same.”

Read what is actually being contemplated. Not apostasy. The man in this verse has not stopped believing in the LORD; he intends to worship him. He is simply curious about method — what did the neighbours do, what worked, what did their ceremonies look like — and he wants to borrow it. And God calls that a snare, and forbids it absolutely: You shall not worship the LORD your God in that way.

The reason follows, and it is the darkest sentence in the chapter: for every abominable thing that the LORD hates they have done for their gods, for they even burn their sons and their daughters in the fire to their gods.

That is where borrowed method ends. Nobody arrives at child sacrifice in one step. It is reached by a long series of small adoptions, each of which seemed at the time like a matter of form rather than substance — and Israel did in fact arrive there, in the valley of Hinnom, centuries later (Jer. 7:31).

Then the closing charter: Everything that I command you, you shall be careful to do. You shall not add to it or take from it.

Both directions again, as at 4:2, and here it is specifically about worship. God is not a blank space that his people fill in according to taste. He has said how he will be approached, and the question in every generation is not whether a form is beautiful, or effective, or moving, but whether he asked for it.

12.theology:
Worship regulated by God's word. God will not be worshiped “in that way” — by the methods of the nations (12:31) — nor by “whatever is right in his own eyes” (12:8). The chapter closes with the charter of the regulative principle: “You shall not add to it or take from it” (12:32). God alone determines how he is approached; both adding and subtracting set human judgment above divine command.

The one chosen place. Israel must seek “the place that the LORD your God will choose… to put his name” (12:5), guarding the purity and unity of worship. This points to Christ, the true temple (John 2:19–21), the one meeting place with God, in whom we worship “in spirit and truth” (John 4:24).

The blood is the life. The repeated prohibition against eating blood — “the blood is the life” (12:23) — enshrines reverence for life as God's sacred gift and points to atonement. The blood poured out anticipates the precious blood of Christ, poured out for the forgiveness of sins, by which alone we have life.
12.examples:
Then: Entering the land, Israel was to tear down every idolatrous shrine, gather to worship and feast at the one place God chose, reverence the blood as the life that belongs to God, and refuse to worship the LORD by the abominable methods of the nations — adding nothing and subtracting nothing from his commands.

Now: We come to God not at a building but through Christ, the true temple and only Mediator, worshiping in spirit and truth. We honor the precious blood of Christ by which we have life, enjoy God's good gifts with thanksgiving, and guard our worship by his Word alone — refusing both to borrow the world's methods and to invent our own, content with the glad, careful obedience that the God of all glory is worthy to receive.

13.title: Warning Against False Prophets: Guard the Heart's Allegiance
13.text: <sup>1</sup>"If a prophet or a dreamer of dreams arises among you and gives you a sign or a wonder,<sup>2</sup>and the sign or wonder that he tells you comes to pass, and if he says, 'Let us go after other gods,' which you have not known, 'and let us serve them,'<sup>3</sup>you shall not listen to the words of that prophet or that dreamer of dreams. For the LORD your God is testing you, to know whether you love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul.<sup>4</sup>You shall walk after the LORD your God and fear him and keep his commandments and obey his voice, and you shall serve him and hold fast to him.<sup>5</sup>But that prophet or that dreamer of dreams shall be put to death, because he has taught rebellion against the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt and redeemed you out of the house of slavery, to make you leave the way in which the LORD your God commanded you to walk. So you shall purge the evil from your midst.<sup>6</sup>"If your brother, the son of your mother, or your son or your daughter or the wife you embrace or your friend who is as your own soul entices you secretly, saying, 'Let us go and serve other gods,' which neither you nor your fathers have known,<sup>7</sup>some of the gods of the peoples who are around you, whether near you or far off from you, from the one end of the earth to the other,<sup>8</sup>you shall not yield to him or listen to him, nor shall your eye pity him, nor shall you spare him, nor shall you conceal him.<sup>9</sup>But you shall kill him. Your hand shall be first against him to put him to death, and afterward the hand of all the people.<sup>10</sup>You shall stone him to death with stones, because he sought to draw you away from the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.<sup>11</sup>And all Israel shall hear and fear and never again do any such wickedness as this among you.<sup>12</sup>"If you hear in one of your cities, which the LORD your God is giving you to dwell there,<sup>13</sup>that certain worthless fellows have gone out among you and have drawn away the inhabitants of their city, saying, 'Let us go and serve other gods,' which you have not known,<sup>14</sup>then you shall inquire and make search and ask diligently. And behold, if it be true and certain that such an abomination has been done among you,<sup>15</sup>you shall surely put the inhabitants of that city to the sword, devoting it to destruction, all who are in it and its cattle, with the edge of the sword.<sup>16</sup>You shall gather all its spoil into the midst of its open square and burn the city and all its spoil with fire, as a whole burnt offering to the LORD your God. It shall be a heap forever. It shall not be built again.<sup>17</sup>None of the devoted things shall stick to your hand, that the LORD may turn from the fierceness of his anger and show you mercy and have compassion on you and multiply you, as he swore to your fathers,<sup>18</sup>if you obey the voice of the LORD your God, keeping all his commandments that I am commanding you today, and doing what is right in the sight of the LORD your God.
13.overview:
Chapter 13 deals with the gravest threat to the covenant community: the temptation to idolatry, no matter how attractive the source. Three scenarios are addressed — a prophet who works signs, a beloved family member who whispers in secret, and an entire city that falls away. In every case, the lure to “go after other gods” must be resisted with uncompromising seriousness, even when it comes from the most credible or beloved source.

The first case is startling: even a prophet whose sign or wonder comes true must be rejected if he says, “Let us go after other gods.” Why? Because “the LORD your God is testing you, to know whether you love the LORD your God with all your heart” (13:3). Miracles do not validate a message that contradicts God's revealed truth. The test of every teacher is fidelity to God's Word, not the impressiveness of his signs.

The second case pierces the heart: if your own brother, child, wife, or dearest friend secretly entices you to idolatry, you must not yield, conceal, or pity. Loyalty to God outranks even the closest human bond.

The third case widens to a whole city given over to idolatry, which is to be devoted to destruction. The seriousness of these measures reflects the seriousness of spiritual defection. To turn from the LORD is not a private preference but covenant treason that imperils the whole community.

For us, the chapter teaches that truth is tested by Scripture, not signs; that no relationship may rival our allegiance to Christ; and that the heart's loyalty must be guarded with all vigilance.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The False Prophet Who Works Wonders
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Even a prophet whose sign comes true must be rejected and put to death if he calls people to follow other gods, for God is testing his people's love, and they must hold fast to him alone.
verseByVerse.theology: Truth is tested by fidelity to God's word, not by signs and wonders; trials of false teaching reveal whether we truly love God with all our heart.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel was to reject even a sign-working prophet who taught idolatry. Now: we test every teaching by Scripture, not by miracles or charisma.

verseByVerse.quote: "If a prophet or a dreamer of dreams arises among you and gives you a sign or a wonder, and the sign or wonder that he tells you comes to pass, and if he says, 'Let us go after other gods,' which you have not known, 'and let us serve them,' you shall not listen to the words of that prophet or that dreamer of dreams. For the LORD your God is testing you, to know whether you love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter puts three cases, each closer to home than the last, and the first is deliberately the hardest to answer.

If a prophet or a dreamer of dreams arises among you and gives you a sign or a wonder, and the sign or wonder that he tells you comes to pass, and if he says, “Let us go after other gods”… you shall not listen.

Take in what has just been conceded. The sign comes true. God does not say the man is a fraud, or that the wonder was a trick, or that it will fail on inspection. The prediction lands, and the man is still to be rejected — because of what he is calling them to.

That single provision settles a question people still get wrong. Supernatural power is not self-authenticating. Pharaoh’s magicians duplicated the first plagues; the Lord Jesus warned that false christs and false prophets will arise and perform great signs and wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect (Matt. 24:24); and Paul says the man of lawlessness comes with all power and false signs and wonders (2 Thess. 2:9). The test of a message has never been whether something remarkable accompanied it. It is what the message says about God.

Then the reason, and it recasts the whole scene: For the LORD your God is testing you, to know whether you love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul.

The false prophet is not an accident that God is dealing with. He is an examination that God is setting. And what is being examined is not doctrinal knowledge but love — the Shema, quoted directly. A man who loves God with all his heart is not moved by a wonder-worker, because he is not shopping.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall walk after the LORD your God and fear him and keep his commandments and obey his voice, and you shall serve him and hold fast to him. But that prophet or that dreamer of dreams shall be put to death, because he has taught rebellion against the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt and redeemed you out of the house of slavery, to make you leave the way in which the LORD your God commanded you to walk. So you shall purge the evil from your midst.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Against the seducer stands the positive command, and it is a chain of six verbs: You shall walk after the LORD your God and fear him and keep his commandments and obey his voice, and you shall serve him and hold fast to him.

Walk, fear, keep, obey, serve, cling. Deuteronomy keeps stacking these because it will not let the life with God be reduced to any one of them. And the last is the strongest: hold fast — dabaq, glued to.

The remedy for seduction is not suspicion. It is attachment. A man is not protected from a false teacher by being sceptical of everybody; he is protected by being fastened to somebody. That is the whole logic of Christian assurance, and it is why the New Testament answers false teaching so often with abide rather than argue — Abide in me, and I in you (John 15:4).

Then the sentence on the prophet, and the reason given for it: because he has taught rebellion against the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt and redeemed you out of the house of slavery.

Note what makes it so grave. The redemption is named. To turn a redeemed people back is not a difference of opinion about religion; it is an attempt to march them back into the house they were bought out of. The crime is measured by the rescue.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–11 — When the Tempter Is a Loved One
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: If a brother, child, spouse, or dearest friend secretly entices to idolatry, one must not yield, conceal, or pity, but resist the temptation, for loyalty to God outranks every human bond.
verseByVerse.theology: Allegiance to God takes precedence over the closest human relationships; no love for family or friend may compromise love for God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel was to resist even a loved one's enticement to idolatry. Now: no relationship may rival Christ; we love family rightly only by loving God supremely.

verseByVerse.quote: "If your brother, the son of your mother, or your son or your daughter or the wife you embrace or your friend who is as your own soul entices you secretly, saying, 'Let us go and serve other gods,' which neither you nor your fathers have known, some of the gods of the peoples who are around you, whether near you or far off from you, from the one end of the earth to the other, you shall not yield to him or listen to him, nor shall your eye pity him, nor shall you spare him, nor shall you conceal him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now the second case, and it is the one that hurts.

If your brother, the son of your mother, or your son or your daughter or the wife you embrace or your friend who is as your own soul entices you secretly…

Read the list slowly. Not a stranger. Not a public figure. A brother — and the text specifies the son of your mother, the closest possible tie. Your own child. The wife you embrace. Your friend who is as your own soul, which is the phrase used of David and Jonathan.

Scripture is being deliberately intimate, and it is naming the five people whose voices carry the most weight with any human being. These are exactly the people we cannot say no to, and God knows it, which is why he lists them by relationship rather than saying anyone.

And note the word secretly. This does not come as a public challenge that can be answered in the open. It comes quietly, from someone with access, in the kind of conversation nobody else hears.

Then five refusals, piled up: you shall not yield to him or listen to him, nor shall your eye pity him, nor shall you spare him, nor shall you conceal him. Five, because one would not be enough. The pull of those relationships is such that God stops the escape at every exit, including the one most of us would use — nor shall you conceal him, which is what love usually wants to do.

The Lord Jesus said the same thing about the same relationships, and it is one of the hardest sentences he ever spoke: Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me (Matt. 10:37). He was not devaluing families. He was ranking them, in exactly the order Deuteronomy 13 ranks them.

verseByVerse.quote: But you shall kill him. Your hand shall be first against him to put him to death, and afterward the hand of all the people. You shall stone him to death with stones, because he sought to draw you away from the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. And all Israel shall hear and fear and never again do any such wickedness as this among you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The penalty is death, carried out by the community, and with a detail that is almost unbearable: Your hand shall be first against him.

The one who was enticed strikes first. Nobody may lay a charge and then step back and let others do it.

Modern readers recoil, and should. Three things need saying, and the third matters most.

First, what this is not. It is not a private killing; the next case (vv. 12–15) requires investigation — you shall inquire and make search and ask diligently — and Deuteronomy elsewhere demands two or three witnesses (19:15). This is judicial, in a nation where God was literally the king, and enticement to idolatry was treason against the head of state.

Second, the requirement that the accuser strike first is a restraint, not a cruelty. It makes it impossible to denounce a family member and keep your hands clean. Anyone who brought such a charge had to be prepared to do the thing himself, in public, which is a considerable deterrent against denunciation.

Third, and this must be said without hedging: no Christian, church or state holds this commission. Israel was a theocracy for a period that ended, and the New Testament transfers the penalty to a different sphere entirely. Paul faces the identical crime — a man teaching what destroys people — and the remedy he commands is exclusion from the fellowship, not execution (1 Cor. 5:1–5; Titus 3:10). The weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh (2 Cor. 10:4). Anyone who has ever used this chapter to justify violence has read it against Christ.

What does carry across is the seriousness. God treats the person who draws his people away from him as doing something worse than any other crime in the code — worse than theft, worse than assault — and a church that finds false teaching a matter of taste has lost something this chapter had.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: If an entire city is led astray to serve other gods, it must be carefully investigated and, if the report is true, devoted to destruction, so that God may turn from his anger and show mercy to a faithful people.
verseByVerse.theology: Idolatry that infects a whole community must be purged; God's people are to take spiritual corruption with utmost seriousness, yet justice requires careful investigation of the truth.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: an apostate city was investigated and judged. Now: the church guards its corporate purity, dealing carefully and seriously with corrupting sin.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you hear in one of your cities, which the LORD your God is giving you to dwell there, that certain worthless fellows have gone out among you and have drawn away the inhabitants of their city, saying, 'Let us go and serve other gods,' which you have not known, then you shall inquire and make search and ask diligently. And behold, if it be true and certain that such an abomination has been done among you, you shall surely put the inhabitants of that city to the sword, devoting it to destruction, all who are in it and its cattle, with the edge of the sword.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third case is a whole city, and what is striking is how much investigation is demanded before anything is done.

Then you shall inquire and make search and ask diligently. And behold, if it be true and certain that such an abomination has been done among you…

Three verbs for finding out. Inquire, search, ask diligently — and then two more words of certainty, true and certain, before a single step may be taken. In the most inflammatory situation the law contemplates, with a whole town accused, the first requirement is patient investigation.

That is a striking feature of biblical justice and it runs against every instinct in a crisis. The greater the outrage, the greater the pressure to act before the facts are in — and the law puts its heaviest evidentiary demands precisely where feelings run hottest.

Note also who is blamed for the city’s fall: certain worthless fellows have gone out among you and have drawn away the inhabitants of their city. The Hebrew is sons of belial — men of no worth. A whole town does not go over at once. It is talked over, by a few persuasive people with nothing to lose, and the rest follow because everybody else is.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall gather all its spoil into the midst of its open square and burn the city and all its spoil with fire, as a whole burnt offering to the LORD your God. It shall be a heap forever. It shall not be built again. None of the devoted things shall stick to your hand, that the LORD may turn from the fierceness of his anger and show you mercy and have compassion on you and multiply you, as he swore to your fathers, if you obey the voice of the LORD your God, keeping all his commandments that I am commanding you today, and doing what is right in the sight of the LORD your God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The city is to be destroyed and its plunder burnt rather than kept — as a whole burnt offering to the LORD your God — and nothing of the devoted thing is to stick to anyone’s hand.

That is the same guard as in chapter 7. The gold is the danger, because a man who keeps something off an idol has kept a thread back to the whole thing.

But the last verse of the chapter is the surprise, and it changes the tone of everything before it.

That the LORD may turn from the fierceness of his anger and show you mercy and have compassion on you and multiply you, as he swore to your fathers.

Mercy, compassion, multiplication — three words of tenderness at the end of the harshest chapter in the book. And they are the purpose. The severity is not an end in itself; it exists so that God can be merciful to the rest, and so that a nation is still standing to receive what he swore to Abraham.

Get that straight, because it is the hardest thing about Deuteronomy for a modern reader. The God of chapter 13 is not two Gods, one fierce and one kind, alternating. He is one God, whose fierceness against what destroys his people is a function of his commitment to them. A physician who will not cut is not gentle; he is negligent.

And the last clause of the chapter — if you obey the voice of the LORD your God, keeping all his commandments — brings it back to where chapter 13 began. The whole thing has been about listening to the right voice. Three seducers speak in this chapter: a prophet with a wonder, a brother in the dark, and a townful of neighbours. Against all three there is one sentence: you shall walk after the LORD your God… and hold fast to him.

13.theology:
Truth tested by God's word, not signs. Even a prophet whose wonder comes true must be rejected if he teaches idolatry (13:1–3). Miracles never validate a message that contradicts God's revealed truth; Satan can counterfeit wonders (2 Thess 2:9). The abiding test of every teacher is fidelity to Scripture.

Supreme allegiance to God. No bond — not spouse, child, friend, or city — may rival our loyalty to God (13:6–8). This anticipates Jesus' words that whoever loves family more than him is not worthy of him (Matt 10:37); rightly ordered love holds even our dearest with an open hand under the supreme love of God.

The seriousness of spiritual defection. The grave penalties reflect the unique theocracy of Old Testament Israel and are not carried into the church age, yet they enshrine an abiding truth: idolatry is covenant treason that imperils the whole community and must be purged — so that God may “turn from his anger and show mercy” (13:17).
13.examples:
Then: Israel was to reject even a sign-working prophet, a beloved family member, or a whole city that enticed to idolatry, taking spiritual defection with deadly seriousness while requiring careful inquiry into the truth — all so that God might turn in mercy to a faithful people.

Now: We test every teaching by Scripture, not by miracles or charisma; we refuse to let any relationship, however precious, rival our allegiance to Christ; and we guard the purity of the church, dealing carefully and seriously with corrupting sin. And we rest in the gospel: the wrath against idolatry that this chapter enforces fell upon Christ, who bore God's fierce anger so that mercy and compassion might flow freely to all who hold fast to him with all their heart.

14.title: A Holy People: Clean Foods, the Tithe, and the Joy of Worship
14.text: <sup>1</sup>"You are the sons of the LORD your God. You shall not cut yourselves or make any baldness on your foreheads for the dead.<sup>2</sup>For you are a people holy to the LORD your God, and the LORD has chosen you to be a people for his treasured possession, out of all the peoples who are on the face of the earth.<sup>3</sup>"You shall not eat any abomination.<sup>4</sup>These are the animals you may eat: the ox, the sheep, the goat,<sup>5</sup>the deer, the gazelle, the roebuck, the wild goat, the ibex, the antelope, and the mountain sheep.<sup>6</sup>Every animal that parts the hoof and has the hoof cloven in two and chews the cud, among the animals, you may eat.<sup>7</sup>Yet of those that chew the cud or have the hoof cloven you shall not eat these: the camel, the hare, and the rock badger, because they chew the cud but do not part the hoof, are unclean for you.<sup>8</sup>And the pig, because it parts the hoof but does not chew the cud, is unclean for you. Their flesh you shall not eat, and their carcasses you shall not touch.<sup>9</sup>"Of all that are in the waters you may eat these: whatever has fins and scales you may eat.<sup>10</sup>And whatever does not have fins and scales you shall not eat; it is unclean for you.<sup>11</sup>"You may eat all clean birds.<sup>12</sup>But these are the ones that you shall not eat: the eagle, the bearded vulture, the black vulture,<sup>13</sup>the kite, the falcon of any kind;<sup>14</sup>every raven of any kind;<sup>15</sup>the ostrich, the nighthawk, the sea gull, the hawk of any kind;<sup>16</sup>the little owl and the short-eared owl, the barn owl<sup>17</sup>and the tawny owl, the carrion vulture and the cormorant,<sup>18</sup>the stork, the heron of any kind; the hoopoe and the bat.<sup>19</sup>And all winged insects are unclean for you; they shall not be eaten.<sup>20</sup>All clean winged things you may eat.<sup>21</sup>"You shall not eat anything that has died naturally. You may give it to the sojourner who is within your towns, that he may eat it, or you may sell it to a foreigner. For you are a people holy to the LORD your God. "You shall not boil a young goat in its mother's milk.<sup>22</sup>"You shall tithe all the yield of your seed that comes from the field year by year.<sup>23</sup>And before the LORD your God, in the place that he will choose, to make his name dwell there, you shall eat the tithe of your grain, of your wine, and of your oil, and the firstborn of your herd and flock, that you may learn to fear the LORD your God always.<sup>24</sup>And if the way is too long for you, so that you are not able to carry the tithe, when the LORD your God blesses you, because the place is too far from you, which the LORD your God chooses, to set his name there,<sup>25</sup>then you shall turn it into money and bind up the money in your hand and go to the place that the LORD your God chooses<sup>26</sup>and spend the money for whatever you desire—oxen or sheep or wine or strong drink, whatever your appetite craves.
