And you shall eat there before the LORD your God and rejoice, you and your household.<sup>27</sup>And you shall not neglect the Levite who is within your towns, for he has no portion or inheritance with you.<sup>28</sup>"At the end of every three years you shall bring out all the tithe of your produce in the same year and lay it up within your towns.<sup>29</sup>And the Levite, because he has no portion or inheritance with you, and the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow, who are within your towns, shall come and eat and be filled, that the LORD your God may bless you in all the work of your hands that you do.
14.overview:
Chapter 14 weaves together what may seem disparate threads — mourning customs, dietary laws, and the tithe — but a single golden cord binds them: “you are a people holy to the LORD your God” (14:2). Israel's whole life, down to what they eat and how they grieve, is to express their distinct identity as God's treasured possession. Holiness is to permeate the ordinary.

The dietary laws, distinguishing clean from unclean animals, served to mark Israel out from the nations and to train them in the constant discrimination between holy and common, pure and impure. Whatever the precise reasons, the great purpose was sanctification — every meal a reminder that they belonged to a holy God.

The chapter then turns to the tithe, presented not as a grim tax but as an act of joyful worship. Israel is to bring the tithe to the chosen place and eat it before the LORD with rejoicing, “that you may learn to fear the LORD your God always” (14:23). And every third year the tithe is for the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow — God's care for those without inheritance or protection.

For the believer, chapter 14 teaches that holiness is comprehensive, touching every corner of life; that worship is meant to be joyful; and that the people of God are marked by generous care for the vulnerable. We are still “a people holy to the LORD,” called to let our distinct identity shape the whole of ordinary life.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–2 — A Holy People, Distinct in Grief
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As God's holy and treasured people, Israel must not adopt the pagan mourning customs of the nations, for their identity sets them apart even in how they grieve.
verseByVerse.theology: Holiness shapes the whole of life, including grief; God's people mourn differently because they belong to him and have hope.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel was forbidden pagan mourning rites. Now: believers grieve with hope, not as those without God (1 Thess 4:13).

verseByVerse.quote: "You are the sons of the LORD your God. You shall not cut yourselves or make any baldness on your foreheads for the dead. For you are a people holy to the LORD your God, and the LORD has chosen you to be a people for his treasured possession, out of all the peoples who are on the face of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are the sons of the LORD your God. You shall not cut yourselves or make any baldness on your foreheads for the dead.

Identity first, then conduct. That order runs through the whole Bible and it is never reversed: God tells his people who they are, and the behaviour follows from it. Israel is not being told to behave well in order to become God’s sons. She is told to stop doing something because she already is.

What is forbidden is a Canaanite mourning practice — gashing the skin and shaving the front of the head for the dead. The prophets of Baal did it on Carmel to get their god’s attention (1 Kgs. 18:28), and it belonged to a world where the dead had to be appeased and grief was expressed by damaging yourself.

Notice that God does not forbid grief. Deuteronomy has funerals in it; Israel mourned Aaron thirty days and Moses thirty more. What is forbidden is a particular kind of grief — the kind with no hope in it, which turns inward and does violence to the body because there is nothing else to do with the pain.

Paul draws exactly this line for Christians and does it without a word of rebuke to the bereaved: that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope (1 Thess. 4:13). Not do not grieve. Not as others do. A believer at a graveside weeps as hard as anybody and is not doing the same thing, because he is a son of the living God and his dead are not gone.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 3–21 — Clean and Unclean: Holiness at the Table
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel is given detailed laws distinguishing clean animals they may eat from unclean ones they may not, training them to discriminate between holy and common in the most ordinary part of life.
verseByVerse.theology: The dietary laws set Israel apart as holy and trained them to live by God's distinctions; in Christ these laws are fulfilled, and all foods are declared clean (Mark 7:19).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel's diet marked them as God's distinct people. Now: holiness pervades ordinary life, though we are no longer bound by the food laws fulfilled in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not eat any abomination. These are the animals you may eat: the ox, the sheep, the goat, the deer, the gazelle, the roebuck, the wild goat, the ibex, the antelope, and the mountain sheep. Every animal that parts the hoof and has the hoof cloven in two and chews the cud, among the animals, you may eat. Yet of those that chew the cud or have the hoof cloven you shall not eat these: the camel, the hare, and the rock badger, because they chew the cud but do not part the hoof, are unclean for you. And the pig, because it parts the hoof but does not chew the cud, is unclean for you. Their flesh you shall not eat, and their carcasses you shall not touch. "Of all that are in the waters you may eat these: whatever has fins and scales you may eat. And whatever does not have fins and scales you shall not eat; it is unclean for you. "You may eat all clean birds. But these are the ones that you shall not eat: the eagle, the bearded vulture, the black vulture, the kite, the falcon of any kind; every raven of any kind; the ostrich, the nighthawk, the sea gull, the hawk of any kind; the little owl and the short-eared owl, the barn owl and the tawny owl, the carrion vulture and the cormorant, the stork, the heron of any kind; the hoopoe and the bat. And all winged insects are unclean for you; they shall not be eaten. All clean winged things you may eat. "You shall not eat anything that has died naturally. You may give it to the sojourner who is within your towns, that he may eat it, or you may sell it to a foreigner. For you are a people holy to the LORD your God. "You shall not boil a young goat in its mother's milk.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then nineteen verses of animals — which chew the cud, which part the hoof, which have fins and scales, which birds are out. Modern readers find this the least promising material in the Pentateuch, and the question they bring is: why?

Scripture does not give a full answer, and it would be dishonest to manufacture one. Hygiene is the popular explanation and it is almost certainly not the point; the text never mentions health, and some of the permitted animals are no safer than the forbidden ones. Other suggestions — that the unclean animals were used in Canaanite ritual, or that the categories mark creatures that do not fit cleanly into the created order of Genesis 1 — have something to them and none is stated.

What the text does say is in verses 2 and 21, and it says it twice: you are a people holy to the LORD your God. The reason is separation. Three times a day, at every meal, in the most ordinary act of human life, an Israelite was reminded that he belonged to God and was not like the people next door. You could not eat dinner in Israel without remembering whose you were.

And that also made the table a boundary. A man who could not eat what his neighbour ate could not easily dine in his house, and a great deal of the social intermingling that led to intermarriage and idolatry was headed off at the kitchen.

Which is why the day these laws were lifted was such an earthquake. Peter, on a roof in Joppa, was shown a sheet of unclean animals and told to kill and eat, three times, and objected — and then found himself in a Gentile’s house, saying God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean (Acts 10:28). Mark states the conclusion flatly: Thus he declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19). The wall came down at a dinner table, because that is where it had been built.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–27 — The Tithe and the Joy of Worship
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel is to bring the tithe of their produce to the chosen place and eat it before the LORD with rejoicing, so that they may learn to fear him always; provision is made for those who live far away.
verseByVerse.theology: The tithe is an act of joyful worship that teaches the fear of the Lord; giving and feasting before God train the heart to revere and trust him.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel feasted joyfully on the tithe before God. Now: giving is to be glad worship, training us to fear and trust the Lord, not a grim duty.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall tithe all the yield of your seed that comes from the field year by year. And before the LORD your God, in the place that he will choose, to make his name dwell there, you shall eat the tithe of your grain, of your wine, and of your oil, and the firstborn of your herd and flock, that you may learn to fear the LORD your God always. And if the way is too long for you, so that you are not able to carry the tithe, when the LORD your God blesses you, because the place is too far from you, which the LORD your God chooses, to set his name there, then you shall turn it into money and bind up the money in your hand and go to the place that the LORD your God chooses and spend the money for whatever you desire—oxen or sheep or wine or strong drink, whatever your appetite craves. And you shall eat there before the LORD your God and rejoice, you and your household. And you shall not neglect the Levite who is within your towns, for he has no portion or inheritance with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now the tithe, in a form that surprises everybody who has heard tithing preached.

You shall eat the tithe of your grain, of your wine, and of your oil… before the LORD your God, in the place that he will choose.

They eat it. This tithe is not handed over and taken away; it is brought to the sanctuary and consumed there by the family who brought it, in God’s presence, as a feast. The stated purpose is that you may learn to fear the LORD your God always — and the method of learning it is a good dinner.

Then the provision for people who live a long way off, and it is extraordinary. If the journey is too far to carry the produce, sell it, take the money, and spend the money for whatever you desire — oxen or sheep or wine or strong drink, whatever your appetite craves. And you shall eat there before the LORD your God and rejoice, you and your household.

Whatever your appetite craves. That is in the Bible, in a law about tithing, with strong drink named in it. God tells a farming family to convert a tenth of the year’s income into cash, travel to the sanctuary, buy whatever they most feel like eating and drinking, and have a party in his presence.

Anyone who has absorbed the idea that God is fundamentally against enjoyment should sit down with verse 26 until it has done its work. He is not merely permitting the feast; he is commanding it, specifying the drink, and calling it worship.

And then, immediately, the guard against it becoming self-indulgence: And you shall not neglect the Levite who is within your towns, for he has no portion or inheritance with you. Bring the man with no land to the party. Joy in God’s presence that leaves out the person who cannot fund his own is not what is being commanded here.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–29 — The Third-Year Tithe for the Vulnerable
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Every third year the tithe is stored in the towns for the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow, so that they may eat and be filled, and God may bless the work of Israel's hands.
verseByVerse.theology: God's people are marked by generous care for those without inheritance or protection; caring for the vulnerable brings God's blessing.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the third-year tithe fed the landless and vulnerable. Now: God's people are still called to generous, structured care for the poor and marginalized.

verseByVerse.quote: "At the end of every three years you shall bring out all the tithe of your produce in the same year and lay it up within your towns. And the Levite, because he has no portion or inheritance with you, and the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow, who are within your towns, shall come and eat and be filled, that the LORD your God may bless you in all the work of your hands that you do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the end of every three years you shall bring out all the tithe of your produce in the same year and lay it up within your towns. And the Levite… and the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow, who are within your towns, shall come and eat and be filled.

Every third year the tithe stays home, and it becomes a local welfare store for four groups — and the four are always the same four in Deuteronomy: the Levite, the foreigner, the orphan, the widow.

What those four have in common is that none of them owned land. In an agricultural economy, land was the only security there was; a man without a field had no way of surviving a bad year and no way of pressing a claim. So God builds provision for them into the tax system of the nation rather than leaving it to charity, and he does it every third year, automatically, whether anybody feels generous or not.

Note also where it happens: within your towns. Not at the sanctuary, not administered by priests — in the local community, where everybody knew exactly which widow and which foreigner was coming to collect. Israel’s care for the poor was designed to be face to face.

And read the promise attached: that the LORD your God may bless you in all the work of your hands that you do. The blessing is tied to the giving. Which is not a transaction — God is not for sale — but it is a stated principle, and the New Testament repeats it without embarrassment: Whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully (2 Cor. 9:6).

14.theology:
A people holy to the LORD. The refrain — “you are a people holy to the LORD your God” (14:2, 21) — binds the chapter together. Holiness shapes the whole of life: how Israel grieves, what they eat, how they worship and give. Though the ceremonial details (food laws) are fulfilled in Christ, who declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19), the call to comprehensive holiness abides: “be holy, for I am holy” (1 Pet 1:16).

The joy of worship. The tithe is brought and eaten before the LORD with rejoicing, “that you may learn to fear the LORD your God always” (14:23). Giving is not grim duty but glad worship; the regular act of giving and feasting before God trains the heart to revere and trust him.

Care for the vulnerable. The third-year tithe provides structured care for the Levite, sojourner, fatherless, and widow (14:28–29). God's people are marked by deliberate, ongoing generosity to those without inheritance or protection, reflecting the heart of God, who draws near to the lowly and blesses those who care for them.
14.examples:
Then: As God's holy and treasured people, Israel let their distinct identity shape even how they grieved and what they ate, brought the tithe to feast joyfully before the LORD, and built into their economy a regular provision for the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow.

Now: We grieve with hope rather than despair, knowing we are God's children; we let holiness pervade the most ordinary corners of life, though freed from the ceremonial food laws fulfilled in Christ; we give not grudgingly but as glad worship that trains us to fear and trust the Lord; and we are marked, as God's people always have been, by generous, structured care for the poor and the marginalized, reflecting the heart of the God who became poor for our sake.

15.title: The Year of Release: Open Wide Your Hand
15.text: <sup>1</sup>"At the end of every seven years you shall grant a release.<sup>2</sup>And this is the manner of the release: every creditor shall release what he has lent to his neighbor. He shall not exact it of his neighbor, his brother, because the LORD's release has been proclaimed.<sup>3</sup>Of a foreigner you may exact it, but whatever of yours is with your brother your hand shall release.<sup>4</sup>But there will be no poor among you; for the LORD will bless you in the land that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance to possess—<sup>5</sup>if only you will strictly obey the voice of the LORD your God, being careful to do all this commandment that I command you today.<sup>6</sup>For the LORD your God will bless you, as he promised you, and you shall lend to many nations, but you shall not borrow, and you shall rule over many nations, but they shall not rule over you.<sup>7</sup>"If among you, one of your brothers should become poor, in any of your towns within your land that the LORD your God is giving you, you shall not harden your heart or shut your hand against your poor brother,<sup>8</sup>but you shall open your hand to him and lend him sufficient for his need, whatever it may be.<sup>9</sup>Take care lest there be an unworthy thought in your heart and you say, 'The seventh year, the year of release is near,' and your eye look grudgingly on your poor brother, and you give him nothing, and he cry to the LORD against you, and you be guilty of sin.<sup>10</sup>You shall give to him freely, and your heart shall not be grudging when you give to him, because for this the LORD your God will bless you in all your work and in all that you undertake.<sup>11</sup>For there will never cease to be poor in the land. Therefore I command you, 'You shall open wide your hand to your brother, to the needy and to the poor, in your land.'<sup>12</sup>"If your brother, a Hebrew man or a Hebrew woman, is sold to you, he shall serve you six years, and in the seventh year you shall let him go free from you.<sup>13</sup>And when you let him go free from you, you shall not let him go empty-handed.<sup>14</sup>You shall furnish him liberally out of your flock, out of your threshing floor, and out of your winepress. As the LORD your God has blessed you, you shall give to him.<sup>15</sup>You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you; therefore I command you this today.<sup>16</sup>But if he says to you, 'I will not go out from you,' because he loves you and your household, since he is well-off with you,<sup>17</sup>then you shall take an awl, and put it through his ear into the door, and he shall be your slave forever. And to your female slave you shall do the same.<sup>18</sup>It shall not seem hard to you when you let him go free from you, for at half the cost of a hired worker he has served you six years. So the LORD your God will bless you in all that you do.<sup>19</sup>"All the firstborn males that are born of your herd and flock you shall dedicate to the LORD your God. You shall do no work with the firstborn of your herd, nor shear the firstborn of your flock.<sup>20</sup>You shall eat it, you and your household, before the LORD your God year by year at the place that the LORD will choose.<sup>21</sup>But if it has any blemish, if it is lame or blind or has any serious blemish whatever, you shall not sacrifice it to the LORD your God.<sup>22</sup>You shall eat it within your towns. The unclean and the clean alike may eat it, as though it were a gazelle or a deer.<sup>23</sup>Only you shall not eat its blood; you shall pour it out on the ground like water.
15.overview:
Chapter 15 reveals the radical economic vision of God's kingdom — a society shaped by grace rather than greed. Every seventh year, the “year of release,” debts among Israelites are to be canceled, and Hebrew slaves are to be set free. The God who released Israel from the bondage of Egypt builds release into the very calendar of their common life.

The vision is breathtaking: “there will be no poor among you” (15:4), the fruit of a community where the redeemed care generously for one another. Yet realism follows: “there will never cease to be poor in the land” (15:11) — and therefore, “you shall open wide your hand to your brother, to the needy and to the poor.” God's people are to be marked by open hands and open hearts, lending freely, giving generously, never hardening against a brother in need.

The freed slave is not to be sent away empty-handed but “furnished liberally” from the master's abundance (15:14), with the master remembering his own redemption from Egypt. Generosity flows from gratitude for grace received.

This whole vision of release and liberation finds its fulfillment in Jesus, who opened his ministry by proclaiming “the year of the Lord's favor” (Luke 4:19) — the true Jubilee, the great release from the debt of sin and the bondage of death. The God who commands open hands is the God whose own hands were opened on the cross for our liberation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Year of Release: Canceling Debts
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Every seventh year, debts owed by fellow Israelites are to be released; if Israel obeys, there will be no poor among them, and they will lend to many nations but borrow from none.
verseByVerse.theology: God builds release and generosity into the rhythm of his people's life; obedience to his economic vision brings blessing and abundance.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel canceled debts every seventh year. Now: God's people are called to open-handed generosity that reflects the grace they have received.

verseByVerse.quote: "At the end of every seven years you shall grant a release. And this is the manner of the release: every creditor shall release what he has lent to his neighbor. He shall not exact it of his neighbor, his brother, because the LORD's release has been proclaimed. Of a foreigner you may exact it, but whatever of yours is with your brother your hand shall release. But there will be no poor among you; for the LORD will bless you in the land that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance to possess— if only you will strictly obey the voice of the LORD your God, being careful to do all this commandment that I command you today. For the LORD your God will bless you, as he promised you, and you shall lend to many nations, but you shall not borrow, and you shall rule over many nations, but they shall not rule over you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the end of every seven years you shall grant a release… every creditor shall release what he has lent to his neighbor.

Every seventh year, debts between Israelites are cancelled. Not rescheduled, not reduced — cancelled, by law, on a fixed date that everybody knew was coming.

There is nothing like it in the ancient world as a standing institution. Kings occasionally proclaimed a general remission of debts on their accession, as a gesture; Israel had one written into the calendar, recurring, independent of who was on the throne. And the reason given is theological rather than economic: because the LORD’s release has been proclaimed. It is his release, not the creditor’s generosity.

Then two statements that appear to contradict each other, four verses apart. Verse 4: there will be no poor among you. Verse 11: there will never cease to be poor in the land.

They are not in conflict; read the conditions attached. Verse 4 is what would happen if only you will strictly obey the voice of the LORD your God — poverty would be eliminated in Israel if the whole nation kept this law. Verse 11 is what will actually happen, because they will not. One is the design; the other is the forecast.

And it is verse 11 the Lord Jesus quotes when a woman pours out expensive ointment and the disciples object: For you always have the poor with you, and whenever you want, you can do good for them (Mark 14:7). He is not shrugging off poverty. He is quoting the verse that commands open-handedness, and the second half of his sentence is the command.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel must not harden their hearts or shut their hands against a poor brother as the year of release approaches, but give freely and ungrudgingly, for there will always be poor in the land to whom they must open wide their hands.
verseByVerse.theology: Generosity is a matter of the heart, not mere outward giving; God commands open-hearted, ungrudging care for the poor, for poverty will always require compassion.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel was to give freely even near the year of release. Now: believers give generously and cheerfully, guarding against a hardened, calculating heart.

verseByVerse.quote: "If among you, one of your brothers should become poor, in any of your towns within your land that the LORD your God is giving you, you shall not harden your heart or shut your hand against your poor brother, but you shall open your hand to him and lend him sufficient for his need, whatever it may be.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If among you, one of your brothers should become poor… you shall not harden your heart or shut your hand against your poor brother, but you shall open your hand to him and lend him sufficient for his need, whatever it may be.

Two images, and they belong together. A hardened heart and a shut hand. God names the inward thing first, because the hand does not close on its own; something has to happen inside first.

And notice how the giving is specified: sufficient for his need, whatever it may be. Not a token. Not a fixed percentage. The measure is the other man’s need, which is an uncomfortable standard because it removes the ceiling and makes each case a judgment.

The word for open is emphatic and gets stronger in verse 11 — open wide your hand. It is the picture of a hand deliberately spread flat so that nothing can be kept back in the palm.

John takes both halves of this — the heart and the hand — and turns them into a test of whether a man is a Christian at all: But if anyone has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does God’s love abide in him? (1 John 3:17). It is the same anatomy: goods, sight, a brother, and a heart that shuts.

verseByVerse.quote: Take care lest there be an unworthy thought in your heart and you say, 'The seventh year, the year of release is near,' and your eye look grudgingly on your poor brother, and you give him nothing, and he cry to the LORD against you, and you be guilty of sin. You shall give to him freely, and your heart shall not be grudging when you give to him, because for this the LORD your God will bless you in all your work and in all that you undertake. For there will never cease to be poor in the land. Therefore I command you, 'You shall open wide your hand to your brother, to the needy and to the poor, in your land.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now God shows that he knows exactly how a shrewd man will handle this law.

Take care lest there be an unworthy thought in your heart and you say, “The seventh year, the year of release is near,” and your eye look grudgingly on your poor brother, and you give him nothing.

The calculation writes itself. It is year six. A neighbour needs a loan. In twelve months the debt will be legally void, so the loan is effectively a gift — and a man who does not want to make a gift finds that he is suddenly unable to help. He has broken no law. He has simply become prudent at the exact moment when generosity would cost him.

God calls that an unworthy thought — literally, a word of belial, worthlessness — and he calls it that before it is ever spoken aloud, because it will never be spoken aloud. Nobody says this. It is a thought in a heart, followed by a regretful conversation about how things are tight this year.

And then: and he cry to the LORD against you, and you be guilty of sin. The poor man does not know he has been calculated against. He goes away and prays, and God hears him, and the prudent man is guilty — of a sin nobody witnessed and he himself could deny with a straight face.

Then the antidote, and it is not about the amount: You shall give to him freely, and your heart shall not be grudging when you give to him. The manner is commanded as well as the act. Which is exactly Paul’s point centuries later, in almost the same words: Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver (2 Cor. 9:7).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A Hebrew slave is to be released in the seventh year and not sent away empty-handed but furnished liberally, in remembrance of Israel's own redemption from slavery in Egypt.
verseByVerse.theology: The redeemed remember their own liberation and extend generous freedom to others; gratitude for grace received fuels generosity given.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the freed slave was sent off with liberal provision. Now: those redeemed by Christ extend liberating, generous grace to others, remembering their own deliverance.

verseByVerse.quote: "If your brother, a Hebrew man or a Hebrew woman, is sold to you, he shall serve you six years, and in the seventh year you shall let him go free from you. And when you let him go free from you, you shall not let him go empty-handed. You shall furnish him liberally out of your flock, out of your threshing floor, and out of your winepress. As the LORD your God has blessed you, you shall give to him. You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you; therefore I command you this today.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The release extends from debts to people. A Hebrew who has sold himself into service — the ancient world’s answer to unpayable debt — goes free in the seventh year.

And then the provision that lifts this above every comparable law in the ancient world: And when you let him go free from you, you shall not let him go empty-handed. You shall furnish him liberally out of your flock, out of your threshing floor, and out of your winepress.

He does not merely leave. He leaves loaded — with animals, grain and wine, enough to start again. Otherwise freedom would be a formality; a man released with nothing is back in servitude within a year, and God closes that door.

And the ground is memory: You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you; therefore I command you this today.

Now go back and look at how Israel left Egypt. The people of Israel… asked the Egyptians for silver and gold jewelry and for clothing… Thus they plundered the Egyptians (Exod. 12:35–36). They did not walk out empty-handed either. God is telling every Israelite slave-owner to do for his servant precisely what God did for him — and the standard of the giving is set by the exodus, not by the market.

That is the pattern of Christian generosity everywhere in Scripture. Not give because it is decent, but give in the manner you were given to. You know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor (2 Cor. 8:9) is Paul making the identical move about a collection for famine relief.

verseByVerse.quote: But if he says to you, 'I will not go out from you,' because he loves you and your household, since he is well-off with you, then you shall take an awl, and put it through his ear into the door, and he shall be your slave forever. And to your female slave you shall do the same. It shall not seem hard to you when you let him go free from you, for at half the cost of a hired worker he has served you six years. So the LORD your God will bless you in all that you do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then a case that is one of the most affecting in the law. A servant, offered his freedom, declines it.

But if he says to you, “I will not go out from you,” because he loves you and your household, since he is well-off with you, then you shall take an awl, and put it through his ear into the door, and he shall be your slave forever.

Consider what has to be true for that scene to happen. Six years of service, and at the end of it a man would rather stay than take his freedom and a herd of animals. It can only mean he has been treated well — that the house was good, the master was kind, and he had come to love them. The law that requires masters to release their servants generously has also produced households that servants do not want to leave.

And the ceremony is public and permanent. An awl through the ear at the doorpost, and a mark he will carry for life. Everybody who saw it would know what it meant: this man belongs here by choice.

The ear is not an accidental choice. It is the organ of hearing and obedience, pinned to the door of the house he has chosen. And a psalm picks that up and puts it in the mouth of somebody else altogether: In sacrifice and offering you have not delighted, but you have given me an open ear… Behold, I have come; in the scroll of the book it is written of me: I delight to do your will, O my God (Ps. 40:6–8) — a passage Hebrews applies directly to Christ (Heb. 10:5–7).

There is one bondservant in history who was under no obligation at all, who could have walked away at any point, and who said I will not go out — and took the nails rather than the awl. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord (John 10:18).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–23 — The Firstborn Devoted to the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The firstborn males of the herd and flock are to be set apart to the LORD, eaten before him at the chosen place if without blemish, but not used for work or shearing; defective animals may be eaten at home.
verseByVerse.theology: The firstborn belongs to God, who claims the best as his own; offering the firstfruits to God is an act of worship and trust.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel devoted the firstborn to God. Now: we give God the first and best, trusting him as the giver of all, and remember Christ the true firstborn given for us.

verseByVerse.quote: "All the firstborn males that are born of your herd and flock you shall dedicate to the LORD your God. You shall do no work with the firstborn of your herd, nor shear the firstborn of your flock. You shall eat it, you and your household, before the LORD your God year by year at the place that the LORD will choose. But if it has any blemish, if it is lame or blind or has any serious blemish whatever, you shall not sacrifice it to the LORD your God. You shall eat it within your towns. The unclean and the clean alike may eat it, as though it were a gazelle or a deer. Only you shall not eat its blood; you shall pour it out on the ground like water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter closes with the firstborn of the herds and flocks, which belong to God and are to be brought to the sanctuary and eaten there before him.

And then a small provision that says a great deal: But if it has any blemish, if it is lame or blind or has any serious blemish whatever, you shall not sacrifice it to the LORD your God. The defective animal is not offered — but neither is it wasted. You shall eat it within your towns.

Two things follow from that. God will not be given the substandard. An animal that would be rejected by a buyer is not a suitable gift to the Almighty, and Malachi will later flay the priests for exactly this: When you offer blind animals in sacrifice, is that not evil?… Present that to your governor; will he accept you? (Mal. 1:8).

And yet the imperfect animal is still food, still a gift of God, still to be enjoyed. The law distinguishes between what may be offered and what may be enjoyed, and does not despise the second.

The whole chapter has been about open hands — debts released, the poor supplied, the servant sent away loaded, and now the best of the flock given back to God. And every one of those commands rests on the same sentence, stated once in the middle of it: you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you. Generosity in Deuteronomy is never a virtue in the abstract. It is the behaviour of people who remember what was done for them.

15.theology:
The economics of grace. Every seventh year debts are canceled and slaves freed (15:1–2, 12). The God who released Israel from Egypt builds release into the calendar. The vision — “there will be no poor among you” (15:4) — is the fruit of a community shaped by gratitude for grace, foreshadowing the gospel's economics, in which those forgiven an unpayable debt are freed to release others.

The open hand and the open heart. “You shall not harden your heart or shut your hand… but you shall open wide your hand” (15:7, 11). Generosity is a matter of the heart, ungrudging and cheerful (cf. 2 Cor 9:7). Because poverty persists in a fallen world, the call to open-handed care is perpetual; Jesus' “you always have the poor with you” (Mark 14:7) mandates, not excuses, ongoing compassion.

Redemption remembered fuels generosity. The freed slave is furnished liberally because “you were a slave… and the LORD your God redeemed you” (15:15). Gratitude for our own redemption is the engine of Christian generosity; the more deeply we grasp how freely Christ saved us, the more freely we give.
15.examples:
Then: Israel was to cancel debts and free slaves every seventh year, send the freed servant away liberally furnished, keep their hearts soft and hands open to the poor, and devote the firstborn and the best to the LORD — all flowing from the memory that they too had been slaves whom God redeemed.

Now: We who have had the infinite debt of sin canceled live with open hands toward the poor, giving cheerfully and sufficiently, never hardening our hearts. We extend liberating, generous grace to others because we remember our own deliverance, give God our first and best, and rejoice in Jesus, who proclaimed the true Jubilee (Luke 4) — the great release from sin and death — and whose pierced hands were opened on the cross for our liberation.

16.title: The Three Pilgrimage Feasts: Rejoice Before the LORD
16.text: <sup>1</sup>"Observe the month of Abib and keep the Passover to the LORD your God, for in the month of Abib the LORD your God brought you out of Egypt by night.<sup>2</sup>And you shall offer the Passover sacrifice to the LORD your God, from the flock or the herd, at the place that the LORD will choose, to make his name dwell there.<sup>3</sup>You shall eat no leavened bread with it. Seven days you shall eat it with unleavened bread, the bread of affliction—for you came out of the land of Egypt in haste—that all the days of your life you may remember the day when you came out of the land of Egypt.<sup>4</sup>No leaven shall be seen with you in all your territory for seven days, nor shall any of the flesh that you sacrifice on the evening of the first day remain all night until morning.<sup>5</sup>You may not offer the Passover sacrifice within any of your towns that the LORD your God is giving you,<sup>6</sup>but at the place that the LORD your God will choose, to make his name dwell in it, there you shall offer the Passover sacrifice, in the evening at sunset, at the time you came out of Egypt.<sup>7</sup>And you shall cook it and eat it at the place that the LORD your God will choose. And in the morning you shall turn and go to your tents.<sup>8</sup>For six days you shall eat unleavened bread, and on the seventh day there shall be a solemn assembly to the LORD your God. You shall do no work on it.<sup>9</sup>"You shall count seven weeks. Begin to count the seven weeks from the time the sickle is first put to the standing grain.<sup>10</sup>Then you shall keep the Feast of Weeks to the LORD your God with the tribute of a freewill offering from your hand, which you shall give as the LORD your God blesses you.<sup>11</sup>And you shall rejoice before the LORD your God, you and your son and your daughter, your male servant and your female servant, the Levite who is within your towns, the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow who are among you, at the place that the LORD your God will choose, to make his name dwell there.<sup>12</sup>You shall remember that you were a slave in Egypt; and you shall be careful to observe these statutes.<sup>13</sup>"You shall keep the Feast of Booths seven days, when you have gathered in the produce from your threshing floor and your winepress.<sup>14</sup>You shall rejoice in your feast, you and your son and your daughter, your male servant and your female servant, the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow who are within your towns.<sup>15</sup>For seven days you shall keep the feast to the LORD your God at the place that the LORD will choose, because the LORD your God will bless you in all your produce and in all the work of your hands, so that you will be altogether joyful.<sup>16</sup>"Three times a year all your males shall appear before the LORD your God at the place that he will choose: at the Feast of Unleavened Bread, at the Feast of Weeks, and at the Feast of Booths. They shall not appear before the LORD empty-handed.<sup>17</sup>Every man shall give as he is able, according to the blessing of the LORD your God that he has given you.<sup>18</sup>"You shall appoint judges and officers in all your towns that the LORD your God is giving you, according to your tribes, and they shall judge the people with righteous judgment.<sup>19</sup>You shall not pervert justice. You shall not show partiality, and you shall not accept a bribe, for a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise and subverts the cause of the righteous.<sup>20</sup>Justice, and only justice, you shall follow, that you may live and inherit the land that the LORD your God is giving you.<sup>21</sup>"You shall not plant any tree as an Asherah beside the altar of the LORD your God that you shall make.<sup>22</sup>And you shall not set up a pillar, which the LORD your God hates.
16.overview:
Chapter 16 sets out Israel's sacred calendar — the three great pilgrimage feasts at which all the men were to appear before the LORD at the chosen place: Passover, the Feast of Weeks (Pentecost), and the Feast of Booths (Tabernacles). The whole year was structured as a rehearsal of redemption, a rhythm of remembrance and rejoicing that kept the mighty acts of God ever before the people.

Passover commemorated the exodus — the night the LORD passed over Israel and brought them out of slavery “in haste.” The Feast of Weeks celebrated the harvest with freewill offerings of gratitude. The Feast of Booths recalled the wilderness wandering, when Israel lived in temporary shelters under God's care.

A striking refrain runs through the feasts: “you shall rejoice before the LORD your God” (16:11, 14). Worship is to be joyful, inclusive — drawing in sons and daughters, servants, Levites, sojourners, the fatherless, and widows — and rooted in the memory of redemption: “you shall remember that you were a slave in Egypt” (16:12).

The chapter then turns to justice, appointing judges and officers and sounding the great cry: “Justice, and only justice, you shall follow” (16:20). Worship and justice belong together; the God who is worshiped in joyful feasts is the God who demands righteousness in the courts. For us, these feasts find their fulfillment in Christ, our Passover Lamb (1 Cor 5:7), the giver of the Spirit at Pentecost (Acts 2), and the One who tabernacled among us (John 1:14).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Passover: Remember the Night of Redemption
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel is to keep the Passover at the chosen place, eating unleavened bread for seven days, remembering the haste of their exodus from Egypt all the days of their life.
verseByVerse.theology: Passover commemorates redemption from slavery and points to Christ, our Passover Lamb, by whose blood we are delivered from death and bondage.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel remembered the exodus each Passover. Now: we celebrate Christ our Passover, whose blood redeems us from sin and death.

verseByVerse.quote: "Observe the month of Abib and keep the Passover to the LORD your God, for in the month of Abib the LORD your God brought you out of Egypt by night. And you shall offer the Passover sacrifice to the LORD your God, from the flock or the herd, at the place that the LORD will choose, to make his name dwell there. You shall eat no leavened bread with it. Seven days you shall eat it with unleavened bread, the bread of affliction—for you came out of the land of Egypt in haste—that all the days of your life you may remember the day when you came out of the land of Egypt. No leaven shall be seen with you in all your territory for seven days, nor shall any of the flesh that you sacrifice on the evening of the first day remain all night until morning. You may not offer the Passover sacrifice within any of your towns that the LORD your God is giving you, but at the place that the LORD your God will choose, to make his name dwell in it, there you shall offer the Passover sacrifice, in the evening at sunset, at the time you came out of Egypt. And you shall cook it and eat it at the place that the LORD your God will choose. And in the morning you shall turn and go to your tents. For six days you shall eat unleavened bread, and on the seventh day there shall be a solemn assembly to the LORD your God. You shall do no work on it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The year opens with Passover, and Deuteronomy adds a phrase to it that is not in Exodus: unleavened bread is the bread of affliction.

You shall eat no leavened bread with it. Seven days you shall eat it with unleavened bread, the bread of affliction — for you came out of the land of Egypt in haste — that all the days of your life you may remember the day when you came out of the land of Egypt.

Flat bread with no yeast is what you make when there is no time to let dough rise. It is the bread of people leaving in a hurry, and it tastes of the night they went. For seven days every year, Israel ate poor food on purpose, so that the memory would go in through the mouth rather than only through the ear.

Note the stated aim: that all the days of your life you may remember. Not for the week — for a lifetime. The feast exists to keep a memory from wearing thin, which is the great preoccupation of this whole book.

And note where it must be kept: not at home, but at the place that the LORD your God will choose. Passover began as a household meal behind a bloodstained door in Egypt; here it becomes a national gathering. The family remembrance grows into a people’s.

Paul takes the leaven and the lamb together and applies both to a church in one sentence: Cleanse out the old leaven that you may be a new lump… For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed (1 Cor. 5:7). And the order is fixed: the lamb first, then the sweeping out. Nobody removes the leaven in order to qualify for the lamb.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–12 — The Feast of Weeks: Rejoice and Remember
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Seven weeks after the harvest begins, Israel is to keep the Feast of Weeks with freewill offerings and joyful, inclusive celebration, remembering their slavery in Egypt.
verseByVerse.theology: The harvest feast expresses grateful joy for God's provision; worship is to be glad and to include the whole community, especially the vulnerable.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel rejoiced at the harvest feast. Now: we celebrate Pentecost, when the Spirit was poured out and the gospel harvest began.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall count seven weeks. Begin to count the seven weeks from the time the sickle is first put to the standing grain. Then you shall keep the Feast of Weeks to the LORD your God with the tribute of a freewill offering from your hand, which you shall give as the LORD your God blesses you. And you shall rejoice before the LORD your God, you and your son and your daughter, your male servant and your female servant, the Levite who is within your towns, the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow who are among you, at the place that the LORD your God will choose, to make his name dwell there. You shall remember that you were a slave in Egypt; and you shall be careful to observe these statutes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seven weeks after the sickle is first put to the grain comes the Feast of Weeks — later called Pentecost — and it is kept with a freewill offering… as the LORD your God blesses you. No fixed amount. Each man brings in proportion to what the harvest gave him.

Then the guest list, and it is the heart of the paragraph: you and your son and your daughter, your male servant and your female servant, the Levite who is within your towns, the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow who are among you.

Seven categories, and after the first three they are all people with no claim on the food. The servants. The landless Levite. The foreigner. The orphan. The widow. God commands the harvest celebration and then fills the table with people who did not own a field.

And the reason follows immediately: You shall remember that you were a slave in Egypt. There it is again. The ground of Israelite generosity is never that the poor deserve it or that giving is admirable. It is that these people were slaves and somebody came and got them, and they are to behave toward the powerless as God behaved toward them when they were powerless.

A harvest festival where the landless eat with the landowners is not a charitable add-on to the worship. It is the worship, and a feast without them would not have been acceptable.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — The Feast of Booths: Joy in God's Provision
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After the ingathering, Israel keeps the Feast of Booths for seven days, rejoicing fully before the LORD; three times a year all the men appear before him, none empty-handed but each giving as God has blessed him.
verseByVerse.theology: Full, abundant joy in God's provision marks true worship; God's people come before him giving in proportion to the blessing they have received.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel dwelt in booths and rejoiced fully. Now: we remember Christ who tabernacled among us, and we worship with full and grateful joy.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall keep the Feast of Booths seven days, when you have gathered in the produce from your threshing floor and your winepress. You shall rejoice in your feast, you and your son and your daughter, your male servant and your female servant, the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow who are within your towns. For seven days you shall keep the feast to the LORD your God at the place that the LORD will choose, because the LORD your God will bless you in all your produce and in all the work of your hands, so that you will be altogether joyful. "Three times a year all your males shall appear before the LORD your God at the place that he will choose: at the Feast of Unleavened Bread, at the Feast of Weeks, and at the Feast of Booths. They shall not appear before the LORD empty-handed. Every man shall give as he is able, according to the blessing of the LORD your God that he has given you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Feast of Booths comes after everything is in — grain threshed, grapes pressed, barns full — and it has one instruction above all others: You shall rejoice in your feast. The same guest list follows, all seven again. And then verse 15: so that you will be altogether joyful.

That is a command to be happy, given by God, in his law, and it is repeated three times in this short chapter (vv. 11, 14, 15). Whatever else Israel’s religion was, it was not grim. God appointed a week of eating and drinking at the point of maximum prosperity and told them to enjoy it thoroughly and to make sure the widow was there.

Then the summary of the three feasts: Three times a year all your males shall appear before the LORD your God at the place that he will choose. Three journeys a year, every year, for every man in the nation — which was a considerable cost in time and in unguarded farms, and which God evidently thought worth it.

And the last provision: They shall not appear before the LORD empty-handed. Every man shall give as he is able, according to the blessing of the LORD your God that he has given you.

Nobody comes with nothing, and nobody is told how much. The measure is what God has given him — which means the poor man who brings little has met the standard exactly as fully as the rich man who brings much, and the rich man who brings little has not. It is the principle the Lord Jesus applied while watching a widow drop in two small coins (Mark 12:41–44), and it is the only measure of giving Scripture ever uses.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel is to appoint judges and officers who will judge righteously, without partiality or bribes, pursuing justice and only justice so that they may live and inherit the land.
verseByVerse.theology: God demands impartial, incorruptible justice; worship and righteousness belong together, for the God of the feasts is the God of the courts.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel's judges were to pursue pure justice. Now: God's people uphold integrity and justice, reflecting the righteous character of God.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall appoint judges and officers in all your towns that the LORD your God is giving you, according to your tribes, and they shall judge the people with righteous judgment. You shall not pervert justice. You shall not show partiality, and you shall not accept a bribe, for a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise and subverts the cause of the righteous. Justice, and only justice, you shall follow, that you may live and inherit the land that the LORD your God is giving you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Straight out of three chapters of feasting, without a pause, comes this: You shall appoint judges and officers in all your towns… and they shall judge the people with righteous judgment.

The juxtaposition is deliberate and it is one of the marks of the Old Testament. A people who have just been commanded to rejoice before God are now told to run honest courts, and the second is not a lesser subject than the first. Worship and justice are not separate departments; the prophets will spend centuries insisting that a nation cannot have the first while neglecting the second (Amos 5:21–24; Isa. 1:11–17).

Three prohibitions follow, tightly stated. You shall not pervert justice. You shall not show partiality — do not recognise faces. And you shall not accept a bribe.

And then the observation about bribery, which is one of the sharpest in Scripture: for a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise and subverts the cause of the righteous. Note whom it blinds. Not fools — the wise. Money does not corrupt only weak or stupid men; it disables good judgment in able ones, and it does it invisibly. Nobody who takes a bribe believes his verdict has been affected.

Then the line that has become the motto of the whole subject: Justice, and only justice, you shall follow. The Hebrew simply repeats the word — tsedeq, tsedeq tirdof, justice, justice you shall pursue. And the verb is pursue, the word used of hunting or chasing down. Justice is not something a society drifts into. It has to be run after.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–22 — No Idolatrous Symbols Beside the Altar
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel must not plant an Asherah or set up a sacred pillar beside the altar of the LORD, for he hates such idolatrous symbols.
verseByVerse.theology: The worship of God must be kept pure and unmixed with idolatry; God hates the corruption of true worship with pagan symbols.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel was to keep God's altar free of idols. Now: we keep our worship pure, refusing to mingle it with the idols of the age.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not plant any tree as an Asherah beside the altar of the LORD your God that you shall make. And you shall not set up a pillar, which the LORD your God hates.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends with two short prohibitions that look like an afterthought and are not.

You shall not plant any tree as an Asherah beside the altar of the LORD your God… And you shall not set up a pillar, which the LORD your God hates.

An Asherah was a wooden pole or living tree representing the Canaanite mother-goddess; a standing pillar was a sacred stone. Both were the ordinary furniture of worship in that world, and both were attractive — a tree is beautiful, and a standing stone looks ancient and serious.

And look where the danger is located: beside the altar of the LORD your God. Not instead of it. Beside it. Nobody is proposing to replace the worship of God; the suggestion is to improve the setting with something the neighbours find moving.

That is the same warning as 12:30, and it is Deuteronomy’s most persistent anxiety about worship. Israel’s great failure was rarely a straight swap of gods. It was addition — the altar of the LORD with an Asherah next to it, on the grounds that it could not do any harm.

And the reason given is startlingly personal: which the LORD your God hates. Not which is unwise, or which will confuse the people. He hates it — because a man whose wife keeps a photograph of somebody else on the bedside table has not committed adultery and has done something.

16.theology:
The calendar of redemption. The three feasts — Passover, Weeks, and Booths — structured the year as a rehearsal of God's mighty acts. They find their fulfillment in Christ: our Passover Lamb (1 Cor 5:7), the giver of the Spirit at Pentecost (Acts 2), and the Word who “tabernacled among us” (John 1:14). The believer keeps a feast of remembrance in the Lord's Supper, recalling our greater exodus from sin and death.

Commanded joy. “You shall rejoice before the LORD your God… so that you will be altogether joyful” (16:11, 15). Worship is to be glad, abundant, and inclusive — drawing in servants, sojourners, orphans, and widows — and rooted in the memory of redemption. A joyless religion misrepresents the God of all delight.

Worship and justice together. “Justice, and only justice, you shall follow” (16:20). The God of the feasts is the God of the courts; impartial, incorruptible righteousness belongs with joyful worship, and pure worship must be kept free of every idol God hates (16:21–22).
16.examples:
Then: Israel's whole year was a rhythm of remembrance and rejoicing — keeping Passover, Weeks, and Booths before the LORD with abundant, inclusive joy rooted in the memory of their redemption — while pursuing pure justice in the courts and keeping God's altar free of every idol.

Now: We celebrate Christ our Passover, the giver of the Spirit, the Word who tabernacled among us, keeping the feast of remembrance at his table. Our worship is to be altogether joyful, glad, and inclusive of the vulnerable; our public life marked by a relentless pursuit of justice; and our devotion kept pure and undivided, refusing to mingle the worship of God with the idols of the age that he hates.

17.title: Kings and Justice: The King Who Reads the Law
17.text: <sup>1</sup>"You shall not sacrifice to the LORD your God an ox or a sheep in which is a blemish, any defect whatever, for that is an abomination to the LORD your God.<sup>2</sup>"If there is found among you, within any of your towns that the LORD your God is giving you, a man or woman who does what is evil in the sight of the LORD your God, in transgressing his covenant,<sup>3</sup>and has gone and served other gods and worshiped them, or the sun or the moon or any of the host of heaven, which I have forbidden,<sup>4</sup>and it is told you and you hear of it, then you shall inquire diligently, and if it is true and certain that such an abomination has been done in Israel,<sup>5</sup>then you shall bring out to your gates that man or woman who has done this evil thing, and you shall stone that man or woman to death with stones.<sup>6</sup>On the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses the one who is to die shall be put to death; a person shall not be put to death on the evidence of one witness.<sup>7</sup>The hand of the witnesses shall be first against him to put him to death, and afterward the hand of all the people. So you shall purge the evil from your midst.<sup>8</sup>"If any case arises requiring decision between one kind of homicide and another, one kind of legal right and another, or one kind of assault and another, any case within your towns that is too difficult for you, then you shall arise and go up to the place that the LORD your God will choose.<sup>9</sup>And you shall come to the Levitical priests and to the judge who is in office in those days, and you shall consult them, and they shall declare to you the decision.<sup>10</sup>Then you shall do according to what they declare to you from that place that the LORD will choose. And you shall be careful to do according to all that they direct you.<sup>11</sup>According to the instructions that they give you, and according to the decision which they pronounce to you, you shall do. You shall not turn aside from the verdict that they declare to you, either to the right hand or to the left.<sup>12</sup>The man who acts presumptuously by not obeying the priest who stands to minister there before the LORD your God, or the judge, that man shall die. So you shall purge the evil from Israel.<sup>13</sup>And all the people shall hear and fear and not act presumptuously again.<sup>14</sup>"When you come to the land that the LORD your God is giving you, and you possess it and dwell in it and then say, 'I will set a king over me, like all the nations that are around me,'<sup>15</sup>you may indeed set a king over you whom the LORD your God will choose. One from among your brothers you shall set as king over you. You may not put a foreigner over you, who is not your brother.<sup>16</sup>Only he must not acquire many horses for himself or cause the people to return to Egypt in order to acquire many horses, since the LORD has said to you, 'You shall never return that way again.'<sup>17</sup>And he shall not acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away, nor shall he acquire for himself excessive silver and gold.<sup>18</sup>"And when he sits on the throne of his kingdom, he shall write for himself in a book a copy of this law, approved by the Levitical priests.<sup>19</sup>And it shall be with him, and he shall read in it all the days of his life, that he may learn to fear the LORD his God by keeping all the words of this law and these statutes, and doing them,<sup>20</sup>that his heart may not be lifted up above his brothers, and that he may not turn aside from the commandment, either to the right hand or to the left, so that he may continue long in his kingdom, he and his children, in Israel.
17.overview:
Chapter 17 continues the theme of justice and turns to the offices that govern God's people — courts, the central tribunal, and most strikingly, the king. The chapter is famous for the “law of the king” (17:14–20), a remarkable charter that subordinates even the monarch to the law of God.

It opens with the demand for justice in worship (no blemished sacrifices) and in the courts (idolatry judged on the testimony of two or three witnesses, with no rash judgment). A central court is established for the hardest cases, and its rulings are to be obeyed — God provides ordered authority to maintain righteousness among his people.

Then comes the law of the king. Israel will one day want a king “like all the nations” (17:14). God permits it but hedges it with restrictions that strike at the very heart of how kings normally behave: the king must not multiply horses (military self-reliance), wives (foreign alliances and divided heart), or silver and gold (greed). Above all, he must write out his own copy of God's law and “read in it all the days of his life” (17:19), so that his heart is not lifted up above his brothers.

Here is the radical vision: a king under the Word, a ruler who is also a humble student of Scripture, a brother among brothers. Israel's kings would largely fail this calling. But it points to the King who would perfectly fulfill it — Christ, the Word made flesh, the humble servant-King whose heart was never lifted up, who came not to be served but to serve.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Justice in Worship and the Courts
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: No blemished sacrifice may be offered, and one accused of idolatry is to be judged carefully on the testimony of two or three witnesses, never on the word of one alone.
verseByVerse.theology: God demands integrity in worship and rigorous justice in judgment; truth must be established by sufficient witnesses, guarding against false condemnation.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: idolatry was judged on multiple witnesses. Now: the church requires careful, corroborated evidence and refuses to condemn on a single testimony.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not sacrifice to the LORD your God an ox or a sheep in which is a blemish, any defect whatever, for that is an abomination to the LORD your God. "If there is found among you, within any of your towns that the LORD your God is giving you, a man or woman who does what is evil in the sight of the LORD your God, in transgressing his covenant, and has gone and served other gods and worshiped them, or the sun or the moon or any of the host of heaven, which I have forbidden, and it is told you and you hear of it, then you shall inquire diligently, and if it is true and certain that such an abomination has been done in Israel, then you shall bring out to your gates that man or woman who has done this evil thing, and you shall stone that man or woman to death with stones.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two demands for integrity open the chapter, one in worship and one in court.

First: You shall not sacrifice to the LORD your God an ox or a sheep in which is a blemish, any defect whatever, for that is an abomination to the LORD your God.

The temptation is obvious and eternal. A farmer with a flock has good animals and damaged ones, and the damaged one is worth less at market. Offering it to God costs him nothing he was going to keep. God calls that an abomination — a word normally reserved for idolatry and the occult — because giving God what you could not sell says something about what you think he is worth. Malachi will make the same charge unanswerable by asking one question: Present that to your governor; will he accept you? (Mal. 1:8).

Then the judicial case: a man or woman found serving other gods is to be executed — but only after you shall inquire diligently, and only if it is true and certain.

That safeguard is the point of the paragraph. In the most inflammatory charge the law recognises, the first requirement is not action but investigation, and the standard is not suspicion or general report but certainty. Israel’s law consistently puts its heaviest evidentiary demands exactly where feeling runs hottest, which is the opposite of what mobs do.

verseByVerse.quote: On the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses the one who is to die shall be put to death; a person shall not be put to death on the evidence of one witness. The hand of the witnesses shall be first against him to put him to death, and afterward the hand of all the people. So you shall purge the evil from your midst.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses the one who is to die shall be put to death; a person shall not be put to death on the evidence of one witness.

Here is one of the foundation stones of biblical justice, and it has outlived Israel by three thousand years. No conviction on a single testimony — however sincere, however respectable, however certain the witness sounds.

The rule exists because one person can be mistaken, and one person can lie, and there is no way to tell the difference from inside the courtroom. Requiring two independent witnesses does not make error impossible; it makes malice expensive, because a false charge now needs a conspiracy.

The New Testament carries the principle straight over and applies it in three different settings: to church discipline — take one or two others along with you, that every charge may be established by the evidence of two or three witnesses (Matt. 18:16); to Paul’s own conduct (2 Cor. 13:1); and, most pointedly, to accusations against a minister — Do not admit a charge against an elder except on the evidence of two or three witnesses (1 Tim. 5:19). God protects the reputation of the accused as carefully as he pursues the guilt of the offender.

And then the requirement that the witnesses cast the first stone. Nobody testifies and walks away. A man who has sworn away another man’s life must be the first to take it, in public, with his own hands — which is the strongest possible deterrent against casual testimony, and the exact provision the men who dragged a woman before Jesus were quietly hoping he would forget (John 8:7).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — The Central Court for Hard Cases
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Cases too difficult for local courts are to be brought to the priests and the judge at the chosen place, whose verdict must be obeyed; presumptuous defiance of the court is a capital offense.
verseByVerse.theology: God provides ordered authority and final courts to maintain justice; submission to legitimate authority guards the community from anarchy.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: hard cases went to the central tribunal. Now: God provides ordered authority in church and society to resolve disputes and uphold justice.

verseByVerse.quote: "If any case arises requiring decision between one kind of homicide and another, one kind of legal right and another, or one kind of assault and another, any case within your towns that is too difficult for you, then you shall arise and go up to the place that the LORD your God will choose. And you shall come to the Levitical priests and to the judge who is in office in those days, and you shall consult them, and they shall declare to you the decision. Then you shall do according to what they declare to you from that place that the LORD will choose. And you shall be careful to do according to all that they direct you. According to the instructions that they give you, and according to the decision which they pronounce to you, you shall do. You shall not turn aside from the verdict that they declare to you, either to the right hand or to the left. The man who acts presumptuously by not obeying the priest who stands to minister there before the LORD your God, or the judge, that man shall die. So you shall purge the evil from Israel. And all the people shall hear and fear and not act presumptuously again.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sets up an appeal court. Cases too difficult for you — the phrase is literally too wonderful, beyond your reach — go up from the local court to the central sanctuary, to the priests and the judge who is in office at the time.

Three things about that arrangement. It assumes local judges will meet cases they cannot settle, and provides for it in advance without shame. It combines priest and judge, so that the hardest questions are decided where worship and law meet rather than in a purely secular room. And its verdict is binding, with severe penalties for defying it, because a legal system with no final court is not a legal system.

The phrase to notice is you shall do according to what they declare to you… you shall not turn aside from the verdict to the right hand or to the left. Neither direction. A man may not evade a judgment by laxity or by scrupulosity.

And there is a reason this matters beyond ancient jurisprudence. A society in which every man is his own final court is exactly what chapter 12 warned about — everyone doing whatever is right in his own eyes — and the remedy God provides is not less freedom but a settled place where hard questions can be brought and answered. God does not expect his people to carry everything alone, and he provides authority precisely so that they need not.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–17 — The King Like the Nations: God's Restrictions
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When Israel desires a king like the nations, God permits one of his choosing from among the brothers, but forbids him to multiply horses, wives, or silver and gold.
verseByVerse.theology: Even the king is subject to God's law; the restrictions guard against military self-reliance, divided allegiance, and greed — the besetting sins of power.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel's king was hedged by God's law. Now: all authority is accountable to God, and leaders must guard against the corruptions of power.

verseByVerse.quote: "When you come to the land that the LORD your God is giving you, and you possess it and dwell in it and then say, 'I will set a king over me, like all the nations that are around me,' you may indeed set a king over you whom the LORD your God will choose. One from among your brothers you shall set as king over you. You may not put a foreigner over you, who is not your brother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now something remarkable. Four centuries before Israel has a king, God legislates for the monarchy — and the way he does it is unlike anything else in the law.

When you come to the land… and then say, “I will set a king over me, like all the nations that are around me,” you may indeed set a king over you whom the LORD your God will choose.

Read that carefully, because two things are held together. God permits a king. And he quotes, in advance, the motive that will actually produce one — like all the nations that are around me — which is not a good motive at all.

When the day came, Israel used almost these exact words: appoint for us a king to judge us like all the nations, and God said to Samuel, they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them (1 Sam. 8:5, 7). God knew the request was a rejection of himself, and he had made provision for it centuries earlier anyway.

That is a striking thing about how God governs. He does not only plan for his people’s obedience. He legislates in advance for their failures, so that when they insist on something they should not have wanted, there is already a way for it to be less ruinous than it might have been. Israel got the king she asked for on the terms God had set before she thought of it.

And the terms begin at once: whom the LORD your God will choose. One from among your brothers. Not a self-made man, and not a foreigner — a king given rather than seized, and one of them rather than over them.

verseByVerse.quote: Only he must not acquire many horses for himself or cause the people to return to Egypt in order to acquire many horses, since the LORD has said to you, 'You shall never return that way again.' And he shall not acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away, nor shall he acquire for himself excessive silver and gold.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three prohibitions follow, and between them they cover the whole anatomy of political corruption.

He must not acquire many horses for himself. Horses meant chariots, and chariots meant military power. And the reason attached is pointed: or cause the people to return to Egypt in order to acquire many horses, since Egypt was the horse market of the region. A king building an army would end up trading with the house of slavery — and the text adds God’s own comment: You shall never return that way again.

And he shall not acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away. Royal marriages in the ancient world were treaties; a wife was a sealed alliance. So this is a prohibition on foreign policy conducted by marriage, and the danger named is not political but personal — lest his heart turn away.

Nor shall he acquire for himself excessive silver and gold. Wealth, and the independence it buys.

Military might, political alliance, personal fortune. Now set that list beside the reign of Solomon: Solomon accumulated chariots and horsemen… and horses were imported for Solomon from Egypt (1 Kgs. 10:26–28); he had 700 wives… and his wives turned away his heart (1 Kgs. 11:3); and the silver he made as common in Jerusalem as stone (1 Kgs. 10:27).

The wisest man who ever lived broke all three clauses of this law, in order, and the historian who records it uses Deuteronomy’s own phrase to explain the ruin: his wives turned away his heart. God had named the exact failure four centuries in advance, and it happened anyway, to the man best equipped to know better.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–20 — The King Who Reads the Law
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king must write his own copy of God's law and read it all the days of his life, so that he fears the LORD, keeps the law, and his heart is not lifted up above his brothers.
verseByVerse.theology: The true king is a humble student of God's word, subject to the law, a brother among brothers; this points to Christ, the King who perfectly embodies the law.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the king was to read the law daily. Now: all leaders are accountable to God's word, and Christ is the King who fulfills it perfectly.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when he sits on the throne of his kingdom, he shall write for himself in a book a copy of this law, approved by the Levitical priests. And it shall be with him, and he shall read in it all the days of his life, that he may learn to fear the LORD his God by keeping all the words of this law and these statutes, and doing them, that his heart may not be lifted up above his brothers, and that he may not turn aside from the commandment, either to the right hand or to the left, so that he may continue long in his kingdom, he and his children, in Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now the climax, and it is one of the most radical political provisions in any ancient document.

And when he sits on the throne of his kingdom, he shall write for himself in a book a copy of this law, approved by the Levitical priests. And it shall be with him, and he shall read in it all the days of his life.

The king must copy out the law by hand. Not commission a scribe — write for himself — and have the copy checked by the priests against the original, so it cannot quietly drift. Then he is to keep it with him and read it every day for as long as he lives.

Consider what that means about where authority sits. In Egypt the king was a god. In Mesopotamia he was the law’s source. In Israel he is the one man in the nation required to write the law out longhand and read it daily, because he is under it. The most powerful person in the country is the most thoroughly governed.

And the stated purposes are two. First, that he may learn to fear the LORD his God — the king is a learner. Second, that his heart may not be lifted up above his brothers.

His brothers. That is what the law is meant to prevent him forgetting — not the technicalities of temple procedure, but that the people he rules are his own family. Power’s characteristic sin is not cruelty; it is the slow, unnoticed conviction that you are of a different kind from the people you govern. A daily hour in the Scriptures is God’s prescription against it.

And there was one King who fulfilled this.
