He was born under the law, knew it well enough to answer the devil out of it three times, said I have kept my Father’s commandments (John 15:10), and whose heart was never lifted up above his brothers — he is not ashamed to call them brothers (Heb. 2:11). Every other king in Israel’s history read this chapter and broke it. He read it and kept it, and then took the curse the breakers had earned.

17.theology:
The king under the Word. The law of the king subordinates even the monarch to God's law (17:18–20). He must write and read Scripture “all the days of his life,” fear God, keep the law, and never let his heart be “lifted up above his brothers.” In a world of god-kings, Israel's king was to be a humble student of the Word and a brother among brothers — the law standing above the throne.

The temptations of power restrained. The king must not multiply horses (military self-reliance), wives (divided allegiance), or silver and gold (greed) (17:16–17). Power concentrates temptation; Solomon violated every prohibition and ruined his kingdom. The restrictions point to the need for a King whose heart would never turn away.

Rigorous, ordered justice. God demands unblemished worship (17:1), corroborated testimony of “two or three witnesses” (17:6), and ordered courts whose verdicts are obeyed (17:8–13). His justice is careful, measured, and protective of truth, and his provision of authority guards the community from anarchy.
17.examples:
Then: Israel was to bring God unblemished offerings, judge carefully on multiple witnesses, submit to ordered courts, and crown a king hedged by God's law — a ruler forbidden the snares of horses, wives, and gold, commanded instead to read the law daily and remain a humble brother among brothers.

Now: We give God our best, for we have been given Christ the unblemished Lamb; we require careful, corroborated evidence and honor legitimate authority in church and society; and we look to the King who perfectly fulfilled the law of the king — the Word made flesh, our brother, whose heart was never lifted up, who trusted God rather than horses, whose love was undivided, who became poor for our sake, and who reigns not by oppression but by self-giving love. Israel's kings failed; Christ alone is the righteous King we long for.

18.title: Prophets, Priests, and the Prophet to Come
18.text: <sup>1</sup>"The Levitical priests, all the tribe of Levi, shall have no portion or inheritance with Israel. They shall eat the LORD's food offerings as their inheritance.<sup>2</sup>They shall have no inheritance among their brothers; the LORD is their inheritance, as he promised them.<sup>3</sup>And this shall be the priests' due from the people, from those offering a sacrifice, whether an ox or a sheep: they shall give to the priest the shoulder and the two cheeks and the stomach.<sup>4</sup>The firstfruits of your grain, of your wine and of your oil, and the first fleece of your sheep, you shall give him.<sup>5</sup>For the LORD your God has chosen him out of all your tribes to stand and minister in the name of the LORD, him and his sons for all time.<sup>6</sup>"And if a Levite comes from any of your towns out of all Israel, where he lives—and he may come when he desires — to the place that the LORD will choose,<sup>7</sup>and ministers in the name of the LORD his God, like all his fellow Levites who stand to minister there before the LORD,<sup>8</sup>then he may have equal portions to eat, besides what he receives from the sale of his patrimony.<sup>9</sup>"When you come into the land that the LORD your God is giving you, you shall not learn to follow the abominable practices of those nations.<sup>10</sup>There shall not be found among you anyone who burns his son or his daughter as an offering, anyone who practices divination or tells fortunes or interprets omens, or a sorcerer<sup>11</sup>or a charmer or a medium or a necromancer or one who inquires of the dead,<sup>12</sup>for whoever does these things is an abomination to the LORD. And because of these abominations the LORD your God is driving them out before you.<sup>13</sup>You shall be blameless before the LORD your God,<sup>14</sup>for these nations, which you are about to dispossess, listen to fortune-tellers and to diviners. But as for you, the LORD your God has not allowed you to do this.<sup>15</sup>"The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, from your brothers—it is to him you shall listen—<sup>16</sup>just as you desired of the LORD your God at Horeb on the day of the assembly, when you said, 'Let me not hear again the voice of the LORD my God or see this great fire any more, lest I die.'<sup>17</sup>And the LORD said to me, 'They are right in what they have spoken.<sup>18</sup>I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers. And I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I command him.<sup>19</sup>And whoever will not listen to my words that he shall speak in my name, I myself will require it of him.<sup>20</sup>But the prophet who presumes to speak a word in my name that I have not commanded him to speak, or who speaks in the name of other gods, that same prophet shall die.'<sup>21</sup>And if you say in your heart, 'How may we know the word that the LORD has not spoken?'—<sup>22</sup>when a prophet speaks in the name of the LORD, if the word does not come to pass or come true, that is a word that the LORD has not spoken; the prophet has spoken it presumptuously. You need not be afraid of him.
18.overview:
Chapter 18 addresses the provision and the dangers surrounding spiritual leadership in Israel — the support of the Levitical priests, the prohibition of pagan occult practices, and, gloriously, the promise of the Prophet to come. It is one of the great messianic chapters of the Old Testament.

The Levites, who have no land inheritance, are to be supported by the offerings of the people, for “the LORD is their inheritance.” God provides for those who serve him at the altar. Then the chapter sweeps away the entire arsenal of pagan spirituality — divination, sorcery, mediums, necromancy — as detestable to the LORD. Israel is not to seek hidden knowledge through occult means but to listen to God's appointed prophet.

And this leads to the chapter's crown: “The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you… it is to him you shall listen” (18:15). Peter, at Pentecost, declares this fulfilled in Jesus (Acts 3:22–23). Here is the supreme Mosaic prophecy of Christ — the Prophet greater than Moses, in whose mouth God puts his very words, to whom all must listen on pain of judgment.

The chapter closes with the test of a true prophet: his words come to pass. But the deepest fulfillment is not in any single Israelite prophet but in the One who is the Word of God himself, the final Prophet through whom God has spoken his last and fullest word (Heb 1:1–2).
18.theology:
The Prophet like Moses. “The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me… it is to him you shall listen” (18:15). Peter declares this fulfilled in Jesus (Acts 3:22–23) — the Prophet greater than Moses, the Word made flesh, in whose mouth God put his words, to whom all must listen on pain of judgment. The Father himself commands, “Listen to him” (Matt 17:5).

The God who speaks versus the silence of idols. Israel must shun all occult practices (18:9–14), humanity's attempt to gain hidden knowledge apart from God. The nations grope in darkness; Israel has the God who speaks. We need not peer into forbidden darkness, for in Christ God has spoken his final and fullest word (Heb 1:1–2).

The LORD is the minister's inheritance. The Levites have no land, “for the LORD is their inheritance” (18:2), and are supported by the people — the principle Paul applies to gospel ministers (1 Cor 9:14). God's servants find their true portion not in earthly inheritance but in God himself.
18.examples:
Then: Israel supported the Levites whose inheritance was the LORD, utterly rejected the occult practices of the nations, and received the great promise of a Prophet like Moses to whom they must listen, tested by the fulfillment of his words.

Now: We support those who labor in the Word, refuse every form of occultism and forbidden quest for hidden knowledge, and listen — as the Father commands — to Jesus, the Prophet greater than Moses, the Word of God made flesh, through whom God has spoken his last and fullest word. To refuse to hear this Prophet is to incur judgment; to listen to him is life. Our whole calling is the glad obedience of listening to the beloved Son in whom the Father is well pleased.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Priests and Their Portion
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The tribe of Levi is given no land. They live on what Israel brings to God, receiving specified portions from every sacrifice and the firstfruits of every harvest — and any Levite from any town may come and serve on equal terms.
verseByVerse.theology: The provision rests on a promise: the LORD is their inheritance, as he promised them (v. 2). Levi has no acres because Levi has God, and the arrangement is a pledge God made and keeps. Paul reasons from this very statute to the support of gospel ministers (1 Cor. 9:13–14) — those who serve at the altar live by the altar.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a whole tribe lived without land, sustained by what the nation carried to God, so that the worship of Israel never depended on somebody being free that week. Now: a congregation that supports those who labour in the Word is not being generous; it is obeying an arrangement God made, and it frees the man to give himself to the work.

verseByVerse.quote: "The Levitical priests, all the tribe of Levi, shall have no portion or inheritance with Israel. They shall eat the LORD's food offerings as their inheritance. They shall have no inheritance among their brothers; the LORD is their inheritance, as he promised them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Levitical priests, all the tribe of Levi, shall have no portion or inheritance with Israel… the LORD is their inheritance, as he promised them.

Moses is preaching now, not legislating. He is standing in front of the whole nation on the plains of Moab, going back over arrangements God made years earlier, and the phrase he adds is the one to notice: as he promised them. Levi’s landlessness is not an oversight or a penalty. It is the discharge of an undertaking God gave, and Moses reminds a tribe with nothing that God said he would do this.

Consider what it meant week to week. Every other Israelite could walk to the edge of his ground and see where it stopped. He could work it badly and be poorer, or work it well and be richer, and either way it was his and his son’s after him. The Levite had no such line to walk. What he had instead was a sentence — and a sentence is only worth as much as the person who said it.

That is why God ties it to a promise rather than to a policy. He is asking a tribe to live its entire history on his word, in public, in front of eleven brothers who can point at their fields. Every generation of Levites was a standing demonstration that the word of God will actually feed a family. And it is the same arrangement every Christian is on, whether he notices or not: your heavenly Father knows that you need them all (Matt. 6:32).

verseByVerse.quote: And this shall be the priests' due from the people, from those offering a sacrifice, whether an ox or a sheep: they shall give to the priest the shoulder and the two cheeks and the stomach. The firstfruits of your grain, of your wine and of your oil, and the first fleece of your sheep, you shall give him. For the LORD your God has chosen him out of all your tribes to stand and minister in the name of the LORD, him and his sons for all time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the specifics, and they are startlingly domestic. They shall give to the priest the shoulder and the two cheeks and the stomach — named cuts off every ox and sheep offered. And the firstfruits of your grain, of your wine and of your oil, and the first fleece of your sheep.

Notice two things. The first is that the priest received specified parts rather than whatever was left. A worshipper could not decide on the day what he felt like handing over; the shoulder was the priest’s before the animal was killed. There is no room in the arrangement for a man to be generous or grudging, and therefore none for the priest to be either flattered or slighted.

The second is the word first, three times. The first of the grain, the first of the wine and oil, the first fleece. Not the tenth after the household had taken what it needed — the first, before anybody knew whether the rest of the harvest would come in. Israel was asked to give away the earliest evidence that the year would be all right, while it was still the only evidence.

And the reason is given in verse 5: the LORD your God has chosen him out of all your tribes to stand and minister in the name of the LORD. The support is not a wage for services rendered. It is the practical shape of a choice God made, and the nation’s part in it was simply to honour what he had decided.

verseByVerse.quote: "And if a Levite comes from any of your towns out of all Israel, where he lives—and he may come when he desires — to the place that the LORD will choose, and ministers in the name of the LORD his God, like all his fellow Levites who stand to minister there before the LORD, then he may have equal portions to eat, besides what he receives from the sale of his patrimony.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A small provision with a large principle inside it. A Levite living out in the country may come to the central sanctuary when he desires, minister there like all his fellow Levites, and — this is the point — he may have equal portions to eat.

Equal. Not a reduced allowance for the newcomer, not a better share for the men who had been there longest, not a distinction between the resident staff and the visitor from a village nobody had heard of. He turns up, he serves, he eats the same as everyone else.

Anyone who has spent time in a church will recognise what this is guarding against. Wherever people serve together, an inner circle forms — the ones who have been here longest, who know how things are done, who are consulted. It happens without anybody deciding it should, and the man who arrives from outside can serve for years without ever quite getting in.

God legislated against it in the ninth verse of a chapter about priests’ dinners. And the New Testament raises the same guard in the plainest possible terms, over a matter as small as where a visitor sits: if you pay attention to the one who wears the fine clothing and say, “You sit here in a good place”… have you not then made distinctions among yourselves? (Jas. 2:3–4).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–14 — No Traffic with the Occult
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nine practices are named and forbidden — child sacrifice heading the list, then every method by which the nations tried to reach the future or the dead. Israel is to be whole before the LORD instead, because she has something the nations do not: a God who speaks.
verseByVerse.theology: The prohibition is not a demand to manage without knowing. It is the near half of an argument whose far half is v. 15: the occult is forbidden and a Prophet is promised, in one breath. God does not shut a door without opening a better one. You shall be blameless (v. 13) — the word is tamim, whole, undivided, all of a piece.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel was surrounded by nations who read livers and consulted the dead, and was told to want none of it. Now: the appetite has not changed and neither has the answer. Horoscopes, mediums and the hunt for hidden knowledge all assume God is silent. He is not, and the reason we may leave the future alone is that it is held by a Father who has already told us what we need.

verseByVerse.quote: "When you come into the land that the LORD your God is giving you, you shall not learn to follow the abominable practices of those nations. There shall not be found among you anyone who burns his son or his daughter as an offering, anyone who practices divination or tells fortunes or interprets omens, or a sorcerer or a charmer or a medium or a necromancer or one who inquires of the dead, for whoever does these things is an abomination to the LORD. And because of these abominations the LORD your God is driving them out before you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the ground goes hard. You shall not learn to follow the abominable practices of those nations, and a list follows that is meant to be exhaustive.

It opens with the worst thing in the Bible: anyone who burns his son or his daughter as an offering. That is what heads the list of Canaanite religion — not a metaphor, not a scholarly dispute, but parents putting children in a fire to secure a harvest or a battle. Every line that follows should be read in the shadow of that one.

Then eight more, and English blurs them, so take them one at a time. To practise divination is to seek a decision by casting or reading signs. To tell fortunes is to forecast a person’s future. To interpret omens is to read meaning in ordinary events — a bird, a spill, a shape in the fire. A sorcerer works with potions and spells. A charmer binds by incantation. A medium and a necromancer and one who inquires of the dead all traffic with the dead. Nine practices, and they cover every route by which the ancient world tried to get at what it could not otherwise know or control.

And then verse 12 gives the reason the Canaanites are losing their land: because of these abominations the LORD your God is driving them out before you. That is a direct answer to the question every honest reader of the conquest asks. God is not clearing a country for a favourite. He is judging a civilisation that had been burning its children for centuries, after four hundred years of waiting for it to stop (Gen. 15:16).

verseByVerse.quote: You shall be blameless before the LORD your God, for these nations, which you are about to dispossess, listen to fortune-tellers and to diviners. But as for you, the LORD your God has not allowed you to do this.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You shall be blameless before the LORD your God, for these nations, which you are about to dispossess, listen to fortune-tellers and to diviners. But as for you, the LORD your God has not allowed you to do this.

The word behind blameless is tamim — whole, entire, all of a piece, the same word used of a sacrificial animal without defect. It does not primarily mean sinless. It means undivided: not a man who consults God on Sunday and a horoscope on Thursday, keeping a second channel open in case the first one goes quiet.

And this is where the chapter turns, so do not read verses 9–14 on their own. God is not telling Israel to manage without knowing. He forbids every method the nations used, and then in the very next sentence promises a Prophet. The two halves are one argument: you may not go to the dead — because I am going to speak to you.

That matters, because the appetite behind the occult is not wickedness so much as fear. People consult mediums because somebody has died and they cannot bear the silence; they read horoscopes because next year is dark and they want a handhold. Saul went to the witch at Endor on the night before he died, and the text says exactly why: when Saul inquired of the LORD, the LORD did not answer him (1 Sam. 28:6). He wanted a word from God and would not wait for one. The alternative God offers here is not stoicism. It is a voice.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God promises a Prophet from among Israel’s own brothers, in whose mouth he will put his words, and to whom the whole nation must listen. The promise answers the people’s own terrified request at Horeb — and God says their fear was right.
verseByVerse.theology: This is the supreme messianic prophecy of the Pentateuch outside Genesis. Peter preaches it as fulfilled in the risen Jesus (Acts 3:22–23) and Stephen repeats it (Acts 7:37); the Father himself echoes its central command on the mount of transfiguration — listen to him (Matt. 17:5). A Prophet like Moses means a mediator of a covenant, an intercessor, and one rejected by his own brothers.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a people who could not bear to hear God directly were given a man to stand between them and the fire. Now: the Mediator has come, and the God whose voice would have killed us has spoken to us in a human voice, at a carpenter’s bench and on a hillside and from a cross.

verseByVerse.quote: "The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, from your brothers—it is to him you shall listen— just as you desired of the LORD your God at Horeb on the day of the assembly, when you said, 'Let me not hear again the voice of the LORD my God or see this great fire any more, lest I die.' And the LORD said to me, 'They are right in what they have spoken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, from your brothers—it is to him you shall listen.

And then Moses explains where the promise came from, and it is not where anyone would guess. Just as you desired of the LORD your God at Horeb on the day of the assembly, when you said, “Let me not hear again the voice of the LORD my God or see this great fire any more, lest I die.”

Go back to that day. The mountain was burning to the heart of heaven, the trumpet was sounding, God was speaking the Ten Commandments in an audible voice, and the entire nation backed away and begged Moses to make it stop. They asked never to hear God again. On the face of it that is the low point of Israel’s history — a people offered the direct voice of God and asking to be spared it.

Now read what God says about that request: They are right in what they have spoken.

He agrees with them. He does not tell them to be braver, or rebuke them for cowardice, or insist that they would manage if they tried. He says they are correct — unmediated contact between the holy God and sinners would kill them, and they were right to say so. And then, out of that agreement, comes the promise of a Prophet.

Which means the greatest messianic prophecy in the book of Deuteronomy grew out of a frightened crowd telling God they could not survive him. He took their terror seriously, called it accurate, and answered it — not by turning down the fire but by providing somebody to stand in it on their behalf.

verseByVerse.quote: I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers. And I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I command him. And whoever will not listen to my words that he shall speak in my name, I myself will require it of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers. And I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I command him.

Two phrases carry the weight. The first is like you — like Moses. Israel had many prophets afterwards and none of them was that. Moses was not merely a man who delivered messages; he mediated a covenant, interceded for a nation under sentence and offered to be blotted out in its place, spoke with God face to face, and was rejected by the brothers he came to rescue. A prophet like Moses is a very particular thing, and the description is uncomfortably specific.

The second is from among their brothers. Not an angel, not a voice out of the fire — one of them. The mediator has to be one of the people he is standing for, which is exactly the argument Hebrews makes about the incarnation: he had to be made like his brothers in every respect (Heb. 2:17).

Then the sanction, and it is severe: whoever will not listen to my words that he shall speak in my name, I myself will require it of him. Not the prophet will require it. God will. To ignore this Prophet is to be dealt with by God personally.

Peter stood in Solomon’s Portico with a healed cripple beside him and quoted this passage word for word to a Jerusalem crowd, and then said who it was about: God, having raised up his servant, sent him to you first, to bless you by turning every one of you from your wickedness (Acts 3:22–26). Stephen quoted it too, minutes before they killed him (Acts 7:37). And on a mountain in Galilee the cloud came down and the Father said the one thing this promise had been waiting fourteen centuries to hear said out loud: This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased; listen to him (Matt. 17:5).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–22 — The Test of a True Prophet
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A prophet who speaks presumptuously in the LORD’s name, or in the name of other gods, is to die. And Israel is given a plain test for telling the difference: does what he says come true?
verseByVerse.theology: With the loyalty test of chapter 13, this gives Israel two objective criteria — a message must agree with what God has already revealed, and its predictions must stand. God does not leave his people defenceless against anyone who claims to speak for him. The final answer, though, is not a better test but a better Prophet: in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son (Heb. 1:1–2).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel could weigh a claimant rather than being at his mercy. Now: the same obligation stands — test the spirits (1 John 4:1) — and the same relief: God has spoken his last and fullest word, and it is not a message but a Person.

verseByVerse.quote: But the prophet who presumes to speak a word in my name that I have not commanded him to speak, or who speaks in the name of other gods, that same prophet shall die.' And if you say in your heart, 'How may we know the word that the LORD has not spoken?'— when a prophet speaks in the name of the LORD, if the word does not come to pass or come true, that is a word that the LORD has not spoken; the prophet has spoken it presumptuously. You need not be afraid of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel is now going to be receiving messages from men claiming to speak for God, so the chapter ends by giving her a way to tell. Two things are named. The prophet who presumes to speak a word in my name that I have not commanded, or who speaks in the name of other gods, is to die. And the test: if the word does not come to pass or come true, that is a word that the LORD has not spoken.

An honest reader asks whether that is workable, since some prophecies take centuries. It is, and the reason is in how false prophets actually operate: the man inventing a message in God’s name is nearly always predicting something near — peace this year, victory in this battle, Babylon will not come. Jeremiah faced exactly that and Hananiah was dead within two months (Jer. 28). The test bites where the lying is done.

And read it alongside chapter 13, which supplies the other half: a prophet whose sign does come true but who says let us go after other gods is to be rejected anyway. So Israel had two criteria — does it come true, and does it agree with what God has already said — and a claimant had to pass both. God does not leave his people at the mercy of anyone confident enough to say thus says the LORD. The obligation continues: do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits (1 John 4:1).

Verse 20 should also make anybody who stands up to preach go quiet for a moment. It is a capital matter to say God has spoken when he has not. The safety of a preacher lies entirely in staying inside what is written, and the man who wanders outside it is not being bold.

But the chapter’s last word is not a test; it is a Person. Israel was given a succession of prophets, and every one of them died and had to be replaced and could be got wrong. Then the succession stopped, because the promise was kept in full: Long ago, at many times and in many ways, God spoke to our fathers by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed the heir of all things (Heb. 1:1–2). The nations strained after the dead for a whisper. Israel was told to wait for a voice. And the voice, when it came, had a face, and ate with sinners, and wept at a grave, and said I am the resurrection and the life.

19.title: Cities of Refuge and the Law of Witnesses
19.text: <sup>1</sup>"When the LORD your God cuts off the nations whose land the LORD your God is giving you, and you dispossess them and dwell in their cities and in their houses,<sup>2</sup>you shall set apart three cities for yourselves in the land that the LORD your God is giving you to possess.<sup>3</sup>You shall measure the distances and divide into three parts the area of the land that the LORD your God gives you as a possession, so that any manslayer can flee to them.<sup>4</sup>"This is the provision for the manslayer, who by fleeing there may save his life. If anyone kills his neighbor unintentionally without having hated him in the past—<sup>5</sup>as when someone goes into the forest with his neighbor to cut wood, and his hand swings the axe to cut down a tree, and the head slips from the handle and strikes his neighbor so that he dies—he may flee to one of these cities and live,<sup>6</sup>lest the avenger of blood in hot anger pursue the manslayer and overtake him, because the way is long, and strike him fatally, though the man did not deserve to die, since he had not hated his neighbor in the past.<sup>7</sup>Therefore I command you, You shall set apart three cities.<sup>8</sup>And if the LORD your God enlarges your territory, as he has sworn to your fathers, and gives you all the land that he promised to give to your fathers—<sup>9</sup>provided you are careful to keep all this commandment, which I command you today, by loving the LORD your God and by walking ever in his ways— then you shall add three other cities to these three,<sup>10</sup>lest innocent blood be shed in your land that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance, and so the guilt of bloodshed be upon you.<sup>11</sup>"But if anyone hates his neighbor and lies in wait for him and attacks him and strikes him fatally so that he dies, and he flees into one of these cities,<sup>12</sup>then the elders of his city shall send and take him from there, and hand him over to the avenger of blood, so that he may die.<sup>13</sup>Your eye shall not pity him, but you shall purge the guilt of innocent blood from Israel, so that it may be well with you.<sup>14</sup>"You shall not move your neighbor's landmark, which the men of old have set, in the inheritance that you will hold in the land that the LORD your God is giving you to possess.<sup>15</sup>"A single witness shall not suffice against a person for any crime or for any wrong in connection with any offense that he has committed. Only on the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses shall a charge be established.<sup>16</sup>If a malicious witness arises to accuse a person of wrongdoing,<sup>17</sup>then both parties to the dispute shall appear before the LORD, before the priests and the judges who are in office in those days.<sup>18</sup>The judges shall inquire diligently, and if the witness is a false witness and has accused his brother falsely,<sup>19</sup>then you shall do to him as he had meant to do to his brother. So you shall purge the evil from your midst.<sup>20</sup>And the rest shall hear and fear, and shall never again commit any such evil among you.<sup>21</sup>Your eye shall not pity. It shall be life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot.
19.overview:
Chapter 19 takes up two matters bound together by a common concern — the protection of innocent blood and the integrity of justice. Israel is to set apart cities of refuge where one who kills another unintentionally may flee from the avenger of blood and find safety until a fair trial. And the law of witnesses guards against the deadly power of false testimony.

The cities of refuge embody a careful balance: the sanctity of human life demands that the deliberate murderer not escape justice, yet mercy and fairness demand that the one who kills accidentally not be slain in hot blood by an avenging relative. The refuge cities, accessible throughout the land, provide a haven where guilt and innocence can be rightly determined.

The church has long seen in the cities of refuge a beautiful shadow of Christ. The guilty one, pursued by the avenger, flees for his life to the appointed place of safety, and within its walls he is secure. So the sinner, pursued by the just demands of the law, flees to Christ, “the hope set before us” to which we “have fled for refuge” (Heb 6:18).

The chapter then guards justice itself, requiring two or three witnesses and dealing severely with the false witness, who is to suffer the very punishment he sought to inflict. The God of refuge is also the God of truth, who will not have his courts corrupted by lies.
19.theology:
Christ our refuge. The cities of refuge shelter the one pursued by the avenger of blood (19:1–7), a shadow of Christ, to whom sinners “flee for refuge” (Heb 6:18). The refuge does not deny guilt but provides shelter from judgment; Christ bears the wrath so that within him we are forever safe. The roads were prepared so none who fled would find refuge out of reach — so the gospel makes Christ near to all who flee to him.

Justice balanced with mercy. The law shelters the innocent-of-intent yet refuses refuge to the deliberate murderer, to “purge the guilt of innocent blood” (19:13). The sanctity of life made in God's image demands justice, yet that justice never crushes the one who erred without malice. God's law is neither careless nor cruel but precisely just.

The integrity of testimony. No one may be condemned on a single witness (19:15), and the false accuser bears the punishment he intended (19:19). The God of refuge is the God of truth, who will not have his courts corrupted by lies — yet the Truth himself was condemned by false witnesses, bearing the unjust sentence for us.
19.examples:
Then: Israel set apart accessible cities of refuge to shelter the one who killed unintentionally while handing over the deliberate murderer, guarded each family's boundary stones, and protected justice by requiring multiple witnesses and punishing the false accuser with the harm he intended.

Now: We flee to Christ, our refuge from the wrath we deserve, secure within him though guilty; we uphold careful, corroborated justice and abhor false witness; and we marvel that the innocent One, condemned by false witnesses and bearing the judgment we earned, has become the only refuge for sinners. Flee to him, and you are safe; there is no other shelter from the avenger.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Three cities, centrally placed with the roads kept clear, where a man who kills without intent may flee from the avenger of blood and stand trial. The deliberate murderer finds no shelter there; the elders hand him over.
verseByVerse.theology: The refuge does not pretend the manslayer is innocent of the death; it shelters him from a vengeance that cannot distinguish accident from murder until the facts are heard. Hebrews takes the picture up for Christians who have fled for refuge to lay hold of the hope set before us (Heb. 6:18). Mercy and justice are not in tension here: the same law that shelters the one who did not intend it hands over the one who did.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: roads were kept clear and the cities placed so that a frightened man could reach one in a day. Now: the refuge is a Person, and the gospel is the road-clearing - our business is to make him reachable, not to make him respectable.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the LORD your God cuts off the nations whose land the LORD your God is giving you, and you dispossess them and dwell in their cities and in their houses, you shall set apart three cities for yourselves in the land that the LORD your God is giving you to possess. You shall measure the distances and divide into three parts the area of the land that the LORD your God gives you as a possession, so that any manslayer can flee to them. "This is the provision for the manslayer, who by fleeing there may save his life. If anyone kills his neighbor unintentionally without having hated him in the past— as when someone goes into the forest with his neighbor to cut wood, and his hand swings the axe to cut down a tree, and the head slips from the handle and strikes his neighbor so that he dies—he may flee to one of these cities and live, lest the avenger of blood in hot anger pursue the manslayer and overtake him, because the way is long, and strike him fatally, though the man did not deserve to die, since he had not hated his neighbor in the past. Therefore I command you, You shall set apart three cities.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three cities of refuge, and the care taken over them is the point.

You shall measure the distances and divide into three parts the area of the land… so that any manslayer can flee to them. The country is to be surveyed and the cities placed so that nobody is ever too far from one — and Jewish tradition adds that the roads to them were kept cleared and signposted, which is exactly what verse 3 implies.

Then the case, and it is beautifully concrete: as when someone goes into the forest with his neighbor to cut wood, and his hand swings the axe to cut down a tree, and the head slips from the handle and strikes his neighbor so that he dies.

Two men working side by side on an ordinary afternoon. A loose axe head. One is dead and the other is a killer, and neither of them did anything wrong. Scripture does not deal in abstract categories here; it puts a specific accident in front of us, with two friends and a tool, because the man this law exists for is not a criminal and needs to be seen clearly.

And the danger is named exactly: lest the avenger of blood in hot anger pursue the manslayer and overtake him, because the way is long, and strike him fatally. In a society without police, the dead man’s nearest relative had the duty of pursuit. He was not a vigilante; he was the only enforcement there was. But he would be riding out on the day of the funeral, in hot anger, and grief cannot tell an accident from a murder at speed.

So the whole institution exists to put distance and time between a death and a killing — long enough for the facts to be heard. That is what God’s justice looks like when it is written into a map: not indifference to blood, but an absolute refusal to let a man die before anyone has found out what he did.

verseByVerse.quote: And if the LORD your God enlarges your territory, as he has sworn to your fathers, and gives you all the land that he promised to give to your fathers— provided you are careful to keep all this commandment, which I command you today, by loving the LORD your God and by walking ever in his ways— then you shall add three other cities to these three, lest innocent blood be shed in your land that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance, and so the guilt of bloodshed be upon you. "But if anyone hates his neighbor and lies in wait for him and attacks him and strikes him fatally so that he dies, and he flees into one of these cities, then the elders of his city shall send and take him from there, and hand him over to the avenger of blood, so that he may die. Your eye shall not pity him, but you shall purge the guilt of innocent blood from Israel, so that it may be well with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God provides for expansion — three more cities if the territory grows — and then the limit.

But if anyone hates his neighbor and lies in wait for him and attacks him and strikes him fatally… then the elders of his city shall send and take him from there, and hand him over to the avenger of blood, so that he may die.

The refuge is not a loophole. A murderer who runs there is fetched out. And the three marks of murder are named: hates, lies in wait, attacks — motive, premeditation, and act. The law is asking what was in the man, not merely what happened.

Then: Your eye shall not pity him. That is a hard sentence and it is aimed at the judges, not the family. A community that will not carry out a just sentence because it finds the sentence distasteful has stopped protecting the next victim.

And the reason given is that the land itself is at stake: so that the guilt of innocent blood be not upon you. Unavenged blood, in Deuteronomy, defiles a country. A nation that shrugs at murder becomes complicit in it.

Hold the two halves of this paragraph together, because they are the same justice. The man who killed by accident is sheltered even from a grieving family; the man who killed on purpose is taken out of sanctuary and handed over. Mercy that cannot distinguish is not mercy, and severity that cannot distinguish is not justice.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: One short command against moving a neighbour’s landmark - the stone that marked where his God-given inheritance began and ended.
verseByVerse.theology: Israel’s land was allotted by God, so a moved boundary stone was theft from God as much as from the neighbour. It is the quietest crime in the law: no violence, no witnesses, and a family slowly loses what it was given. Proverbs returns to it twice, and both times attaches the widow and the fatherless (Prov. 22:28; 23:10-11).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a stone moved a foot in the night, and a poor family a little poorer every year. Now: the same theft happens by increments in contracts, expenses and estimates - and God, who says of the fatherless their Redeemer is strong, still takes their case.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not move your neighbor's landmark, which the men of old have set, in the inheritance that you will hold in the land that the LORD your God is giving you to possess.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One verse, dropped into the middle of a chapter about killing, and it looks like a change of subject: You shall not move your neighbor’s landmark, which the men of old have set, in the inheritance that you will hold.

It is not a change of subject. Israel’s land was allotted by God, tribe by tribe and family by family, and the boundary stones marked what he had given. To shift one was to steal from a neighbour and to redraw God’s map.

And consider the crime itself, because it is the quietest one in the law. No violence. No confrontation. A man goes out at dusk and moves a stone eighteen inches, and does it again in a few years, and there are no witnesses and nothing to report. Meanwhile a family who cannot afford a surveyor is a little poorer every harvest and cannot say why.

That is why Scripture keeps returning to it, and notice who turns up in the company each time: Do not move the ancient landmark or enter the fields of the fatherless, for their Redeemer is strong; he will plead their cause against you (Prov. 23:10–11). The people this is done to are the ones who cannot fight back, and God appoints himself their advocate.

The modern version needs no stone. It is done in contracts, in invoices, in a fee structure a client cannot follow, in a margin quietly taken from somebody who will never audit it. Nobody calls it theft, and no one is ever charged. The verse is in the Bible for exactly that reason.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–21 — Two Witnesses, and the False One
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: No charge may stand on one testimony. A malicious witness is investigated by priests and judges, and if he is proved false, the punishment he intended for his brother falls on him.
verseByVerse.theology: Two witnesses make malice expensive, because a false charge now needs a conspiracy. And the penalty on the false witness is exact retribution: he receives what he meant to inflict. The lex talionis of v.21 is not a licence for private revenge but a ceiling on punishment - the sentence may not exceed the crime.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a man who would use the courts to destroy a neighbour had to reckon with receiving the sentence himself. Now: the principle stands wherever reputations are handled - Christ himself was condemned by false witnesses (Matt. 26:59-60), and bore the sentence he had not earned.

verseByVerse.quote: "A single witness shall not suffice against a person for any crime or for any wrong in connection with any offense that he has committed. Only on the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses shall a charge be established. If a malicious witness arises to accuse a person of wrongdoing, then both parties to the dispute shall appear before the LORD, before the priests and the judges who are in office in those days. The judges shall inquire diligently, and if the witness is a false witness and has accused his brother falsely, then you shall do to him as he had meant to do to his brother. So you shall purge the evil from your midst. And the rest shall hear and fear, and shall never again commit any such evil among you. Your eye shall not pity. It shall be life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the law of witnesses, and its foundation: A single witness shall not suffice against a person for any crime… Only on the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses shall a charge be established.

Not because one person always lies, but because one person cannot be checked. Requiring two independent testimonies does not make error impossible; it makes malice expensive, since a false charge now needs a conspiracy rather than a grudge.

Then the case of the man who lies anyway: If a malicious witness arises… then both parties to the dispute shall appear before the LORD, before the priests and the judges… The judges shall inquire diligently.

Notice the procedure. Both parties present, before God and the court, with diligent investigation — and the burden falls on the accuser to make his charge stand rather than on the accused to disprove it.

And the penalty is the most exact in the law: then you shall do to him as he had meant to do to his brother. The false witness receives precisely the sentence he was trying to obtain. A man who swore away his neighbour’s life loses his own; a man who tried to have him fined pays the fine. The lie comes back down the same road it went out on.

Then verse 21, which is one of the most misunderstood in the Bible: It shall be life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth.

This is not permission for revenge; it is a ceiling on it. In a world where a slight could start a feud that killed a family, the law says: one eye, no more. The punishment may not exceed the crime. It is a limit written to restrain vengeance, not to license it — which is exactly why the Lord Jesus could take it further in the same direction without contradicting it: You have heard that it was said, “An eye for an eye”… But I say to you, Do not resist the one who is evil (Matt. 5:38–39). Moses capped retaliation at one eye. Christ asks his people to give it up altogether, and then went to a court where false witnesses were heard and the sentence exceeded the crime by an infinite margin, and said nothing.

20.title: Laws of War: The LORD Goes With You to Fight
20.text: <sup>1</sup>"When you go out to war against your enemies, and see horses and chariots and an army larger than your own, you shall not be afraid of them, for the LORD your God is with you, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt.<sup>2</sup>And when you draw near to the battle, the priest shall come forward and speak to the people<sup>3</sup>and shall say to them, 'Hear, O Israel, today you are drawing near for battle against your enemies: let not your heart faint. Do not fear or panic or be in dread of them,<sup>4</sup>for the LORD your God is he who goes with you to fight for you against your enemies, to give you the victory.'<sup>5</sup>Then the officers shall speak to the people, saying, 'Is there any man who has built a new house and has not dedicated it? Let him go back to his house, lest he die in the battle and another man dedicate it.<sup>6</sup>And is there any man who has planted a vineyard and has not enjoyed its fruit? Let him go back to his house, lest he die in the battle and another man enjoy its fruit.<sup>7</sup>And is there any man who has betrothed a wife and has not taken her? Let him go back to his house, lest he die in the battle and another man take her.'<sup>8</sup>And the officers shall speak further to the people, and say, 'Is there any man who is fearful and fainthearted? Let him go back to his house, lest he make the heart of his fellows melt like his own.'<sup>9</sup>And when the officers have finished speaking to the people, then commanders shall be appointed at the head of the people.<sup>10</sup>"When you draw near to a city to fight against it, offer terms of peace to it.<sup>11</sup>And if it responds to you peaceably and it opens to you, then all the people who are found in it shall do forced labor for you and shall serve you.<sup>12</sup>But if it makes no peace with you, but makes war against you, then you shall besiege it.<sup>13</sup>And when the LORD your God gives it into your hand, you shall put all its males to the sword,<sup>14</sup>but the women and the little ones, the livestock, and everything else in the city, all its spoil, you shall take as plunder for yourselves. And you shall enjoy the spoil of your enemies, which the LORD your God has given you.<sup>15</sup>Thus you shall do to all the cities that are very far from you, which are not cities of the nations here.<sup>16</sup>But in the cities of these peoples that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance, you shall save alive nothing that breathes,<sup>17</sup>but you shall devote them to complete destruction, the Hittites and the Amorites, the Canaanites and the Perizzites, the Hivites and the Jebusites, as the LORD your God has commanded,<sup>18</sup>that they may not teach you to do according to all their abominable practices that they have done for their gods, and so you sin against the LORD your God.<sup>19</sup>"When you besiege a city for a long time, making war against it in order to take it, you shall not destroy its trees by wielding an axe against them. You may eat from them, but you shall not cut them down. Are the trees in the field human, that they should be besieged by you?<sup>20</sup>Only the trees that you know are not trees for food you may destroy and cut down, that you may build siegeworks against the city that makes war with you, until it falls.
20.overview:
Chapter 20 sets out the laws of warfare for Israel — and they are unlike the war manuals of any other ancient nation. For Israel, war was not a matter of raw military power but of faith in the God who fights for his people. The priest, not the general, addresses the troops first, and his message is not strategy but trust: “Do not fear… for the LORD your God is he who goes with you to fight for you” (20:3–4).

Remarkably, God provides generous exemptions from battle — the man with a new house, a new vineyard, a new wife, and even the fearful — so that Israel's army was deliberately reduced to those who would fight in faith. God does not want a great host; he wants a believing remnant, so that the victory is plainly his.

For distant cities, Israel must first offer terms of peace; war is not Israel's first resort but its last. Yet for the Canaanite nations within the land, devoted to destruction because of their complete wickedness, no such terms apply — this was the unique judicial judgment of God upon peoples whose iniquity was full.

Even in war, restraint is commanded: the fruit trees are not to be destroyed, “for the tree of the field is man's food” (20:19). Israel is not to wage scorched-earth devastation. The God of holy war is also the God who cares for his creation and limits the destruction of war. For us, the chapter points to the God who fights for his people and to Christ, the true Warrior who has won the decisive victory over sin, death, and the devil.
20.theology:
The LORD fights for his people. Before battle, the priest preaches not strategy but faith: “the LORD your God is he who goes with you to fight for you… to give you the victory” (20:4). Holy war rests on God's presence, not human strength. The believer's spiritual warfare follows the same pattern — we conquer not by our own power but by the One who goes before us (Rom 8:31).

God saves by a believing remnant. The generous exemptions deliberately reduce the army to those who fight in faith (20:5–8), so the victory is plainly God's, not man's (cf. Gideon, Judg 7). God is not impressed by numbers or resources; he delights to save by the few who trust him, that the glory may be his alone.

Justice tempered by restraint. War is not Israel's first resort; terms of peace must precede the siege (20:10), and even in war the fruit trees are spared (20:19). The judgment of the Canaanites was God's unique judicial act upon a people whose wickedness was complete — pointing to the cross, where judgment fell on Christ, and to the gospel's offer of peace to all who will receive it.
20.examples:
Then: Israel went to war not trusting in horses and chariots but in the God who fought for them, with an army reduced to the believing, offering peace before the siege, executing God's unique judgment on the Canaanites, and sparing even the fruit trees from needless destruction.

Now: We face our spiritual battles knowing the Lord goes with us to give the victory; we trust him to save by the faithful few rather than by human strength and numbers; and we rejoice that the God of holy war offers peace to the world in the gospel, having borne his own judgment against sin at the cross. Christ is the true Warrior who has triumphed over sin, death, and the devil, and in him we are more than conquerors.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Before the Battle: the Priest and the Exemptions
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The priest, not the general, speaks first, and his word is not tactics but faith. Then the officers send men home - the one with a new house, the one with a new vineyard, the newly betrothed, and anyone who is afraid.
verseByVerse.theology: Israel goes to war on the ground of who is with her: the LORD your God is he who goes with you to fight for you (v.4). And the army is deliberately reduced rather than maximised, so that the victory can belong to nobody else. Gideon will be whittled to three hundred for the same stated reason (Judg. 7:2).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a man with an unfinished house went home, because God would not have his people lose the good gifts he had given them in a war he intended to win himself. Now: the same God is not served by people driven past what he asked of them, and the church’s strength has never been its numbers.

verseByVerse.quote: "When you go out to war against your enemies, and see horses and chariots and an army larger than your own, you shall not be afraid of them, for the LORD your God is with you, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt. And when you draw near to the battle, the priest shall come forward and speak to the people and shall say to them, 'Hear, O Israel, today you are drawing near for battle against your enemies: let not your heart faint. Do not fear or panic or be in dread of them, for the LORD your God is he who goes with you to fight for you against your enemies, to give you the victory.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When you go out to war against your enemies, and see horses and chariots and an army larger than your own, you shall not be afraid of them.

Notice that God grants the facts first. The enemy does have horses and chariots, and the army is larger. Israel had no cavalry and no chariot corps; against a chariot force on open ground an infantry army was at a severe disadvantage, and everybody involved knew it.

And then something extraordinary happens: when you draw near to the battle, the priest shall come forward and speak to the people.

Not the general. The priest addresses the army on the morning of a battle, and what he delivers is not a strategy or a rallying speech but a sermon, and it opens with the words of the Shema: Hear, O Israel. The same call that opens the confession of faith opens the briefing before combat.

His message is four negatives and one positive. Let not your heart faint. Do not fear or panic or be in dread of them, for the LORD your God is he who goes with you to fight for you against your enemies, to give you the victory.

Four different words for fear, because fear comes in more than one form and God addresses all of them. And against them, not an argument about Israel’s capability but a single fact about God’s presence. That is the pattern of every battle speech in Scripture, and it is the shape of Paul’s question when he has finished eight chapters of argument: If God is for us, who can be against us? (Rom. 8:31).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the officers shall speak to the people, saying, 'Is there any man who has built a new house and has not dedicated it? Let him go back to his house, lest he die in the battle and another man dedicate it. And is there any man who has planted a vineyard and has not enjoyed its fruit? Let him go back to his house, lest he die in the battle and another man enjoy its fruit. And is there any man who has betrothed a wife and has not taken her? Let him go back to his house, lest he die in the battle and another man take her.' And the officers shall speak further to the people, and say, 'Is there any man who is fearful and fainthearted? Let him go back to his house, lest he make the heart of his fellows melt like his own.' And when the officers have finished speaking to the people, then commanders shall be appointed at the head of the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the officers begin sending men home, and the exemptions are astonishing.

Is there any man who has built a new house and has not dedicated it?… who has planted a vineyard and has not enjoyed its fruit?… who has betrothed a wife and has not taken her? Let him go back.

A new house, a young vineyard, a fiancée. God releases men from military service so that they will not die before enjoying the good things he has given them. A vineyard takes four or five years before its fruit may be eaten; a man who had planted one and not yet tasted it is sent home. That is not military logic. It is a Father protecting his children’s joy in a war he intends to win himself.

And then the fourth exemption, which no army in history would grant: Is there any man who is fearful and fainthearted? Let him go back to his house.

Anyone who is frightened may leave, publicly, without penalty. The stated reason is practical — lest he make the heart of his fellows melt like his own, because fear is contagious and travels faster than courage. But the effect is that the army is deliberately reduced to men who actually believe God will do what he said.

God does not want the largest possible force. He wants a believing one, and he will strip the numbers down to make sure nobody can misattribute the result — which is exactly what he says to Gideon: The people with you are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hand, lest Israel boast over me, saying, “My own hand has saved me” (Judg. 7:2).

There is a lesson here for anybody who measures a work of God by its headcount. He has never been impressed by the size of the army, and he has more than once made it smaller on purpose.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–18 — Terms of Peace, and the Cities of Canaan
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Distant cities must first be offered peace, and only besieged if they refuse. The seven nations inside the land are under a different and unrepeatable command.
verseByVerse.theology: Two régimes are set side by side deliberately. War outside Canaan begins with an offer of peace and spares women and children - a striking restraint by ancient standards. The herem inside Canaan is judicial, bounded by a named list, and given a stated protective reason in v.18. It is a model for nobody; the New Testament forecloses it (John 18:36; 2 Cor. 10:3-4).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the offer of peace went out first, and judgment fell only where it was refused. Now: the order is unchanged - we implore you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God (2 Cor. 5:20) - and the terms are far better than any city in Canaan was offered.

verseByVerse.quote: "When you draw near to a city to fight against it, offer terms of peace to it. And if it responds to you peaceably and it opens to you, then all the people who are found in it shall do forced labor for you and shall serve you. But if it makes no peace with you, but makes war against you, then you shall besiege it. And when the LORD your God gives it into your hand, you shall put all its males to the sword, but the women and the little ones, the livestock, and everything else in the city, all its spoil, you shall take as plunder for yourselves. And you shall enjoy the spoil of your enemies, which the LORD your God has given you. Thus you shall do to all the cities that are very far from you, which are not cities of the nations here.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When you draw near to a city to fight against it, offer terms of peace to it.

Israel’s wars are to begin with an offer. Not a demand for surrender after a siege has already starved a city, but terms extended before a blow is struck. If the city accepts, its people become subject labourers; if it refuses and fights, then the siege follows, and the men are killed — but the women and the little ones, the livestock, and everything else in the city… you shall take as plunder.

Modern readers find that harsh, and by our standards it is. Measured against the actual practice of the ancient Near East it is a remarkable restraint. Assyrian kings recorded, with pride, the flaying of prisoners and the building of pillars from severed heads; total annihilation of a resisting city was normal and boasted about. Israel is required to offer peace first, and is forbidden to kill the women and children even of a city that chose war.

And the offer of peace preceding judgment is not merely a rule of engagement here. It is how God himself operates throughout Scripture. Nineveh got forty days and a preacher. Judah got centuries of prophets. And the shape of the gospel is the same: we implore you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God (2 Cor. 5:20) — terms offered, freely, before anything falls.

verseByVerse.quote: But in the cities of these peoples that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance, you shall save alive nothing that breathes, but you shall devote them to complete destruction, the Hittites and the Amorites, the Canaanites and the Perizzites, the Hivites and the Jebusites, as the LORD your God has commanded, that they may not teach you to do according to all their abominable practices that they have done for their gods, and so you sin against the LORD your God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the exception, and it is stated as an exception: But in the cities of these peoples that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance, you shall save alive nothing that breathes.

Everything in the previous paragraph applies to all the cities that are very far from you. This is different, and the difference is the whole point. What is commanded here is not Israel’s foreign policy; it is a bounded judicial act inside one territory, against six named nations, at one moment in history.

And a reason is given, in verse 18, which is the only reason Deuteronomy ever gives: that they may not teach you to do according to all their abominable practices that they have done for their gods, and so you sin against the LORD your God.

The stated purpose is protective. Not conquest, not land-hunger, not racial superiority — containment of a religion that burned children (12:31), so that it would not be taught to Israel. And the tragic footnote is that Israel did not carry it out, and it was taught to her, and within a few centuries Israelites were burning their own children in the valley of Hinnom (Jer. 7:31). The thing God said would happen is exactly what happened.

Three things must be said and held together. This is judgment, executed after four centuries of divine patience (Gen. 15:16). It is unrepeatable, and no nation, church or person has ever held this commission since; the New Testament removes the possibility (John 18:36). And it remains hard, and Scripture does not remove the difficulty — what it does is put alongside it a God who, when judgment finally fell on sin in earnest, arranged for it to fall on himself.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–20 — Do Not Destroy the Trees
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In a long siege, Israel may cut timber for siegeworks but may not touch the fruit trees. The question God asks is unanswerable: are the trees in the field human, that you should besiege them?
verseByVerse.theology: Even a war God has authorised is fenced. What sustains life is not to be destroyed to win a battle, and the restraint is grounded in the nature of the thing itself rather than in Israel’s advantage. It is the seed of every later principle of proportion in warfare.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: an army under orders left the olive groves standing. Now: the same God still asks whether the thing we are about to destroy in order to win was ever the enemy.

verseByVerse.quote: "When you besiege a city for a long time, making war against it in order to take it, you shall not destroy its trees by wielding an axe against them. You may eat from them, but you shall not cut them down. Are the trees in the field human, that they should be besieged by you? Only the trees that you know are not trees for food you may destroy and cut down, that you may build siegeworks against the city that makes war with you, until it falls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And then, at the end of a chapter about siege warfare, this: When you besiege a city for a long time… you shall not destroy its trees by wielding an axe against them. You may eat from them, but you shall not cut them down.

Scorched earth was standard practice. An army besieging a city cut down the orchards — for timber, for siege ramps, and to ruin the district so it could not recover. It took an olive tree fifteen years to bear well and decades to reach full yield; destroying the groves meant a generation of poverty for whoever was left.

God forbids it. Israel may cut any tree that does not bear food, and must leave the fruit trees standing, even while starving out the city they belong to.

And then the question, which is one of the strangest and most humane sentences in the Pentateuch: Are the trees in the field human, that they should be besieged by you?

The tree is not the enemy. It has done nothing, it cannot fight, and it will still be feeding people long after this quarrel is settled. War does not license the destruction of everything within reach; there is a distinction between the combatant and the field he stands in, and God draws it in the middle of a manual on siegecraft.

That single verse is the ancestor of every later principle of proportion in warfare, and it comes from a God whose care runs down into things nobody thought to protect. He notices the sparrow and he notices the olive grove, and he asks the men with the axes a question they cannot answer.

21.title: Various Laws: A Hanged Man Is Cursed by God
21.text: <sup>1</sup>"If in the land that the LORD your God is giving you to possess someone is found slain, lying in the open country, and it is not known who killed him,<sup>2</sup>then your elders and your judges shall come out, and they shall measure the distance to the surrounding cities.<sup>3</sup>And the elders of the city that is nearest to the slain man shall take a heifer that has never been worked and that has not pulled in a yoke.<sup>4</sup>And the elders of that city shall bring the heifer down to a valley with running water, which is neither plowed nor sown, and shall break the heifer's neck there in the valley.<sup>5</sup>Then the priests, the sons of Levi, shall come forward, for the LORD your God has chosen them to minister to him and to bless in the name of the LORD, and by their word every dispute and every assault shall be settled.<sup>6</sup>And all the elders of that city nearest to the slain man shall wash their hands over the heifer whose neck was broken in the valley,<sup>7</sup>and they shall testify, 'Our hands did not shed this blood, nor did our eyes see it shed.<sup>8</sup>Accept atonement, O LORD, for your people Israel, whom you have redeemed, and do not set the guilt of innocent blood in the midst of your people Israel, so that their blood guilt be atoned for.'<sup>9</sup>So you shall purge the guilt of innocent blood from your midst, when you do what is right in the sight of the LORD.<sup>10</sup>"When you go out to war against your enemies, and the LORD your God gives them into your hand and you take them captive,<sup>11</sup>and you see among the captives a beautiful woman, and you desire to take her to be your wife,<sup>12</sup>and you bring her home to your house, she shall shave her head and pare her nails.<sup>13</sup>And she shall take off the clothes in which she was captured and shall remain in your house and lament her father and her mother a full month. After that you may go in to her and be her husband, and she shall be your wife.<sup>14</sup>But if you no longer delight in her, you shall let her go where she wants. But you shall not sell her for money, nor shall you treat her as a slave, since you have humiliated her.<sup>15</sup>"If a man has two wives, the one loved and the other unloved, and both the loved and the unloved have borne him children, and if the firstborn son belongs to the unloved,<sup>16</sup>then on the day when he assigns his possessions as an inheritance to his sons, he may not treat the son of the loved as the firstborn in preference to the son of the unloved, who is the firstborn,<sup>17</sup>but he shall acknowledge the firstborn, the son of the unloved, by giving him a double portion of all that he has, for he is the firstfruits of his strength. The right of the firstborn is his.<sup>18</sup>"If a man has a stubborn and rebellious son who will not obey the voice of his father or the voice of his mother, and, though they discipline him, will not listen to them,<sup>19</sup>then his father and his mother shall take hold of him and bring him out to the elders of his city at the gate of the place where he lives,<sup>20</sup>and they shall say to the elders of his city, 'This our son is stubborn and rebellious; he will not obey our voice; he is a glutton and a drunkard.'<sup>21</sup>Then all the men of the city shall stone him to death with stones. So you shall purge the evil from your midst, and all Israel shall hear, and fear.<sup>22</sup>"And if a man has committed a crime punishable by death and he is put to death, and you hang him on a tree,<sup>23</sup>his body shall not remain all night on the tree, but you shall bury him the same day, for a hanged man is cursed by God. You shall not defile your land that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance.
21.overview:
Chapter 21 gathers a series of laws governing difficult cases in community life — the unsolved murder, the captive woman taken as a wife, the rights of the firstborn, the incorrigibly rebellious son, and the disposal of the body of an executed criminal. Through them all runs a deep concern for the value of human life, the purging of bloodguilt, and the holiness of the community before God.

The law of the unsolved murder (vv. 1–9) reveals how seriously God regards innocent blood: even when no killer can be found, the community must enact a solemn ritual to purge the guilt of bloodshed from the land. No murder is too obscure to matter to God.

Other laws protect the dignity of the vulnerable — the captive woman is not to be treated as mere property, and the rights of the firstborn cannot be set aside by a father's favoritism. The law of the rebellious son, severe as it is, underscores the gravity of persistent, unrepentant defiance against parents and against God.

The chapter's crown, for the Christian, is verses 22–23: the executed criminal hung on a tree is “cursed by God.” Paul seizes on this verse to proclaim the heart of the gospel: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us—for it is written, ‘Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree'” (Gal 3:13). The Lord Jesus, hung on the tree of Calvary, took upon himself the curse we deserved, that we might receive the blessing. Here the law's stern provision becomes the foundation of our redemption.
21.theology:
Christ became a curse for us. “A hanged man is cursed by God” (21:23). Paul finds here the heart of redemption: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Gal 3:13). On the tree of Calvary, the sinless Son bore the curse we deserved, so that the blessing might flow to us — the law's sternest word becoming the gospel's sweetest comfort.

The preciousness of innocent blood. Even an unsolved murder must be solemnly addressed to “purge the guilt of innocent blood” (21:9). God places immense value on human life made in his image; no bloodshed is too obscure to matter to him. All defilement is finally purged not by a heifer's blood but by the blood of Christ (Heb 9:14).

Justice that protects the vulnerable and takes rebellion seriously. The law guards the dignity of the captive woman and the rights of the firstborn (21:10–17), refusing to let power or favoritism override justice. And the severity toward the incorrigibly rebellious son (21:18–21) underscores that rebellion against authority and God is deadly serious — a rebellion the gospel addresses by Christ bearing our judgment, that rebels might become beloved children.
21.examples:
Then: Israel solemnly purged the guilt of even unsolved bloodshed, protected the dignity of captive women and the rights of the firstborn against favoritism, took rebellion against parents and God with utmost seriousness, and buried the hanged criminal the same day because he bore God's curse.

Now: We rest in the gospel proclaimed from this chapter: Christ, hung on the tree, became a curse for us, bearing the judgment we deserved so that we might receive the blessing forever. We honor the value of human life, defend the vulnerable, refuse to let favoritism corrupt justice, and marvel that the God who would not overlook a single drop of innocent blood has dealt fully with all our guilt at the cross, where the blessed One was cursed that the cursed might be blessed.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A body is found in open country and nobody knows who did it. The elders of the nearest town measure the distance, break a heifer’s neck in an untilled valley, wash their hands over it and swear they neither shed the blood nor saw it shed.
verseByVerse.theology: Innocent blood pollutes the land, and God will not let an unsolved killing be quietly forgotten. The ritual is a corporate confession that a death has occurred which the community cannot account for, and a plea: Accept atonement, O LORD, for your people Israel, whom you have redeemed (v.8). Even where no one can be charged, atonement is sought.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a whole town stopped work over a stranger nobody could name, because his blood mattered to God. Now: a society that can absorb unexplained deaths without flinching has lost something this ritual existed to protect, and the blood that finally answers for all of it was not a heifer’s.

verseByVerse.quote: "If in the land that the LORD your God is giving you to possess someone is found slain, lying in the open country, and it is not known who killed him, then your elders and your judges shall come out, and they shall measure the distance to the surrounding cities. And the elders of the city that is nearest to the slain man shall take a heifer that has never been worked and that has not pulled in a yoke. And the elders of that city shall bring the heifer down to a valley with running water, which is neither plowed nor sown, and shall break the heifer's neck there in the valley. Then the priests, the sons of Levi, shall come forward, for the LORD your God has chosen them to minister to him and to bless in the name of the LORD, and by their word every dispute and every assault shall be settled. And all the elders of that city nearest to the slain man shall wash their hands over the heifer whose neck was broken in the valley, and they shall testify, 'Our hands did not shed this blood, nor did our eyes see it shed. Accept atonement, O LORD, for your people Israel, whom you have redeemed, and do not set the guilt of innocent blood in the midst of your people Israel, so that their blood guilt be atoned for.' So you shall purge the guilt of innocent blood from your midst, when you do what is right in the sight of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A body is found in open country, and nobody knows who did it. In most societies, ancient or modern, that is where the matter ends — no suspect, no evidence, no case.

In Israel it triggers a ceremony. Your elders and your judges shall come out, and they shall measure the distance to the surrounding cities. Grown men with measuring lines, walking out into a field to establish which town is nearest to a corpse nobody can name.

Then the elders of that town take a heifer that has never been worked and that has not pulled in a yoke, bring it down to a valley with running water which is neither plowed nor sown, and break its neck there. Untouched animal, untouched ground, running water. And then they wash their hands over it and swear: Our hands did not shed this blood, nor did our eyes see it shed.

Two things are happening. The first is a denial of responsibility, made under oath by the men who bear authority nearest the scene — which also means that if anyone in that town knew anything, the ceremony would give him a very uncomfortable morning.

The second is the prayer, and it is the heart of the passage: Accept atonement, O LORD, for your people Israel, whom you have redeemed, and do not set the guilt of innocent blood in the midst of your people. They ask for atonement for a crime they did not commit and cannot solve — because blood shed in the land defiles the land, and somebody must deal with it before God whether or not anybody can be charged.

What that whole ritual says is that no human life is too obscure to matter. A man nobody could identify, killed by somebody nobody could find, in a field outside a town that had nothing to do with him — and the entire leadership of that town stops work, walks out, and stands before God about it. Set that beside a world that scrolls past a body on the news, and you can measure the distance between two views of what a human being is.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — The Captive Woman and the Unloved Wife’s Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two laws protecting people with no advocate: a woman taken in war, who must be given a month to mourn and may never be sold or treated as a slave; and the firstborn of a wife her husband does not love, whose double portion may not be given to a favourite’s son.
verseByVerse.theology: Neither law describes God’s ideal; both restrain a fallen practice and put a floor under the powerless. The captive is given time, dignity and — if the marriage fails — freedom rather than sale. The unloved wife’s son is protected from a father’s partiality, because justice may not be bent by affection.
