verseByVerse.examples: Then: the two people in Israel least able to defend themselves were named in the law and given rights. Now: the test of any household, church or company is still what happens to the person in it who cannot appeal to anyone.

verseByVerse.quote: "When you go out to war against your enemies, and the LORD your God gives them into your hand and you take them captive, and you see among the captives a beautiful woman, and you desire to take her to be your wife, and you bring her home to your house, she shall shave her head and pare her nails. And she shall take off the clothes in which she was captured and shall remain in your house and lament her father and her mother a full month. After that you may go in to her and be her husband, and she shall be your wife. But if you no longer delight in her, you shall let her go where she wants. But you shall not sell her for money, nor shall you treat her as a slave, since you have humiliated her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now a law that troubles modern readers, and it should be read for what it actually does rather than for what it permits.

A soldier sees a captive woman and wants to marry her. In every other army of the ancient world, that is the end of the story and she has no say in any of it; captured women were spoil, and what happened to them needs no describing.

Here it is stopped. You shall bring her home to your house — home, not the camp. She shaves her head, pares her nails and takes off the clothes in which she was captured, which are the signs of mourning, and then: she shall remain in your house and lament her father and her mother a full month.

A full month. He may not touch her for thirty days, while she grieves for parents who are almost certainly dead in the battle he fought. He has to live in the same house as her sorrow, and watch it, before anything can happen at all.

Then marriage — and she shall be your wife, a wife and not a concubine, with a wife’s standing. And then the provision that closes the last door: if you no longer delight in her, you shall let her go where she wants. But you shall not sell her for money, nor shall you treat her as a slave, since you have humiliated her.

She cannot be sold. She cannot be demoted. If the marriage fails she walks out free, and the law says plainly why — you have humiliated her, which is God taking her side in the statute book against the man who owns everything.

This is not God’s picture of marriage and nobody should pretend it is. It is God regulating a brutal practice in a brutal world and putting a floor beneath a woman who had no advocate, no family and no rights. He does the same thing repeatedly in the law — meeting people where they are, restraining the worst, and protecting the person nobody else will protect. The Lord Jesus said as much about divorce: Because of your hardness of heart Moses allowed you… but from the beginning it was not so (Matt. 19:8).

verseByVerse.quote: "If a man has two wives, the one loved and the other unloved, and both the loved and the unloved have borne him children, and if the firstborn son belongs to the unloved, then on the day when he assigns his possessions as an inheritance to his sons, he may not treat the son of the loved as the firstborn in preference to the son of the unloved, who is the firstborn, but he shall acknowledge the firstborn, the son of the unloved, by giving him a double portion of all that he has, for he is the firstfruits of his strength. The right of the firstborn is his.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second law protects a different powerless person: the son of a wife whose husband does not love her.

If a man has two wives, the one loved and the other unloved… he may not treat the son of the loved as the firstborn in preference to the son of the unloved, who is the firstborn.

Notice that God does not endorse the situation. Polygamy in Genesis and the histories is uniformly a source of misery, and the phrase the one loved and the other unloved is lifted almost directly from the household of Jacob, where Leah was the unloved one and Reuben was her firstborn (Gen. 29:31). The law is written about a mess God did not design.

And it protects the boy. He gets a double portion of all that he has — not because he is better, or preferred, or even liked, but because he is the firstborn and the law says so. A father’s affection may not rewrite an inheritance.

That is a very particular kind of justice: the sort that protects somebody precisely where he is least likely to be defended, in his own home, from his own father. There is no court a boy can appeal to against being loved less. So God writes it into the law instead.

And notice what God repeatedly does with unloved sons. The unloved wife’s firstborn in Jacob’s house was Reuben — and it was Leah, the unloved one, through whose son Judah the Messiah came. God’s habit of preferring the overlooked is not a sentimental idea about him. It runs through the genealogies.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–21 — The Stubborn and Rebellious Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: An incorrigible adult son, a glutton and a drunkard who has rejected all discipline, is brought by his own parents to the elders at the gate and stoned by the men of the city.
verseByVerse.theology: The safeguards are as striking as the severity: the parents themselves must bring the charge, the elders must hear it publicly, and the son is described as an adult given to drink, not a disobedient child. The civil penalty belonged to Israel’s theocracy and is not carried into the church age; the seriousness of rebellion against God-given authority is.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a community was warned that unchecked rebellion in one house spreads to a nation. Now: the gospel deals with exactly this rebel - not by stoning him, but by another Son bearing the sentence in his place.

verseByVerse.quote: "If a man has a stubborn and rebellious son who will not obey the voice of his father or the voice of his mother, and, though they discipline him, will not listen to them, then his father and his mother shall take hold of him and bring him out to the elders of his city at the gate of the place where he lives, and they shall say to the elders of his city, 'This our son is stubborn and rebellious; he will not obey our voice; he is a glutton and a drunkard.' Then all the men of the city shall stone him to death with stones. So you shall purge the evil from your midst, and all Israel shall hear, and fear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is among the most severe laws in the Old Testament, and it needs to be read carefully rather than either dismissed or brandished.

Start with who is described. Not a small child; the Hebrew word covers a young man, and he is a glutton and a drunkard — which is not a description of a toddler in a tantrum but of an adult with an established way of life. He will not obey the voice of his father or the voice of his mother, and, though they discipline him, will not listen. Discipline has already been tried, repeatedly, and has failed.

Then the safeguards, and they are formidable. His father and his mother shall take hold of him and bring him out to the elders. Both parents. The charge must be brought by the two people in the world least likely to want their son executed, and no parent brings such a case lightly or in a temper — which rules out the abusive father using the law as a weapon.

Then it goes to the elders of his city at the gate, in public, and the community judges. It is not a family matter settled at home, and the parents do not carry out the sentence.

Jewish tradition held that this law was never actually applied, and that the safeguards were designed to make it nearly impossible to apply. That may or may not be so; what is certain is that its stated purpose is deterrent: all Israel shall hear, and fear.

And the theology underneath it is that rebellion against parents is the seedbed of everything else. The fifth commandment stands at the hinge of the two tables because the family is where a person first meets authority, and a society in which that goes unchecked in one generation is ungovernable in the next.

The civil penalty belonged to a theocracy that ended, and no church or parent holds it now. But do not miss where the chapter is going. Israel is told to bring the rebellious son out to be stoned — and two verses later we are told what happens to a man hung on a tree. There is a rebellious son in this story, and it is every one of us; and there was a Son who was not rebellious at all, and he is the one who was taken outside the city and executed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–23 — A Hanged Man Is Cursed by God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The body of an executed criminal hung on a tree must not stay there overnight. It is to be buried the same day, for a hanged man is under the curse of God, and the land must not be defiled.
verseByVerse.theology: Paul takes this verse and builds the doctrine of the atonement on it: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us — for it is written, “Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree” (Gal. 3:13). The law’s severest sentence becomes the gospel’s deepest comfort, and even the requirement of same-day burial was kept at Calvary (John 19:31).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a body on a tree was the visible sign of God’s curse, and Israel was to get it down before sunset. Now: we look at a man on a tree and see the curse we had earned, borne by someone else, and taken down before dark.

verseByVerse.quote: "And if a man has committed a crime punishable by death and he is put to death, and you hang him on a tree, his body shall not remain all night on the tree, but you shall bury him the same day, for a hanged man is cursed by God. You shall not defile your land that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now the two verses on which Paul builds the doctrine of the atonement.

And if a man has committed a crime punishable by death and he is put to death, and you hang him on a tree, his body shall not remain all night on the tree, but you shall bury him the same day, for a hanged man is cursed by God.

Take first what the law is describing. This is not execution by hanging; Israel executed by stoning. The body was hung up afterwards, on a pole or a tree, as a public display — and the display meant one thing: this man is under the curse of God. Everybody who walked past knew it.

And even that had a limit. The body must come down before sunset, because a corpse left hanging defiles the land. Even a cursed man is not to be left up overnight in a country where God lives.

Now hold that verse in one hand and a Friday afternoon outside Jerusalem in the other.

Every Jew watching a crucifixion knew this text. It is why a crucified Messiah was not merely implausible to them but blasphemous — the one place a man could hang and prove he was under God’s curse was the last place the Christ could ever be. Paul had thought exactly that, and had persecuted the church over it.

And then, converted, he took the verse that had made Christianity impossible and made it the centre of the gospel: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us — for it is written, “Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree” (Gal. 3:13).

The logic is exact. The law pronounces a curse on everyone who does not keep it (27:26), which is everybody. The curse had to fall somewhere. And on a hill outside the city, the one man who had never earned it took the position the law reserved for the cursed, and hung there in public, so that the sentence would land on him. He was not merely killed. He was, in the terms of this statute, made a curse — and Paul chooses that appalling phrase deliberately, as he chooses he made him to be sin (2 Cor. 5:21).

And they took him down before dark. Since it was the day of Preparation… the Jews asked Pilate that their legs might be broken and that they might be taken away (John 19:31) — men keeping Deuteronomy 21:23 to the letter while the Son of God hung under its curse for them.

The chapter that begins with a murder nobody could atone for ends with the atonement for everything. Israel washed her hands over a heifer and asked God to accept it. He accepted something else instead.

22.title: Laws on Community Life: Love Your Neighbor in the Details
22.text: <sup>1</sup>You shall not see your brother's ox or his sheep going astray and ignore them. You shall take them back to your brother... <sup>4</sup>You shall not see your brother's donkey or his ox fallen down by the way and ignore them. You shall help him to lift them up again.
22.overview:
Chapter 22 takes the great command to love your neighbor and works it out in the concrete details of daily life — lost animals, fallen burdens, roof safety, the mixing of kinds, and a series of laws governing sexual ethics and the protection of marriage. The chapter reveals that holiness is not merely a matter of grand religious gestures but of everyday faithfulness in countless small responsibilities toward one another.

The opening laws are beautifully practical: if you see your neighbor's straying ox or his donkey fallen under its load, you must not “ignore” it — literally, hide yourself from it — but help. Love is active; it does not look away. These are the very situations Jesus would later illuminate in the parable of the Good Samaritan, who refused to “pass by on the other side.”

Other laws guard life (a parapet on the roof to prevent falls) and preserve the God-ordained distinctions woven into creation (not mixing kinds of seed, cloth, or animals) — teaching Israel to honor the boundaries and order God has established.

The latter part of the chapter deals with sexual ethics and the protection of marriage, treating these matters with great seriousness because marriage and sexual integrity lie at the foundation of the community and reflect deep truths about covenant faithfulness. Through it all, the principle holds: to love God is to love one's neighbor in the details of ordinary life, honoring God's order and protecting the wellbeing and dignity of others.

sections.title: Do Not Ignore Your Neighbor's Need
sections.commentary:
The chapter opens with a stream of homely, practical love: if you see your brother's ox or sheep wandering off, “you shall not ignore them” but take them back; if you don't know whose they are, keep them safe until the owner seeks them; the same for a lost garment or anything lost. And if you see your brother's donkey or ox fallen under its load, “you shall not… ignore them. You shall help him to lift them up again” (v. 4).

The repeated phrase — translated “ignore,” but literally “hide yourself” — is striking. The temptation is always to look away, to pretend we did not see, to make the neighbor's trouble none of our business. God forbids this self-protective blindness. Love does not hide itself; it sees, stops, and helps. Keller observed that biblical love is intensely practical and inconvenient — it interrupts our plans to meet the actual, mundane needs of others, from a stray animal to a fallen burden.

These very scenarios illuminate Jesus' parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10), where the priest and Levite “passed by on the other side” — hiding themselves from the wounded man — while the Samaritan stopped and helped. Begg notes that the question Jesus answered, “Who is my neighbor?”, is anticipated here: your neighbor is anyone whose need crosses your path. Calvin saw in these small laws the great commandment in miniature: to love your neighbor as yourself is worked out not in grand gestures but in returning a lost animal and lifting a fallen burden. The believer is called to this same active, seeing, helping love — refusing to hide ourselves from the needs around us, but stooping to serve as Christ, our Good Samaritan, stooped to bind up our wounds.

sections.title: Honoring God's Order: Distinctions and Boundaries
sections.commentary:
A cluster of laws follows that guard life and honor the distinctions woven into creation. A parapet is required on the flat roof of a new house, “that you may not bring the guilt of blood upon your house if anyone should fall from it” (v. 8) — a striking concern for safety and the prevention of needless death. Calvin notes the principle: we are responsible to take reasonable care for the lives of others, and negligence that endangers life carries guilt before God. This is love of neighbor expressed in practical foresight.

Other laws forbid mixing kinds — not sowing two kinds of seed in a vineyard, not plowing with an ox and donkey yoked together, not wearing cloth of wool and linen mixed (vv. 9–11). The mother bird is not to be taken with her young (vv. 6–7), a tenderness toward creation and the preservation of life. These laws about distinctions taught Israel to honor the God-ordained boundaries and order of creation, cultivating a disposition that respected the way God had made the world. Wenham notes that the categories of mixing and distinction trained Israel to think in terms of God's order — that things have their proper place and kind.

The command also addresses the blurring of the distinction between male and female in dress (v. 5), reflecting the goodness and intentionality of God's creation of male and female (Gen 1:27). While the ceremonial details (mixed cloth, mixed seed) were specific to Israel's calling to be a distinct people and are fulfilled in Christ, the underlying principle abides: God is a God of order, not confusion, and his people are to honor the good distinctions and boundaries he has woven into creation. Ferguson notes that even these seemingly minor laws cultivated a reverence for God's created order and a holiness that touched every corner of life.

sections.title: Protecting Marriage and a Wife's Honor
sections.commentary:
The chapter turns to the protection of marriage, beginning with a case of false accusation. A man who, having married a woman, then slanders her by falsely charging that she was not a virgin, is to be punished, fined, and may never divorce her (vv. 13–19). The law protects a wife from a husband's malicious slander, guarding her honor and security against false accusation. Sproul observed that this reflects God's concern to protect the vulnerable — here, a woman whose reputation and future could be destroyed by a lying husband.

Yet the law also takes sexual integrity within marriage with the utmost seriousness. The deep concern of these laws is the holiness of marriage and the truthfulness of the marriage covenant. Marriage in Scripture is not merely a social arrangement but a sacred covenant that reflects deep spiritual realities — ultimately the covenant between God and his people, and between Christ and his church (Eph 5:31–32). To corrupt or falsify the marriage covenant is therefore a grave matter.

Calvin notes that the severity of these laws reflects the foundational importance of marriage and sexual fidelity to the health of the entire community. Where marriage is dishonored, the whole social and spiritual fabric unravels. Ferguson observes that the seriousness with which God surrounds marriage and sexuality testifies to their sacredness and their power for good or ruin. For the believer, these laws — set within their ancient context — point to the abiding truth that marriage is holy, that sexual integrity matters profoundly to God, and that the marriage covenant is to be protected and honored. They point ultimately to the faithful love of Christ for his bride, the church, the covenant that no slander can break and no unfaithfulness can finally destroy, for the Bridegroom is faithful even when his people are not.

sections.title: Sexual Ethics and the Seriousness of Covenant Faithfulness
sections.commentary:
The chapter concludes with a series of laws addressing sexual sin — adultery, the violation of a betrothed woman, and related cases (vv. 22–30). These laws distinguish carefully between consent and coercion: the case of the woman in the open country who cried out but was not heard is treated as the crime of the man alone (vv. 25–27), with the principle stated, “this case is like that of a man attacking and murdering his neighbor.” The law protects the victim and places guilt where it belongs.

The severity of the penalties for adultery and sexual violation reflects how seriously God regards the sanctity of marriage and the dignity of persons. Sproul stressed that sexual sin is never trivial in Scripture; it strikes at the heart of the covenant order God has established, betraying vows, wounding persons, and corrupting the community. The careful distinctions in these laws — weighing consent, circumstance, and culpability — reveal a God concerned for true justice, who neither excuses the guilty nor condemns the innocent.

While the specific penalties belonged to Israel's unique civil order under the old covenant, the abiding principles shine through: marriage is sacred, sexual integrity matters supremely to God, the vulnerable are to be protected, and guilt is to be assessed justly. The prohibition that closes the chapter (v. 30) guards the boundaries of family relationships, reflecting the same concern for order and holiness. Ferguson notes that these laws, far from being arbitrary or repressive, express God's wise design for human flourishing — for sexuality finds its proper place within the covenant of marriage, and its abuse brings ruin. The believer is called to sexual holiness not as a joyless restriction but as the honoring of God's good design, and ultimately as a reflection of the faithful, covenant love that Christ pours out upon his bride. To love God is to love one's neighbor even here, in the most intimate matters, with truthfulness, fidelity, and honor.

22.theology:
Love your neighbor in the details. The chapter works out the second great commandment in the homely details of life — returning a lost animal, lifting a fallen burden, building a safe roof (22:1–8). Love does not “hide itself” (the literal sense of “ignore”) but sees, stops, and helps — the very disposition of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10). Holiness is everyday faithfulness toward one another.

Honoring God's created order. The laws about distinctions and boundaries (22:5–12) trained Israel to honor the order God has woven into creation. God is a God of order, not confusion (1 Cor 14:33); though the ceremonial details are fulfilled in Christ, the principle abides — his people reverence the good distinctions he has established.

The sanctity of marriage and sexual integrity. The marriage and sexuality laws (22:13–30) treat these matters with utmost seriousness, protecting the vulnerable and assessing guilt justly, because marriage is a sacred covenant reflecting Christ and his church (Eph 5:31–32). Sexual holiness honors God's good design and points to the faithful covenant love of the Bridegroom for his bride.
22.examples:
Then: Israel lived out love of neighbor in countless practical ways — recovering lost animals, lifting fallen burdens, building safe roofs — while honoring God's created order and protecting the sanctity of marriage and sexual integrity with great seriousness and careful justice.

Now: We are called to the same active, seeing love that refuses to hide itself from a neighbor's need, stooping to serve as Christ our Good Samaritan stooped to bind our wounds. We honor God's good order in creation, and we treasure marriage and sexual holiness not as joyless restriction but as the honoring of God's wise design and a reflection of the faithful covenant love that Christ pours out upon his bride, the church. To love God is to love our neighbor even in the smallest and most intimate details of life.

23.title: The Assembly of the LORD: Holiness and Compassion
23.text: <sup>14</sup>Because the LORD your God walks in the midst of your camp, to deliver you and to give up your enemies before you, therefore your camp must be holy, so that he may not see anything indecent among you and turn away from you.
23.overview:
Chapter 23 gathers laws concerning who may enter “the assembly of the LORD,” the holiness of the war camp, and a range of community matters — the runaway slave, lending, vows, and respect for a neighbor's property. The unifying theme is the holiness that must mark a people in whose midst the holy God dwells: “your camp must be holy, so that he may not see anything indecent among you” (23:14).

The opening laws about exclusion from the assembly remind us that fellowship with a holy God is not to be taken lightly; there are barriers that sinful and broken humanity cannot cross on its own. Yet even here, the gospel will break through: in Christ, the very ones once excluded — the eunuch, the foreigner — are brought near (Isa 56; Acts 8).

The holiness of the camp, even in matters of bodily function and waste, teaches that God's presence sanctifies the whole of life, down to its most ordinary and private details. The God who walks in their midst calls for comprehensive holiness.

The chapter also reveals God's tender compassion: the runaway slave is to be given refuge, not returned to his master; lending to a brother is not to be at interest; vows are to be kept faithfully; and a neighbor's vineyard or field may be eaten from to satisfy hunger but not plundered for gain. Holiness and compassion, reverence and mercy, walk together in the life of God's people.

sections.title: Who May Enter the Assembly of the LORD
sections.commentary:
The chapter opens with restrictions on entering “the assembly of the LORD” — the gathered worshiping community. Certain persons are excluded: the emasculated, those of forbidden birth, and the Ammonites and Moabites (because of their hostility to Israel during the wilderness journey), while the Edomites and Egyptians may enter after the third generation. These boundaries underscore that approach to the holy God is not a casual matter; fellowship with him is hedged about with seriousness.

We must read these laws in the sweep of redemptive history. Sproul observed that such restrictions taught Israel the holiness of God and the gravity of drawing near to him — there are barriers that sinful, broken humanity cannot simply ignore or cross on its own. The assembly of the LORD was a holy gathering, and the exclusions dramatized that not everyone could presume to enter God's presence.

Yet the glory of the gospel is that these very boundaries are transcended in Christ. Isaiah 56 explicitly promises that the eunuch and the foreigner, once excluded, will be given “a name better than sons and daughters” and brought into God's house. And in Acts 8, the Ethiopian eunuch — doubly excluded under this law — is the first Gentile convert, joyfully baptized into the people of God. Ferguson notes the breathtaking reversal: the barriers that the law erected to teach the holiness of God are torn down in Christ, who by his blood brings near “those who were far off” (Eph 2:13). The dividing wall is broken down (Eph 2:14); in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free. The very ones once shut out are welcomed in, not because the holiness of God has diminished, but because Christ has fulfilled the law and opened a new and living way into the presence of God for all who come to him by faith.

sections.title: A Holy Camp: God Walks Among You
sections.commentary:
When Israel goes to war and encamps, the camp must be kept holy — even in matters of bodily emission and the disposal of human waste, which is to be buried outside the camp (vv. 9–14). The reason given is profound: “Because the LORD your God walks in the midst of your camp, to deliver you and to give up your enemies before you, therefore your camp must be holy, so that he may not see anything indecent among you and turn away from you” (v. 14).

The holiness commanded here extends to the most ordinary and private details of life — even sanitation. Sproul stressed the deep theological point: because God dwells among his people, the whole of life, down to its most mundane functions, falls under the call to holiness. There is no secular zone, no private corner exempt from the presence of the holy God who walks in their midst. Begg notes the astonishing intimacy and the corresponding seriousness: the God of all glory walks among his people, and that presence both blesses (“to deliver you”) and demands (“your camp must be holy”).

For the believer, this principle finds its fullest application in the New Testament truth that we are now the dwelling place of God by the Spirit: “your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit” (1 Cor 6:19), and the church is “a holy temple in the Lord… a dwelling place for God by the Spirit” (Eph 2:21–22). If Israel's camp had to be holy because God walked among them, how much more are God's people now to pursue holiness, for God dwells within them. Ferguson observes that the presence of God is both our greatest comfort and our highest call to holiness. The God who walks in our midst calls for a holiness that touches every corner of life, public and private, sacred and ordinary, because he is always present with his people.

sections.title: Compassion: The Runaway Slave and Just Lending
sections.commentary:
Now the chapter reveals God's tender compassion. A runaway slave who has escaped to Israel is not to be returned to his master but given refuge: “he shall dwell with you, in your midst… you shall not wrong him” (vv. 15–16). This was extraordinary in the ancient world, where extradition of escaped slaves was the universal norm. Israel was to be a refuge for the oppressed, not a partner in their re-enslavement. Keller saw here the heart of a God who sides with the oppressed and provides sanctuary for those fleeing bondage — a foreshadowing of the gospel's liberation of all who flee to Christ from the slavery of sin.

The chapter also forbids charging interest on loans to a fellow Israelite (vv. 19–20), though interest from a foreigner in commercial dealings was permitted. The principle was that within the covenant community, lending to a needy brother was an act of compassion, not a means of profit. Calvin, who wrote thoughtfully on lending and interest, saw the underlying concern: the poor brother must not be exploited or driven deeper into poverty by the burden of interest. Loans to the needy were to be acts of mercy, reflecting the generosity God himself shows.

Sproul stressed that these laws reveal a God who cares deeply for the vulnerable and the oppressed, who refuses to let his people use the misfortune of others for gain. The same compassion that gives refuge to the runaway slave forbids profiting off the poverty of a brother. Ferguson notes the consistent pattern: holiness toward God and compassion toward neighbor are never separated in Scripture. The people in whose midst the holy God walks are to reflect his character — holy in their reverence, generous in their lending, and merciful toward the oppressed and the poor.

sections.title: Keeping Vows and Respecting a Neighbor's Property
sections.commentary:
The chapter closes with laws on vows and a neighbor's produce. Concerning vows: “If you make a vow to the LORD your God, you shall not delay fulfilling it… You shall be careful to do what has passed your lips” (vv. 21, 23). One is not required to make vows, but a vow once made to God must be kept; to break a vow to the LORD is sin. Sproul stressed the seriousness with which God regards our words and promises, especially those made to him; we are accountable for what passes our lips. Calvin notes that rash vows are to be avoided, but solemn commitments to God are sacred and binding. Ecclesiastes echoes this: “When you vow a vow to God, do not delay paying it… It is better that you should not vow than that you should vow and not pay” (Eccl 5:4–5). The believer is called to integrity of word — to be the kind of person whose “yes” is yes (Matt 5:37).

Finally, a beautiful provision of neighborly generosity: a passerby may eat his fill of grapes from a neighbor's vineyard or pluck heads of grain by hand from his field to satisfy hunger, but may not put any in a container to carry away or use a sickle to harvest for gain (vv. 24–25). The hungry traveler is welcome to eat freely; the would-be thief is forbidden to plunder. This balances generosity and the protection of property with great wisdom. Jesus and his disciples enjoyed this very provision when they plucked heads of grain on the Sabbath (Matt 12:1). Begg notes the gracious balance: the law provides for genuine need while guarding against exploitation. The community in whose midst God dwells is to be marked by both integrity (keeping vows) and open-handed generosity (sharing food with the hungry), reflecting the character of the God who keeps his every promise and feeds his people freely.

23.theology:
The holiness of God's dwelling place. “Your camp must be holy, so that he may not see anything indecent among you” — for “the LORD your God walks in the midst of your camp” (23:14). God's presence sanctifies the whole of life, down to its most private details. Now God's people are themselves his temple (1 Cor 6:19; Eph 2:21–22), called all the more to comprehensive holiness because he dwells within us.

Barriers broken in Christ. The exclusions from the assembly (23:1–8) taught the holiness of God and the gravity of approaching him. Yet in Christ the very ones once shut out — the eunuch, the foreigner — are brought near (Isa 56; Acts 8; Eph 2:13–14). Christ has opened a new and living way into God's presence for all who come by faith.

Holiness wedded to compassion. The runaway slave is given refuge (23:15–16), the poor brother is not charged interest (23:19), vows are faithfully kept (23:21–23), and the hungry traveler is freely fed (23:24–25). Reverence toward God and mercy toward neighbor are never separated; the people among whom the holy God walks reflect his holiness and his compassion alike.
23.examples:
Then: Israel honored the holiness required of a people among whom God walked — even in the ordinary details of the camp — while extending compassion to runaway slaves, lending without interest to the poor, keeping their vows faithfully, and feeding the hungry traveler from their fields.

Now: We are God's temple, indwelt by the Spirit, called to a holiness that touches every corner of life because he dwells within us. We rejoice that in Christ the barriers that once excluded are broken down, and the far-off are brought near. And we reflect the character of God by joining reverent holiness with open-handed compassion — keeping our word, lifting the oppressed, refusing to profit from a brother's poverty, and feeding the hungry, for the God among us is both holy and merciful.

24.title: Laws Protecting the Vulnerable: Remember You Were a Slave
24.text: <sup>18</sup>...but you shall remember that you were a slave in Egypt and the LORD your God redeemed you from there; therefore I command you to do this. <sup>15</sup>You shall give him his wages on the same day, before the sun sets... lest he cry against you to the LORD, and you be guilty of sin.
24.overview:
Chapter 24 is a tapestry of laws woven together by a single golden thread: the protection of the vulnerable and the remembrance of redemption. Again and again the refrain sounds — “you shall remember that you were a slave in Egypt” (24:18, 22) — grounding compassion in gratitude for grace received. Because God redeemed Israel from bondage, they must deal mercifully with the poor, the worker, the widow, the orphan, and the sojourner.

The chapter opens with the regulation of divorce — not commanding or commending it, but limiting it and protecting the woman from being treated as a casual possession. Jesus would later teach that this provision was given “because of your hardness of heart” (Matt 19:8), a merciful concession to human sinfulness, not God's original design for marriage.

Other laws protect the dignity and survival of the poor: a newlywed exempted from war and duty for a year to bring joy to his wife; the millstone not taken in pledge, for that would be taking a man's livelihood; the pledged cloak returned by nightfall so the poor man can sleep warm; the worker's wages paid the same day, before he goes hungry.

The gleaning laws leave the edges of the harvest for the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow. Through it all, God reveals himself as the defender of the defenseless, who hears the cry of the oppressed and commands his redeemed people to reflect his mercy. The God who remembered Israel in their slavery calls them to remember the vulnerable in their midst.

sections.title: Divorce Regulated, Not Commended
sections.commentary:
The chapter opens with a law concerning divorce and remarriage. If a man divorces his wife and she marries another, who then divorces her or dies, the first husband may not take her back again, for that would be “an abomination before the LORD” (v. 4). The precise legal point is debated, but the broader significance is clear from Jesus' own interpretation.

When the Pharisees cited this passage to justify easy divorce, Jesus corrected them: “Because of your hardness of heart Moses allowed you to divorce your wives, but from the beginning it was not so” (Matt 19:8). Sproul stressed this crucial distinction: the law did not command or commend divorce but regulated a practice that arose from human sinfulness, limiting its damage and protecting the woman. The certificate of divorce, far from licensing casual abandonment, gave the woman legal standing and protection, preventing her from being cast off without recourse and treated as a mere possession to be discarded and reclaimed at whim.

Calvin observed that God in his mercy often regulates and restrains the sins he does not approve, hedging human hardness with protections for the vulnerable. The law here is a concession to the hardness of the human heart, not a statement of God's ideal, which was always the lifelong union of one man and one woman (Gen 2:24). Ferguson notes the tender concern beneath the legal language: the protection of the woman, who in the ancient world was the more vulnerable party in divorce. For the believer, this passage teaches both the sanctity of marriage in God's original design and the reality of God's merciful accommodation to human weakness — and it points to Christ, who came to heal hard hearts and to restore marriage to its created glory as a picture of his own unbreakable covenant love for his bride.

sections.title: Joy in Marriage and the Mercy of the Pledge
sections.commentary:
A delightful law follows: a newly married man is exempted from military service and public duty for one full year, “to be happy with his wife whom he has taken” (v. 5). God cares about the joy of a new marriage and protects the precious first year of a couple's life together from the demands of war and work. Begg notes the tenderness of this — God is not indifferent to human happiness but actively provides for the flourishing of marriage and the deepening of love in its first year. The God who gives marriage delights in its joy.

Then come laws protecting the poor in the matter of pledges. A creditor may not take a millstone (or even its upper stone) as security for a loan, “for that would be taking a life in pledge” (v. 6) — the millstone was essential for grinding grain into daily bread, so to seize it would be to take away a family's means of survival. And if a poor man's cloak is taken in pledge, it must be returned by sunset, for it is his only covering at night: “in what else shall he sleep?” (v. 13). When the poor man sleeps warm in his cloak, “he will bless you, and it shall be righteousness for you before the LORD your God.”

Sproul stressed how these laws reveal a God who sees and cares for the poor in the most practical ways — his daily bread, his nightly warmth. The creditor's rights are real, but they may never be exercised at the cost of a poor man's survival or dignity. Calvin notes that God here teaches his people a compassion that looks past legal rights to human need. The principle is unforgettable: God's people must never use their legal advantages to crush the vulnerable, but must temper every right with mercy. The God who clothes the lilies and feeds the sparrows watches over the poor man's cloak, and his people are to share his tender care.

sections.title: The Worker's Wages and Individual Responsibility
sections.commentary:
God's care for the worker is striking: “You shall not oppress a hired worker who is poor and needy… You shall give him his wages on the same day, before the sun sets, for he is poor and counts on it, lest he cry against you to the LORD, and you be guilty of sin” (vv. 14–15). The day-laborer lived hand to mouth; to withhold his wages even overnight could mean his family went hungry. So God commands payment the same day. And he warns that the worker's cry reaches his ears — “lest he cry against you to the LORD.” The God of heaven hears the cry of the underpaid laborer.

James echoes this very law in the New Testament: “the wages of the laborers… which you kept back by fraud, are crying out against you, and the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of hosts” (James 5:4). Keller stressed that the prompt, fair payment of workers is a matter of justice that God takes with utmost seriousness; the exploitation of labor is a sin that cries to heaven. The believer is called to deal justly and promptly with all who work for us, never using their dependence to delay or defraud them of what they are owed.

Verse 16 establishes the principle of individual responsibility in justice: “Fathers shall not be put to death because of their children, nor shall children be put to death because of their fathers. Each one shall be put to death for his own sin.” Justice is personal; one may not be punished for another's crime. Sproul noted that this guards against the corruption of collective punishment. And the chapter grounds all this compassion in the great refrain: “you shall remember that you were a slave in Egypt and the LORD your God redeemed you” (v. 18). Mercy flows from memory; because Israel was once oppressed and was redeemed, they must not oppress others. Gratitude for grace is the engine of justice and compassion.

sections.title: Gleaning: Leaving Margin for the Poor
sections.commentary:
The chapter closes with the beautiful gleaning laws. When Israel harvests the field, the forgotten sheaf is not to be retrieved; when they beat their olive trees or gather their grapes, they are not to go over the boughs or vines again. What is left is for “the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow” (vv. 19–21). The harvesters are to leave margin — deliberate inefficiency — so that the poor may gather what remains and feed themselves with dignity.

This is a profound model of structured generosity. Keller, who wrote much on this theme, observed that the gleaning laws provided for the poor not through handouts that demean but through opportunity that dignifies — the poor gleaned with their own hands, working for their bread. The landowner left margin in his harvest as an act of worship and justice, building care for the vulnerable into the very economy of the land. The book of Ruth shows these laws in beautiful action, as Ruth the Moabite widow gleans in the field of Boaz, who deliberately leaves extra for her (Ruth 2) — and from that gleaning came the line of David, and ultimately of Christ.

Again the chapter grounds the command in redemption: “You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt; therefore I command you to do this” (v. 22). The whole chapter pulses with this logic of grace: because you were redeemed, be merciful; because God remembered you in your bondage, remember the vulnerable in their need. Sproul stressed that the memory of one's own deliverance is the great motive for generosity. For the believer, this is the gospel pattern: having been shown infinite mercy in Christ, redeemed from a slavery far deeper than Egypt's, we are to leave generous margin in our lives for the poor, reflecting the boundless grace we have received. The God who provides for the gleaner is the God who became poor that we might become rich.

24.theology:
Compassion grounded in redemption. The refrain — “you shall remember that you were a slave in Egypt and the LORD your God redeemed you” (24:18, 22) — grounds every law of mercy in gratitude for grace received. Because God remembered Israel in bondage, they must remember the vulnerable. Having been shown infinite mercy in Christ, we leave generous margin for the poor, reflecting the grace we received.

God defends the defenseless. The poor man's cloak (24:13), the worker's wages (24:15), the gleaner's portion (24:19–21) — God watches over the survival and dignity of the vulnerable and hears their cry (cf. James 5:4). His people may never use legal rights to crush the weak but must temper every right with mercy.

Marriage and merciful accommodation. The divorce regulation (24:1–4) did not command or commend divorce but limited and protected against the hardness of the human heart (Matt 19:8); God's design was always the lifelong union of Genesis 2:24. The exemption for the newlywed (24:5) shows God's delight in the joy of marriage — pointing to Christ, who heals hard hearts and restores marriage as a picture of his unbreakable covenant love.
24.examples:
Then: Israel regulated divorce to protect the vulnerable, guarded the joy of new marriage, refused to take a poor man's livelihood or nightly covering in pledge, paid the worker his wages the same day, and left the gleanings of the harvest for the widow, orphan, and sojourner — all because they remembered they were once slaves whom God redeemed.

Now: Redeemed from a slavery deeper than Egypt's, we reflect the boundless mercy we have received by dealing justly and generously with the poor, the worker, and the vulnerable, never using our advantages to crush the weak. We honor marriage as God designed it and look to Christ, who heals hard hearts, hears the cry of the oppressed, and became poor that we might become rich — and whose grace is the engine of all our compassion.

25.title: Levirate Marriage and Honest Weights: Justice in the Details
25.text: <sup>15</sup>A full and fair weight you shall have, a full and fair measure you shall have, that your days may be long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you. <sup>16</sup>For all who do such things, all who act dishonestly, are an abomination to the LORD your God.
25.overview:
Chapter 25 brings the body of covenant law toward its close with a cluster of laws on justice, dignity, family preservation, and honesty in commerce. The unifying concern is righteousness in the practical details of life — that punishment be proportionate and not degrading, that the worker (even the ox) not be muzzled, that family lines be preserved, that commerce be honest, and that Amalek's wickedness be remembered.

The law of limited beating (vv. 1–3) ensures that even a guilty person retains his dignity — “lest… your brother be degraded in your sight.” Justice is to be measured, never cruel or humiliating. The brief command not to muzzle the ox as it treads grain (v. 4) reflects God's care even for working animals — and Paul applies it to the support of gospel workers (1 Cor 9:9; 1 Tim 5:18).

The law of levirate marriage (vv. 5–10) provides for the preservation of a deceased brother's name and line through his widow — a provision beautifully fulfilled in the story of Ruth and Boaz, in the very line of Christ.

The chapter's great ethical heart is the demand for honest weights and measures (vv. 13–16): “A full and fair weight you shall have… For all who act dishonestly are an abomination to the LORD.” God cares passionately about integrity in the marketplace. And the closing command to blot out Amalek (vv. 17–19) reminds us that God remembers both faithfulness and wickedness, and that he will finally deal with all his enemies.

sections.title: Proportionate Justice and the Dignity of Persons
sections.commentary:
The chapter opens with a remarkable law about judicial punishment. When a guilty man is sentenced to be beaten, the number of strokes must be proportionate to the offense and is capped at forty, “lest, if one should go on to beat him with more stripes than these, then your brother be degraded in your sight” (v. 3). Even the guilty, even the one justly punished, retains his dignity as a fellow human being — “your brother.” Punishment may be just, but it must never be cruel or degrading.

Sproul observed the profound humanity of this law: the criminal does not cease to be a person made in God's image, and justice must never descend into the dehumanizing brutality common in the ancient world. The Jews so revered this limit that they administered only thirty-nine stripes to ensure they never exceeded forty — the very “forty lashes less one” that Paul received five times (2 Cor 11:24). Calvin notes that God's justice is always measured, fitting the punishment to the crime and guarding the dignity of even the condemned.

The brief but weighty command of verse 4 follows: “You shall not muzzle an ox when it is treading out the grain.” The working ox must be allowed to eat as it labors. This reveals God's tender care even for animals (Prov 12:10), but Paul seizes on it for a greater principle: “Is it for oxen that God is concerned? … It was written for our sake” — namely, that those who labor in the gospel deserve their support (1 Cor 9:9–10; 1 Tim 5:18). Ferguson notes the consistent thread: God cares for the worker, whether ox or apostle, and his people must not deprive the laborer of his due. The dignity of persons and the just treatment of all who labor flow from the character of a God who is both perfectly just and tenderly compassionate.

sections.title: Levirate Marriage: Preserving a Brother's Name
sections.commentary:
The law of levirate marriage (from the Latin levir, “brother-in-law”) provides for a widow whose husband has died without a son. His brother is to marry her, and their firstborn son “shall succeed to the name of his dead brother, that his name may not be blotted out of Israel” (v. 6). This preserved the deceased man's name, line, and inheritance — a matter of great importance in a culture where one's name and posterity carried deep significance and where the widow's security depended on it.

The provision protected the widow, who would otherwise be left without support or standing, and honored the memory and inheritance of the dead. The law also addressed the brother who refused this duty: the widow could publicly shame him by removing his sandal and spitting in his face, marking him as “the house of him who had his sandal pulled off” (vv. 7–10) — a public reproach for failing his familial responsibility.

This law shines most beautifully in the book of Ruth, where Boaz acts as a “kinsman-redeemer” to Ruth the Moabite widow, marrying her to preserve the name of her dead husband and the line of Elimelech (Ruth 4). And from that union came Obed, the father of Jesse, the father of David — and ultimately, the line led to Jesus Christ himself (Matt 1:5). Sproul and others have delighted to trace how this provision for preserving a name in Israel became, in God's providence, a strand in the genealogy of the Redeemer. Ferguson notes that the kinsman-redeemer points to Christ, our great Redeemer, who takes us as his bride, gives us his name, and secures our inheritance forever. The God who would not let a poor man's name be blotted out of Israel is the God who has written our names in the Lamb's book of life.

sections.title: Honest Weights: Integrity in the Marketplace
sections.commentary:
After a brief law guarding modesty and proportionate justice in a physical altercation (vv. 11–12), the chapter reaches its great ethical heart: the demand for honest weights and measures. “You shall not have in your bag two kinds of weights, a large and a small. You shall not have in your house two kinds of measures, a large and a small. A full and fair weight you shall have, a full and fair measure you shall have” (vv. 13–15). The dishonest merchant kept two sets of weights — a heavy one for buying and a light one for selling — to cheat his customers. God forbids it utterly.

The verdict is severe: “all who act dishonestly are an abomination to the LORD your God” (v. 16). The same word used for idolatry and the grossest sins is applied to the cheating businessman. Sproul stressed that God cares passionately about integrity in the marketplace; the fudged scale, the rigged measure, the deceptive practice are not minor matters but abominations in his sight. Proverbs repeats this again and again: “A false balance is an abomination to the LORD, but a just weight is his delight” (Prov 11:1). Calvin observed that commercial dishonesty is a form of theft that wears the mask of legitimate business, and that God sees through every clever deception.

This is a searching word for every believer who works, buys, and sells. Keller noted that the Bible's concern for justice extends fully into the world of commerce; the Christian businessperson is called to scrupulous honesty, fair dealing, and transparency, refusing every form of deception that gains at another's expense. The promise attached — “that your days may be long in the land” — links integrity to blessing and flourishing. The God who is himself perfectly true and faithful calls his people to reflect his character in the most ordinary transactions. A full and fair weight is not a small thing; it is the worship of an honest God expressed in the marketplace.

sections.title: Remember Amalek: God Will Deal with His Enemies
sections.commentary:
The chapter closes with a sobering command: “Remember what Amalek did to you on the way as you came out of Egypt, how he attacked you on the way when you were faint and weary, and cut off your tail, those who were lagging behind you, and he did not fear God” (vv. 17–18). Amalek had attacked Israel cowardly and cruelly, preying on the weak and exhausted stragglers at the rear. God commands that when Israel has rest in the land, they must “blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven. You shall not forget” (v. 19).

Two things stand out. First, the particular wickedness of Amalek: they attacked the faint and weary, the vulnerable stragglers, “and he did not fear God.” This cruelty toward the weak, this contempt for the helpless, this absence of the fear of God, marked Amalek as an enemy under divine judgment. Sproul noted that God takes special note of cruelty toward the vulnerable and the defenseless; such wickedness does not escape his memory or his justice. The God who cares for the gleaner and the widow remembers those who prey upon the weak.

Second, the command reveals that God remembers — both faithfulness and wickedness. “You shall not forget” is matched by God's own remembering. The judgment on Amalek would unfold across Israel's history (1 Sam 15), and it stands as a witness that God will finally deal with all his enemies and all the unrepentant wickedness of the world. Ferguson notes that this points to the final judgment, when every evil that has preyed on the weak and defied God will be fully and justly recompensed. For the believer, this is both warning and comfort: God does not forget the wrongs done to his people, and he will set all things right. The same God who is an abomination to the dishonest and a judge of the cruel is the refuge of the faint and weary, who will one day blot out all evil and wipe away every tear.

25.theology:
Integrity in the marketplace. “A full and fair weight you shall have… all who act dishonestly are an abomination to the LORD” (25:13–16). God cares passionately about honesty in commerce; the rigged scale is as much an abomination as idolatry (cf. Prov 11:1). The believer is called to scrupulous honesty in every transaction, reflecting the character of the God who is perfectly true.

The dignity of persons and the worker. Even the guilty are not to be degraded (25:3), and the ox is not muzzled as it works (25:4) — which Paul applies to the support of gospel laborers (1 Cor 9:9; 1 Tim 5:18). God's justice is measured, never cruel, and his care extends to all who labor.

The kinsman-redeemer. Levirate marriage preserved a dead brother's name and protected his widow (25:5–10), beautifully fulfilled in Ruth and Boaz — in the very line of Christ. The kinsman-redeemer points to Jesus, our great Redeemer, who takes us as his bride, gives us his name, and secures our inheritance forever, having written our names in the Lamb's book of life.
25.examples:
Then: Israel administered measured, dignity-preserving justice, cared even for the working ox, preserved a dead brother's name through levirate marriage, kept honest weights in the marketplace as an abomination-free people, and remembered that God would deal with cruel Amalek who preyed on the weak.

Now: We pursue scrupulous honesty in all our dealings, knowing the rigged scale is an abomination to the God of truth; we honor and support those who labor for us and for the gospel; we rejoice in Christ, our kinsman-Redeemer, who gave us his name and secured our inheritance; and we trust the God who remembers every wrong done to the weak and will finally blot out all evil, being himself the refuge of the faint and weary who will one day wipe away every tear.

26.title: Firstfruits and Covenant Affirmation: You Are His Treasured Possession
26.text: <sup>5</sup>‘A wandering Aramean was my father. And he went down into Egypt... <sup>9</sup>And he brought us into this place and gave us this land...’ <sup>18</sup>And the LORD has declared today that you are a people for his treasured possession, as he has promised you...
26.overview:
Chapter 26 brings the great body of covenant law (chs. 12–26) to a moving climax with two liturgies — the offering of firstfruits and the presentation of the third-year tithe — and a solemn affirmation of the covenant bond between God and his people. After all the commandments, the chapter returns to worship, gratitude, and the mutual belonging that lies at the heart of the covenant.

The firstfruits liturgy (vv. 1–11) is one of the most beautiful acts of worship in the Old Testament. As the Israelite brings the first of his harvest to the LORD, he recites the story of redemption: “A wandering Aramean was my father… the LORD brought us out of Egypt… and gave us this land.” Worship is rooted in the rehearsal of God's saving acts; the gift in the hand is accompanied by the gospel on the lips.

The tithe liturgy (vv. 12–15) confirms the worshiper's faithful care for the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow — generosity to the vulnerable as an integral part of covenant obedience.

The chapter closes with the great covenant affirmation (vv. 16–19): “You have declared today that the LORD is your God… And the LORD has declared today that you are a people for his treasured possession.” Here is the heart of the covenant — mutual belonging. God is theirs, and they are his. He has chosen them to be “a people holy to the LORD,” set high above all nations for praise, fame, and honor. The covenant is not merely law but love, the joyful bond between the redeeming God and his redeemed people — fulfilled in Christ, in whom we become God's own treasured possession forever.

sections.title: The Firstfruits Liturgy: Worship Rooted in Redemption
sections.commentary:
When Israel comes into the land and gathers its first harvest, each one is to take some of the firstfruits of the ground, put it in a basket, and bring it to the chosen place — to the priest at the altar. The firstfruits, the very first and best of the harvest, are offered to God before anything else, as an acknowledgment that the whole harvest, and indeed the whole land, comes from his hand.

Sproul observed the deep theology of firstfruits: by giving God the first and best, the worshiper confesses that everything belongs to God and comes from him. The firstfruits offering is an act of faith — trusting that the God who gave the first will give the rest — and an act of gratitude, returning to God a portion of what he has so generously provided. Calvin notes that the order matters: God receives the first, not the leftovers, for he is worthy of our best.

The setting is significant. The Israelite does not bring the offering in silence but accompanies it with a recited declaration, a liturgy of remembrance. This is worship in which gift and word, action and confession, go together. Begg notes the beauty of structured, corporate worship that rehearses the story of redemption; the firstfruits ceremony ensured that the act of giving was always wrapped in the remembrance of God's saving acts. For the believer, the principle of firstfruits abides: we give God our first and best — of our time, our resources, our energy — as an act of worship and faith, trusting the God who has given us all things in Christ. And as we give, we too rehearse the story of our redemption, for true giving flows from a grateful heart that remembers what God has done.

sections.title: ‘A Wandering Aramean Was My Father’: The Gospel on the Lips
sections.commentary:
Here is the heart of the firstfruits liturgy, one of the great confessions of faith in the Old Testament. As he presents his offering, the Israelite recites the story of redemption: “A wandering Aramean was my father. And he went down into Egypt and sojourned there, few in number, and there he became a nation, great, mighty, and populous. And the Egyptians treated us harshly and humiliated us… Then we cried to the LORD… and the LORD heard our voice… and brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand… And he brought us into this place and gave us this land” (vv. 5–9).

This is gospel preaching in miniature — the whole story of grace condensed into a worshiper's confession: from the precarious wandering of the patriarch, to the bondage and crying out in Egypt, to the mighty deliverance, to the gift of the land. Notice the movement from “my father” to “us” to “we” — the worshiper personally appropriates the redemption of his people as his own. Sproul stressed that biblical worship is always rooted in the recitation of God's saving acts; we worship not in a vacuum but in response to what God has done in history. Ferguson notes the beauty of a faith that is confessed, rehearsed, and personalized — the worshiper makes the story of redemption his own testimony.

And the response is joy: “you shall rejoice in all the good that the LORD your God has given to you” (v. 11), with the Levite and the sojourner included in the celebration. Begg observes that grateful remembrance of redemption produces joyful, generous worship. For the Christian, this confession finds its fuller voice in the gospel: we too rehearse our redemption — we were lost and enslaved to sin, we cried out, and God heard us and delivered us by the mighty hand of Christ, bringing us into the inheritance of his kingdom. The gift in our hands and the gospel on our lips belong together. True worship is always the grateful confession of God's saving grace, overflowing in joy and generosity.

sections.title: The Tithe Liturgy: Faithful Care for the Vulnerable
sections.commentary:
The second liturgy concerns the third-year tithe, which (as we saw in chapter 14) was stored locally for the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow. Having distributed it faithfully, the worshiper makes a solemn declaration before God: “I have removed the sacred portion out of my house, and moreover, I have given it to the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow, according to all your commandment… I have not transgressed any of your commandments” (vv. 13). Then he prays: “Look down from your holy habitation, from heaven, and bless your people Israel and the ground that you have given us” (v. 15).

This liturgy reveals that care for the vulnerable was not optional or peripheral but an integral part of covenant faithfulness, to be solemnly affirmed before God. Keller stressed that in the biblical vision, true worship and care for the poor are inseparable; one could not claim to have obeyed God while neglecting the Levite, the immigrant, the orphan, and the widow. The worshiper must be able to declare honestly before God that he has cared for the vulnerable as God commanded.

Calvin notes the seriousness of the declaration — it is made before God himself, who sees whether the care of the poor has truly been rendered. And the prayer that follows links generosity to blessing: having cared for God's vulnerable ones, the worshiper asks God to look down and bless his people and their land. Ferguson observes the consistent pattern of Deuteronomy: worship, obedience, and compassion belong together; the people who rejoice before God in the firstfruits are the same people who provide for the widow and the sojourner. For the believer, this is a searching reminder that our worship is hollow if it does not overflow in care for the vulnerable (James 1:27). The God who blesses from his holy habitation is the God who identifies with the poor and commands his people to reflect his compassion.

sections.title: The Covenant Affirmation: Mutual Belonging
sections.commentary:
The chapter — and the whole body of covenant law — climaxes with a solemn affirmation of the covenant bond, expressed as a mutual declaration. On Israel's side: “You have declared today that the LORD is your God, and that you will walk in his ways… and will obey his voice” (v. 17). And on God's side, magnificently: “And the LORD has declared today that you are a people for his treasured possession, as he has promised you… and that you are a people holy to the LORD your God” (vv. 18–19).

Here is the heart of the covenant — mutual belonging. God is theirs, and they are his. This is the great covenant formula that echoes throughout Scripture: “I will be your God, and you shall be my people.” Sproul cherished this as the essence of all covenant relationship: not merely a contract of obligations but a bond of belonging, a marriage of love between the redeeming God and his redeemed people. The phrase “treasured possession” (segullah) returns from chapter 7 — Israel is God's personal treasure, his private hoard of precious things, set high “above all nations… for praise and for fame and for honor” (v. 19).

Begg observes the wonder of being declared God's treasured possession — not because of any worth in us, but because God has set his love upon us and claimed us as his own. Ferguson notes that this mutual declaration is the beating heart of the covenant: the God who gives himself to his people receives them as his own treasure. For the believer, this finds its fullness in Christ, through whom we become God's own people: “you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession” (1 Pet 2:9). The covenant of love sealed at Sinai and renewed on the plains of Moab is consummated in the new covenant in Christ's blood, in which God declares over every believer, “You are mine,” and we declare in return, “The LORD is my God.” This mutual belonging is the deepest joy and security of the redeemed: we are God's treasured possession forever.

26.theology:
Worship rooted in redemption. The firstfruits liturgy weds gift and word: as the offering is presented, the worshiper recites the story of grace — “A wandering Aramean was my father… the LORD brought us out” (26:5–9). True worship always rehearses God's saving acts and personalizes them; the gift in the hand and the gospel on the lips belong together, overflowing in joy and generosity.

Worship inseparable from compassion. The tithe liturgy requires the worshiper to declare before God that he has cared for the Levite, sojourner, fatherless, and widow (26:12–13). Care for the vulnerable is integral to covenant faithfulness; worship is hollow without it (James 1:27).

Mutual belonging. The covenant climaxes in a double declaration: Israel declares the LORD their God, and the LORD declares them his “treasured possession” (26:17–18). This is the heart of the covenant — not mere contract but a bond of love. Fulfilled in Christ, God declares over every believer, “You are mine” (1 Pet 2:9), and we are his treasured possession forever.
26.examples:
Then: The Israelite brought the firstfruits of his harvest while reciting the story of his redemption, declared before God his faithful care for the vulnerable, and entered with all Israel into the solemn covenant affirmation in which God claimed them as his treasured possession and they claimed him as their God.

Now: We give God our first and best as worship rooted in gratitude, rehearsing our own redemption — lost and enslaved, we cried out, and Christ delivered us by his mighty hand into the inheritance of his kingdom. Our worship overflows in joyful care for the poor and vulnerable. And we rest in the deepest joy of the redeemed: in Christ, God declares over us, “You are mine,” and we answer, “The LORD is my God” — his treasured possession, set apart and beloved forever.

27.title: The Covenant at Shechem and the Curses
27.text: <sup>26</sup>‘Cursed be everyone who does not confirm the words of this law by doing them.’ And all the people shall say, ‘Amen.’
27.overview:
Chapter 27 turns from the giving of the law to its solemn ratification. Moses commands a great covenant ceremony to be held at Shechem, between Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal, once Israel enters the land. The law is to be written on plastered stones, an altar built, and the tribes positioned on the two mountains to proclaim the blessings and the curses of the covenant.

The ceremony makes the covenant vivid and binding. Six tribes stand on Mount Gerizim for the blessing, six on Mount Ebal for the curse, and the Levites proclaim a series of curses upon specific covenant violations — idolatry, dishonoring parents, injustice, sexual sin, violence — to each of which all the people answer, “Amen.” By their “Amen,” the whole nation binds itself to the covenant, agreeing that those who break it justly fall under its curse.

The chapter culminates in the comprehensive curse of verse 26: “Cursed be everyone who does not confirm the words of this law by doing them.” Paul quotes this verse (Gal 3:10) to prove that the law cannot justify, for it demands perfect, comprehensive obedience that no sinner can render — and thus places all under a curse.

Here the law does its great work: it shuts every mouth and drives us to Christ. For the curse pronounced from Mount Ebal, the curse that falls on all who fail to keep the whole law, is the very curse that Christ bore for us, “becoming a curse for us” on the tree (Gal 3:13). The mountain of cursing points to Calvary, where the curse was exhausted and the blessing secured.

sections.title: The Law Written on Stones; an Altar Built
sections.commentary:
Moses commands that when Israel crosses the Jordan, they are to set up large stones, coat them with plaster, and write on them “all the words of this law” (vv. 2–3, 8). They are also to build an altar of uncut stones on Mount Ebal and offer burnt offerings and peace offerings, rejoicing before the LORD (vv. 5–7). The law is to be publicly displayed, permanently inscribed, for all to see and read.

The writing of the law on stones underscores its abiding authority and public character. This is no secret code for an elite but God's covenant terms displayed openly before the whole nation. Calvin notes that God's law is meant to be known, read, and obeyed by all his people; he does not hide his will but proclaims it plainly. The permanence of stone signifies the enduring nature of God's covenant word.

Significantly, the altar is built of uncut stones — “you shall wield no iron tool on them” (v. 5). No human tool, no human improvement, may be applied to the altar of God; it is to be built as God commands, not embellished by human skill. Sproul saw in this the principle that we do not improve on God's appointed means of approach; the altar of atonement is God's provision, not man's invention. And the altar is striking: it stands on Mount Ebal, the mountain of cursing. Right at the place where the curse will be proclaimed, an altar of sacrifice is built, with burnt offerings and peace offerings and rejoicing. Ferguson notes the profound foreshadowing: where the curse falls, there the altar of atonement stands. The only hope of a people under the curse of the law is the altar — the sacrifice that bears the curse. Even here, at the mountain of cursing, the gospel of atonement is present, pointing to the cross where the curse and the sacrifice would meet in the body of Christ.

sections.title: Today You Have Become the People of the LORD
sections.commentary:
Moses and the Levitical priests address all Israel: “Keep silence and hear, O Israel: this day you have become the people of the LORD your God. You shall therefore obey the voice of the LORD your God, keeping his commandments” (vv. 9–10). The covenant ceremony marks a decisive moment — a renewal and reaffirmation of Israel's identity as God's covenant people.

Notice the order, which is the gospel order throughout Scripture: “this day you have become the people of the LORD your God. You shall therefore obey.” Identity precedes obedience; belonging precedes duty. Israel does not obey in order to become God's people; they obey because they already are God's people. Sproul stressed this fundamental pattern of grace: God first claims us as his own, and obedience flows as the grateful response to that prior belonging, never as its cause. The indicative (“you have become”) grounds the imperative (“you shall obey”).

Calvin observes that the call to “keep silence and hear” summons the people to reverent attention before the word of God; the covenant is received in humble listening. Begg notes the tender solemnity of the moment — Israel is being reminded who they are, that their whole life now flows from their identity as the people of the LORD. For the believer, this is the very heart of Christian living: we obey not to earn God's favor but because, in Christ, we have already become the people of God. “You are a chosen race… God's own people” (1 Pet 2:9) — therefore live as such. Ferguson notes that the imperatives of the Christian life always rest on the indicatives of grace; we are summoned to become what God has already declared us to be in Christ. The believer's obedience is the joyful working out of an identity freely given by grace.

sections.title: The Tribes on the Mountains; the Curses Proclaimed
sections.commentary:
Moses arranges the great ceremony: six tribes stand on Mount Gerizim to pronounce the blessing, and six on Mount Ebal for the curse (vv. 12–13). The Levites then proclaim a series of specific curses to all the people, who respond to each with “Amen” — binding themselves corporately to the covenant. The curses target hidden and grievous sins: idolatry, dishonoring parents, moving a neighbor's landmark, misleading the blind, perverting justice for the vulnerable, sexual sins, violence, and bribery to shed innocent blood (vv. 15–25).

Strikingly, many of these are secret sins — the idol “made in secret” (v. 15), the one who “misleads a blind person on the road” (v. 18), the one who “strikes down his neighbor in secret” (v. 24). The curses reach into the hidden places of life, where no human eye sees but God sees all. Sproul observed that the covenant binds not only outward conduct but the secret heart; God's law penetrates to what is done in darkness. There is no escaping the all-seeing eye of God.

The repeated “Amen” from all the people is profoundly significant. By saying “Amen” to each curse, the whole nation publicly agrees that those who commit such sins justly fall under God's curse — they ratify the justice of the covenant sanctions and bind themselves to its terms. Calvin notes that this corporate “Amen” made the covenant binding and the people accountable; they could never claim ignorance or injustice. Ferguson observes that the people, in their “Amen,” pronounce judgment on the very sins they are all too capable of committing — a sobering act of self-condemnation. The ceremony exposes the impossibility of the people's situation: they bind themselves to a law they cannot perfectly keep, agreeing that the curse is just. The mountain of cursing thus prepares the heart for the gospel, for it reveals that all stand under the curse and need a Redeemer who can bear it for them.

sections.title: Cursed Be Everyone Who Does Not Keep the Whole Law
sections.commentary:
The series of curses culminates in a comprehensive, sweeping declaration: “Cursed be everyone who does not confirm the words of this law by doing them. And all the people shall say, ‘Amen'” (v. 26). This final curse gathers up all the rest. It is no longer aimed at this or that specific sin but at any failure to keep the whole law. The standard is total, comprehensive, perfect obedience — and the curse falls on everyone who falls short of it.

Paul seizes on this very verse to make one of the great arguments of the gospel: “For all who rely on works of the law are under a curse; for it is written, ‘Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the Book of the Law, and do them'” (Gal 3:10). The logic is devastating and liberating. The law demands perfect, comprehensive obedience; no sinner can render it; therefore everyone who relies on law-keeping for justification stands under the curse of verse 26. The law, far from being a ladder to heaven, becomes a chain of condemnation, shutting every mouth and proving all guilty before God (Rom 3:19–20).

This is the law doing its great and necessary work: it drives us out of all self-righteousness and into the arms of Christ. For the curse pronounced from Mount Ebal — the curse that falls on all who fail to keep the whole law — is the very curse that Christ bore for us. Paul continues: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us—for it is written, ‘Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree'” (Gal 3:13). Sproul exulted in this exchange: the curse we earned, Christ absorbed; the “Amen” of self-condemnation we pronounced, Christ answered with his own body on the tree. Begg notes the staggering grace: the mountain of cursing points straight to Calvary, where the curse was exhausted and the blessing of Abraham flows to all who believe. The law's last word is curse; the gospel's last word is Christ, who became the curse that we might receive the blessing.

27.theology:
The curse of the law drives us to Christ. “Cursed be everyone who does not confirm the words of this law by doing them” (27:26). Paul quotes this to prove that the law cannot justify, for it demands perfect, comprehensive obedience no sinner can render (Gal 3:10). The law's great work is to shut every mouth and drive us to Christ, “who redeemed us from the curse… by becoming a curse for us” (Gal 3:13) on the tree.

The altar at the mountain of cursing. The altar of atonement is built on Mount Ebal, the mountain of curse (27:5–7), of uncut stones untouched by human tools. Where the curse falls, there the altar of sacrifice stands — a profound foreshadowing of the cross, where the curse and the sacrifice met in the body of Christ.

Identity precedes obedience. “This day you have become the people of the LORD your God. You shall therefore obey” (27:9–10).
