Sproul and many others have delighted to trace this: the law (Moses) brings us to the border and shows us the promise, but it cannot carry us across; only Joshua-Jesus brings us in.

Ferguson draws out the rich typology: the inability of Moses and the success of Joshua dramatize the great truth of the gospel — “the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17). The law cannot save; it can only reveal the inheritance and our inability to reach it. But the One who bears the name of salvation does what the law could never do — he leads his people through the waters of death into the everlasting inheritance. Begg observes the comfort: we are not left to be brought home by the law, which can only condemn, but by Jesus, who has gone before us and brings us in. The God who equipped Joshua by his Spirit to lead Israel into Canaan is the God who has given us his Spirit and his Son to bring us into the rest that remains for the people of God. Where Moses falls silent, Joshua rises; where the law fails, Christ saves.

sections.title: There Has Not Arisen a Prophet Like Moses
sections.commentary:
The book closes with a tribute to Moses' unparalleled greatness: “And there has not arisen a prophet since in Israel like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face, none like him for all the signs and the wonders that the LORD sent him to do… and for all the mighty power and all the great deeds of terror that Moses did in the sight of all Israel” (vv. 10–12). Moses stands alone — the prophet who knew God “face to face,” who performed the signs of the exodus, who mediated the covenant. No one since had equaled him.

This is a fitting epitaph for the greatest figure of the old covenant. Yet the very statement, “there has not arisen a prophet since like Moses,” leaves the reader looking forward. For Moses himself had prophesied: “The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me… it is to him you shall listen” (18:15). The closing words of Deuteronomy, lamenting that no prophet like Moses had yet arisen, create a longing and an expectation that point beyond the old covenant to the Prophet who would come.

And that Prophet did come. The New Testament declares that Jesus is the Prophet greater than Moses (Acts 3:22–23; Heb 3:1–6). Where Moses knew God “face to face” as a servant, Jesus is the eternal Son who is “in the bosom of the Father” (John 1:18) and has made him known. Where Moses' face shone with reflected glory that faded (2 Cor 3:7), Christ is the very radiance of God's glory (Heb 1:3). Where Moses was “faithful in all God's house as a servant,” Christ is “faithful over God's house as a son” (Heb 3:5–6). Sproul stressed the surpassing greatness of Christ over Moses: as glorious as Moses was, he was but a servant pointing to the Son. Ferguson notes the deliberate open-endedness of the ending — Deuteronomy closes with a death and an unfulfilled longing, looking forward to the One who would not only see the land but bring his people in, and who would be the Prophet, Priest, and King that Moses could only foreshadow. The law-giver dies outside the land; the Savior brings us home. And so the book of remembrance and obedience ends, pointing past its greatest servant to the greater Prophet, the true Joshua, our Lord Jesus Christ, who does for us all that Moses could not — and brings us, at last, into the rest of God.

34.theology:
The law cannot bring us in; only the Savior can. Moses, the law-giver and mediator of the old covenant, sees the land but cannot enter it (34:4). The law shows us the inheritance and our inability to reach it, but it cannot carry us across the Jordan. Only Joshua — Yeshua, Jesus — leads the people in (34:9), for “the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17). Where the law fails, Christ saves.

The servant of the LORD. Moses' deepest identity, even in death, was “the servant of the LORD” (34:5), faithful to the end. God himself buried him in a secret grave, guarding against idolatry of the messenger and keeping the focus on the One who sent him. The faithful servant finished his course; God's purposes did not die with him.

The Prophet greater than Moses. “There has not arisen a prophet since in Israel like Moses” (34:10) — yet Moses himself foretold the Prophet to come (18:15). The book ends in longing, pointing to Jesus, the eternal Son, faithful over God's house as a Son (Heb 3:5–6), the radiance of God's glory (Heb 1:3), who is everything Moses foreshadowed and infinitely more.
34.examples:
Then: Moses, the greatest prophet of the old covenant, climbed Mount Nebo, saw the Promised Land he could never enter, and died as the servant of the LORD in Moab, buried by God in a secret grave — while Joshua, full of the Spirit, took up the leadership to bring Israel into the land Moses could not.

Now: We see in the death of Moses the great truth of the gospel: the law brings us to the border and shows us the promise, but it cannot carry us home; only Jesus — the true Joshua, the Prophet greater than Moses — leads his people through the waters of death into the everlasting inheritance. Where the law-giver falls silent, the Savior rises. And so Deuteronomy, the book of remembering and obeying, ends by pointing past its greatest servant to the greater Prophet, our Lord Jesus Christ, who does for us all that Moses could not, and brings us at last into the rest of God.
